Sauv. gen. 233. Lin. 198. Vog. 92. Sag. gen. 178.** <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>: Purulenta, Calculosa, Hemorrhoidalis, &c. **ORDER V. PROFLUVIA.** **GENUS XL. CATARRHUS.** The **CATARRH.** Catarrhus, Sauv. gen. 186. Vog. 98. Sag. gen. 145. Coryza, Lin. 174. Vog. 100. Sag. gen. 196. Rheuma, Sauv. gen. 142. Tussis, Sauv. gen. 142. Lin. 155. Vog. 205. Sag. gen. 245, 255. Junck. 30. Tussis catarrhalis et rheumatica, Hoffm. III. 109. Sp. I. Catarrh from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">Cold</a>. Catarrhus a frigore, Cul. Catarrhus benignus, Sauv. sp. 1. Catarrhus pectoreus, Sauv. sp. 6. Coryza catarrhalis, Sauv. sp. 1. Coryza phlegmatorrhagia, Sauv. sp. 2. Salmuth. Obs. cent. 1, 37. Junck. 28. Morgagni de sed. xiv. 21. Coryza fabricosa, Sauv. sp. 6. Tussis catarrhalis, Sauv. sp. 1. N. Rosen. Diss. apud. Haller, Disput. Pract. tom. ii. Rheuma catarrhale, Sauv. sp. 1. Amphimerina catarrhalis, Sauv. sp. 2. Amphimerina tussiculosa, Sauv. sp. 13. Cephalalgia catarrhalis, Sauv. sp. 10. Sp. II. Sp. II. Catarrh from Contagion. Catarrhus a contagio, Cul. Catarrhus epidemicus, Sauv. sp. 3. Rheuma epidemicum, Sauv. sp. 2. Synocha catarrhalis, Sauv. sp. 5. There are several symptomatic species: as, Catarrhus Rubeculosus; Tussis Variolosa, Verminosa, Calculosa, Phthisica, Hysterica, a dentitione, Gravidarum, Metallicolarum, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a>. The catarrh is an increased excretion of mucus from the mucous membrane of the nose, fauces and bronchiae, attended with pyrexia. Practical writers and nosologists have distinguished the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> by different appellations, according as it happens to affect different parts of the mucous membrane, one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less than the other: but Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a> is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the disease in those different parts is always of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and proceeds from the same cause in the one as in the other. Very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> indeed, those different parts are affected at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and therefore there is little room for the distinction mentioned. The disease has been frequently treated of under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of tussis or cough; and a cough, indeed, always attends the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> form of catarrh, that is, the increased excretion from the bronchiae; but as it is so often also a symptom of many other affections, which are very different from one another, it is improperly used as a generic title. The disease generally begins with some difficulty of breathing through the nose, and with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of some fulness stopping up that passage. This again is often attended with some dull pain and a sense of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in the forehead, as well as a stiffness in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the eyes. These feelings, sometimes at their very first beginning, and always soon after, are attended with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of a thin fluid from the nose, and sometimes from the eyes; and these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> are often found to be somewhat acid, both by their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and by their fretting the parts over which they <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. These symptoms constitute the coryza and gravedo of authors, and are commonly attended with a sense of lassitude over the whole body. Sometimes cold shiverings are felt; at least the body is more sensible than usual to the coldness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and with all this the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> is more frequent than ordinary, especially in the evenings. These symptoms have seldom <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before they are accompanied with some hoarseness, and a sense of roughness and soreness in the trachea, with some difficulty of breathing, expressed by a sense of straitness in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, and with a cough which seems to arise from some irritation felt at the glottis. This cough is generally at first dry and painful, occasioning pains about the chest, and more especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; sometimes, together with these symptoms, pains resembling those of the rheumatism are felt in several parts of the body, particularly about the neck and head. With all these symptoms, the appetite is impaired, some thirst arises, and a feverish lassitude is felt all over the body. These symptoms mark the height and violence of the disease; but commonly it does not continue long. By degrees the cough comes to be attended with a more copious excretion of catarrh mucus; which is at first thin, but gradually becoming thicker, is brought up with less frequent and less laborious coughing. The hoarseness and soreness of the trachea are also relieved or removed; and the febrile symptoms abating, the expectoration becomes again less considerable, and the cough less frequent, till at length they cease altogether. Such is generally the course of this disease, neither tedious nor dangerous; but it is sometimes in both respects otherwise. The body subjected to catarrh seems to be more than usually liable to be affected by cold air; and upon exposure of the body to fresh cold, the disease, which seemed to be yielding, is often brought back with greater violence than before, and is rendered not only more tedious than otherwise it would be, but also more dangerous by the supervening of other diseases. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the cynanche tonsillaris often accompanies the catarrh; and when this is aggravated by a fresh application of cold, the cynanche also becomes more violent and dangerous from the cough which is present at the same time. When a catarrh has been occasioned by a violent cause, when it has been aggravated by improper management, and especially when it has been rendered more violent by fresh and repeated applications of cold, it often passes into a pneumonic inflammation, attended with the utmost danger. Unless, however, such accidents as these happen, a catarrh, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> persons not far advanced in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, is always a slight and safe disease; but in persons of a phthisical disposition, a catarrh may readily produce a haemoptysis, or perhaps form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>, in the lungs; and still more readily in persons who have tubercles already formed in the lungs, an accidental catarrh may occasion the inflammation of these tubercles, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> produce a phthisis pulmonalis. In elderly persons, a catarrh sometimes proves a dangerous disease. Many persons, as they advance in life, and especially after they have arrived at old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, have the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> mucus of the lungs poured out in greater <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, and requiring a frequent expectoration. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, therefore, a catarrh happen to such persons, and increase the influx of fluids to the lungs, with some degree of inflammation, it may produce the peripneumonia notha, or more properly chronic catarrh, a disease continuing often for many years, or at least returning regularly every winter; which in such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> is very often fatal. Causes, &c. The proximate cause of catarrh seems to be an increased influx of fluids to the mucous membrane of the nose, fauces, and bronchiae, along with some degree of inflammation affecting the same. The latter circumstance is confirmed by this, that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of catarrh, the blood drawn from a vein commonly exhibits the same inflammatory crust which appears in the case of phlegmasiae. The remote cause of catarrh is most commonly cold applied to the body. This application of cold producing catarrh is generally evident; and Dr Cullen is of opinion that it would always be so, were men acquainted with and attentive to the circumstances which determine cold to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon the body. The application of cold which occasions a catarrh probably operates by stopping the discharge usually made going off they are renewed by any fresh application of catarrhus cold. **Prognosis.** Considering the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons who are affected with catarrh, of either the one species or the other, and escape from it quickly without any hurt, it may be allowed to be a disease commonly free from danger; but it is not always to be treated as such; for in some persons it is accompanied with pneumonic inflammation. In the phthisically disposed, it often accelerates the coming on of phthisis; and in elderly persons it often proves fatal in the manner we have explained above, viz. by degenerating into its chronic state. But though chronic catarrh be often the termination of that species which arises from cold, we have not, in any case, observed it to arise as a consequence of a catarrh from contagion. This species of catarrh, however, is not unfrequently followed by phthisis; or rather, where a phthisical tendency before existed, the affection has been begun and its progress accelerated from this cause. **Cure.** The cure of catarrh is nearly the same, whether it proceeds from cold or contagion; only in the latter case remedies are commonly more necessary than in the former. In the cases of a moderate disease, it is commonly sufficient to avoid cold, or to abstain from animal food for some days. In some cases, where the febrile symptoms are considerable, it is proper for that length of time to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and, by taking frequently some mild and diluted drink, a little warmed, to promote a very gentle sweat; and after this to take care to return very gradually only to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the free air. When the disease is more violent, not only the antiphlogistic regimen, exactly observed, but various remedies also, become necessary. To take off the phlogistic diathesis which always attends this disease, blood-letting, more or less, according as the symptoms shall require, is the proper remedy. After blood-letting, for restoring the determination of the fluids to the surface of the body, and at the same time for expediting the secretion of mucus in the lungs, which may take off the inflammation of its membrane, vomiting is the most effectual means. For the last-mentioned purpose, it has been supposed that squills, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-ammoniac, the volatile alkali, and some other medicines, might be useful; but their efficacy has never been found considerable: and if squills have ever been very useful, it seems to have been rather by their emetic than by their expectorant powers. When the inflammatory affections of the lungs seem to be considerable, it is proper, besides blood-letting, to apply blisters to the back or sides. As a cough is often the most troublesome circumstance of this disease, so demulcents may be employed to alleviate it. But after the inflammatory symptoms are much abated, if the cough still remains, opiates afford the most effectual means of relieving it; and, in the circumstances <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now mentioned, they may be very safely employed. Very considerable advantage is often derived from employing opiates in such a manner as to act more immediately on the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-pipe. For this purpose, opium may often be advantageously conjoined with demulcents, melting slowly in the mouth. And perhaps no form is more convenient, or answers the purpose better, than the *trochisci glycyrrhizae cum opio* of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Pharmacopoeia.

HYPOCHONDRIAC AFFECTION

Pages 425-425

Hypochondriasis, Sauv. gen. 220. Lin. 76. Vog. 218. Sag. 332. Morbus hypochondriacus, Boerh. 1998. Malum hypochondriacum, Hoffm. III. 65. Junck. 36. Although some of the nosological writers, particularly Sauvages, have considered this genus as consisting of different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a> is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that there is only one idiopathic species, the hypochondriasis melancholica. He considers not only the hypochondriasis hysterica, phthisica, and asthmatica, but also the biliosa, sanguinea, and pituitosa, as being only symptomatic; but he views the true melancholic hypochondriasis as being a proper idiopathic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, perfectly distinct from hysteria, with which it has often been confounded. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a>. The symptoms of hypochondriasis are, stretching, pressing, gripping, and tormenting pains under the ribs, and chiefly in the left side; which sometimes are exasperated, and become pungent, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lancinating. Frequently there is an inflation of the left hypochondrium, which sometimes becomes <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> was taken for a symptom of an enlarged spleen. When these symptoms take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hypochondrium, they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> attended with colic pains, uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> heats, especially in the head, with a transient redness of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and very frequently an edematous swelling of the feet succeeds. To these are superadded almost all the affections of the stomach occurring in dyspepsia, besides a variety of other symptoms, such as palpitations, sleepless nights, and the like. But besides these, there occurs also a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of danger, which may be considered as one of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> characteristic symptoms of the disease. Causes, &c. The general causes of the hypochondriac affection are said to be a plethora, and preternatural thickness of the blood; suppressions of customary evacuations; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and full diet, together with a sparing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of drink; an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> disposition; indolence; atony of the intestines; violent passions of the mind, &c. Prognosis. The hypochondriac affection, when left to itself, is more troublesome than dangerous; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> improperly treated, it may bring on various diseases of a more fatal tendency, such as the melancholy, bloody urine and nephritis, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, vertigo, palsy, apoplexy, &c. Cure. This is to be attempted by such medicines as counteract occasional causes, and obviate urgent symptoms, which may be all comprehended under bleeding, gentle evacuants, chalybeates, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CINCHONA">cinchona</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, especially riding on horseback, which in this disease is greatly preferable to any other. When the circumstances of the patient can afford it, a voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, or some of the warmer countries in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be of great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. GENUS XLVII. CHLOROSIS.

IMMEDIATE

Pages 230-230
or INTERMEDIATE, something that stands betwixt and connects two or more terms considered as extremes; in which sense it stands opposed to immediate.

JAMES HENTHORN

Pages 379-380

Secretary. After this report, we cannot help thinking that the British legislature would be fully warranted for passing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> prohibiting the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a> of smallpox under very severe penalties, and ordering all those who may be subjected to smallpox by accidental contagion to be confined to lazaretos, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least to their own houses, under a proper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of infection, till their complete <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. By such an act, there is good ground to believe, that the loathsome and dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> of smallpox would in a few years be exterminated in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. But although <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> has thus furnished mankind with an easy <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of preserving their offspring from the danger of smallpox, by the inoculation of the cow-pox at an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, yet not a few deaths from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> small-pox have occurred in Britain even during the course of the present year. When the preventive has not been duly employed, after the contagion of variola is introduced into the body, nothing yet known <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> prevent the disease from running its course, either under the mild or confluent form; and the endeavours of the medical practitioner are altogether to be employed in rendering that course as favourable as possible by mitigating symptoms. In the mild or distinct smallpox, the strictest antiphlogistic regimen is to be enjoined. Gentle refrigerant cathartics are often useful, and mild diluents should be copiously employed. Under these remedies the disease will generally run its course without much inconvenience. But it will sometimes be necessary to employ remedies for obviating particular urgent symptoms, such as gargarisms or blisters for affections of the throat. In the malignant smallpox, besides the same refrigerant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of cure which is best accommodated to the mild, as the secondary fever shows evident marks of a putrid tendency, it is necessary to employ those remedies which are accommodated to typhus, and accordingly recourse is not only had to opiates and cardiae, but to wine, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CINCHONA">cinchona</a>, and the mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. GENUS XXIX. VARICELLA.

President. Royal College of Physicians, 10th of April, 1807. JA. HERVEY, Register.

MATRIX

Pages 25-25

in Anatomy, the womb, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> of any kind, wherein the fetus is conceived and nourished till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its delivery. See Anatomy, No 168. Matrix is also applied to places proper for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of vegetables, minerals, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is the matrix wherein seeds sprout; and marcasites are by many considered as the matrices of metals. The matrix of ores is the earthy and stony substance in which these metallic matters are enveloped; these are various, as lime and heavy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>, flours, &c.

MATRON

Pages 25-25

an elderly married woman. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">Jury</a> of Matrons. When a widow feigns herself with child in order to exclude the next heir, and a supposititious birth is suspected to be intended, then, upon the writ de ventre inspiciendo, a jury of women is to be impannelled to try the question whether the woman is with child <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not. So, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a woman is convicted of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offence, and, being condemned to suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, pleads in stay of execution, that she is pregnant, a jury of matrons is impannelled to inquire into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the allegation; and, if they find it true, the convict is respited till after her delivery.

MATRONA

Pages 25-25

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river separating Gallia Celtica from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a> (Cæsar). Now the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>; which, rising in Champagne near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANGRES">Langres</a>, runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west, and then west, and passing by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a> falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> at Charenton, two leagues to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>.

MATRONALIA

Pages 25-25

a Roman festival instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, and celebrated on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>. It was kept by matrons in particular, and bachelors were entirely excluded from any share in the solemnity. The men during this feast sent presents to the women, for which a return was made by them at the Saturnalia: And the women gave the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> to their servants now which the men gave to theirs at the feast of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, serving them at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and treating them as superiors.

MATROSSES

Pages 25-25

are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the train of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, who are next to the gunners, and assist them in loading, firing, and spunging the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns. They carry firelocks, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> along with the store wagons, both as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and to give their assistance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a waggon should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>.

MATSYS

Pages 25-26

Quintin, painter of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and portraits, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1465, and for several years followed the trade of a blacksmith <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARRIER">farrier</a>, at least till he was in his 25th year. Authors vary in their accounts of the cause of his quitting his first occupation, and attaching himself to the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. Some affirm, that the first unfolding of his genius was occasioned by the sight of a print which accidentally was shown to him by a friend who came to pay him a visit while he was in a declining state of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> from the labour of his former employment, and that by his copying the print with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of success, he was animated with a desire to learn the art of painting. Others say, he fell in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with a young woman of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a painter, and they allege that love alone wrought the miracle, as he could have no prospect of obtaining her except by a distinguished merit in the profession of painting: for which reason he applied himself with incessant labour to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and practise the art, till he became so eminent as to be entitled to demand her in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and he succeeded. Whatever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> may be in either of these accounts, it is certain that he appeared to have an uncommon genius; his manner was singular, not resembling the manner of any other <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; and his pictures were strongly coloured and carefully finished, but yet they are somewhat dry and hard. By many competent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> judges it was believed, when they observed the strength of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> in some of his compositions, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had studied in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to acquire some knowledge of the antiques and the great masters of the Roman school, he would have proved one of the most eminent painters of the Low Countries. But he only imitated ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and seemed more inclined, or at least more qualified, to imitate the defects than the beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Some historical compositions of this master deserve commendation; particularly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">Descent</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a>, which is in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> at Antwerp; and it is justly admired for the spirit, skill, and delicacy of the whole. But the most remarkable and best known <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Matsys, is that of the Two Misers in the gallery at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>. He died in 1529.

MATTER

Pages 26-26

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is a word of the same import with body, and denotes that which is tangible, visible, and extended; but among philosophers it signifies that substance of which all bodies are composed; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with the word ELEMENT. It is only by the senses that we have any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> world; but the immediate objects of sense, philosophers have in general agreed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> qualities, which they conceive as inhering in something which is called their subject <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> substratum. It is this substratum of sensible qualities which, in the language of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, is denominated matter; so that matter is not that which we immediately see or handle, but the concealed subject or support of visible and tangible qualities. What the moderns term qualities, was by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and his followers called form; but so far as the two doctrines are intelligible, there appears to be no essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them. From the moderns we learn, that body consists of matter and qualities; and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> taught the same thing, when they said that body is composed of matter and form. How philosophers were led to analyze body into matter and form, or, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> language, into matter and qualities; what kind of existence they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to each; and whether matter must be conceived as self-existent or created—are questions which shall be considered afterwards (See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>). It is sufficient here to have defined the term.

MATTHEW

Pages 26-27
or Gospel of St Matthew, a canonical book of the New Testament. St Matthew wrote his gospel in Judea, at the request of those he had converted; and it is thought he began in the year 41, eight years after Christ's resurrection. It was written, according to the testimony of all the ancients, in the Hebrew or Syrian language; but the Greek version, which now passes for the original, is as old as the apostolical times. St Matthew the Evangelist's Day, a festival of the Christian church, observed on September 21st. St Matthew, the son of Alpheus, was also called Levi. He was of a Jewish origin, as both his names discover, and probably Galilean. Before his call to the apostolate, he was a publican or toll-gatherer to the Romans; an office of bad repute among the Jews, on account of the covetousness and exaction of matters, those who managed it; St Matthew's office particularly consisting in gathering the customs of all merchandise that came by the sea of Galilee, and the tribute that passengers were to pay who went by water. And here it was that Matthew sat at the receipt of customs, when our Saviour called him to be a disciple. It is probable, that, living at Capernaum, the place of Christ's usual residence, he might have some knowledge of him before he was called. Matthew immediately expressed his satisfaction in being called to this high dignity, by entertaining our Saviour and his disciples at a great dinner at his own house, whither he invited all his friends, especially those of his own profession, hoping, probably, that they might be influenced by the company and conversation of Christ. St Matthew continued with the rest of the apostles till after our Lord's ascension. For the first eight years afterwards, he preached in Judea. Then he betook himself to propagating the gospel among the Gentiles, and chose Ethiopia as the scene of his apostolical ministry; where it is said he suffered martyrdom, but by what kind of death is altogether uncertain. It is pretended, but without any foundation, that Hyrtacus, king of Ethiopia, desiring to marry Iphigenia, the daughter of his brother and predecessor Ægillus, and the apostle having represented to him that he could not lawfully do it, the enraged prince ordered his head immediately to be cut off. Baronius tells us, the body of St Matthew was transported from Ethiopia to Bithynia, and from thence was carried to Salernum in the kingdom of Naples in the year 954, where it was found in 1082, and where Duke Robert built a church bearing his name. St Matthew, a town of Spain, in the kingdom of Arragon, seated in a pleasant plain, and in a very fertile country watered with many springs. W. Long. o. 15. N. Lat. 40. 22. Matthew of Paris. See PARIS. Matthew of Westminster, a Benedictine monk and accomplished scholar, who wrote a history from the beginning of the world to the end of the reign of Edward I, under the title of Flores Historiarum; which was afterwards continued by other hands. He died in 1382. St Matthias, an apostle, was chosen instead of Judas. He preached in Judea and part of Ethiopia, and suffered martyrdom. See the Acts of the Apostles, chap. i. There was a gospel published under Matthias's name, but rejected as spurious; as likewise some traditions, which met with the same fate. St Matthias's Day, a festival of the Christian church, observed on the 24th of February. St Matthias was an apostle of Jesus Christ, but not of the number of the twelve chosen by Christ himself. He obtained this high honour upon a vacancy made in the college of the apostles by the treason and death of Judas Iscariot. The choice fell on Matthias by lot; his competitor being Joseph called Barsabas, and surmamed Justus. Matthias was qualified for the apostleship, by having been a constant attendant upon our Saviour all the time of his ministry. He was, probably, one of the 70 disciples. After our Lord's resurrection, he preached the gospel first in Judea. Afterwards Afterwards it is probable he travelled eastward, his residence being principally near the irruption of the river Apsarus and the haven Hyssus. The barbarous people treated him with great rudeness and inhumanity; and, after many labours and sufferings in converting great numbers to Christianity, he obtained the crown of martyrdom; but by what kind of death, is uncertain.—They pretend to show the relics of St Matthias at Rome; and the famous abbey of St Matthias near Treves boasts of the same advantage; but doubtless both without any foundation. There was a gospel ascribed to St Matthias; but it was universally rejected as spurious. MATTIACÆ AQUÆ, or MATTIACI FONTES, in Ancient Geography, now Wiesbaden, opposite to Mentz, in Wetteravia. E. Long. 8. N. Lat. 50. 6.

MATTIACUM

or Mattium, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Mattiaci, a branch of the Catti in Germany. Now Marpurg in Hesse. E. Long. 8. 40. N. Lat. 50. 40.

MATTINS

Pages 27-27

the first canonical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the daily <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.

MATY

Pages 27-27

MATTHEW, M. D. an eminent physician and polite writer, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in the year 1718. He was the son of a clergyman, and was originally intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of some mortifications his father met with from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, on account of the peculiar sentiments he entertained about the doctrine of the Trinity, turned his thoughts to physic. He took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M. D. at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; and in 1740 came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in England, his father having determined to quit Holland for ever. In order to make himself known, he began in 1749 to publish in French an account of the productions of the English press, printed at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> under the name of the Journal Britannique. This journal, which continues to hold its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> amongst the best of those which have appeared since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Bayle, answered the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> end he intended by it, and introduced him to the acquaintance of some of the most respectable literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he had made his own. It was to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and uninterrupted friendship he owed the places he afterwards possessed. In 1758 he was chosen fellow, and in 1765, on the resignation of Dr Birch, who died a few months after, and had made him his executor, secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. He had been appointed one of the under librarians of the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at its first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> in 1753, and became <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> librarian at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> in 1772. Useful in all these situations, he promised to be eminently so in the last, when he was seized with a languishing disorder, which in 1776 put an end to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> which had been uniformly devoted to the pursuit of science and the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. He was an early and active advocate for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a>; and when there was a doubt entertained that one might have the smallpox this way a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, tried it upon himself unknown to his family. He was a member of the medical club (with the Drs Parsons, Templeman, Maty, Fothergill, Watson and others), which met every Mauberge, fortnight in St Paul's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">Churchyard</a>. He was twice married, viz. the first time to Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Boisragon; and the second to Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Deners. He left a son and three daughters. He had nearly finished the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Chesterfield; which were completed by his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Mr Justamond, and prefixed to that nobleman's Miscellaneous Works, 1777, 2 vols 4to. Maty, Paul Henry, M. A. F. R. S. son of the former, was born in 1745, and was educated at Westminster and Trinity <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and had their travelling fellowship for three years. He was afterwards chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Stormont at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and soon after vacated his next fellowship by marrying one of the three daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Clerk, Esq. and sister of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Clerk (who succeeded to the command on the death of Captain Cook). On his father's death in 1776, he was appointed to the office of one of the under librarians of the British Museum, and was afterwards preferred to a superior department, having the care of the antiquities, for which he was eminently qualified. In 1776 he also succeeded his father in the office of secretary to the Royal Society. On the disputes respecting the reinstatement of Dr Hutton in the department of secretary for foreign correspondence in 1784, Mr Maty took a warm and distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and resigned the office of secretary; after which he undertook to assist gentlemen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ladies in perfecting their knowledge of the Greek, Latin, French, and Italian classics. Mr Maty was a thinking conscientious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and having conceived some doubts about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> he had subscribed in early life, he never could be prevailed upon to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferment, though his connexions were amongst those who could have served him essentially in this point; and soon after his father's death he withdrew himself from ministering in the established church, his reasons for which he published in the 27th volume of the Gent. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, p. 466. His whole life was thenceforwards taken up in literary pursuits. He received 100l. from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, with a copy of that beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the Gramma Marlboroughensis, of which only 100 copies were worked off for presents; and of which Mr Maty wrote the French account, as Mr Bryant did the Latin. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1782 he set on foot a Review of publications, principally foreign, which he carried on, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to himself and satisfaction to the public, for near five years, when he was obliged to discontinue it from ill <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. He had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> laboured under an asthmatic complaint, which at times made great ravages in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and at last put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his life in Jan. 1787, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 42; leaving behind him one son.—Mr Maty was eminently acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> literature, and particularly conversant in critical researches. The purity and probity of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> were unquestionable; and his humanity was as exquisite as it would have been extensive, had it been seconded by his fortune.

MAUBEUGE

Pages 27-28

a fortified town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in Hainault, which formerly contained an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of canonesses, who were noble both by the father and mother's side. In 1678 this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was ceded to France, in whose possession it still remains. In September MAU 1793; the Austrians formed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of this place, but were driven from their position in the following <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. It is seated on the river Sambre, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 2'. N. Lat. 50° 16'.

MAUCAUCO

Pages 28-28

MACACO, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Maki, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order Primates. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MAUNCH

Pages 28-28

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> coat sleeve, borne in many gentlemen's escutcheons.

MAUNDY THURSDAY

Pages 28-28

is the Thursday in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; which was called Maunday, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mandate Thursday, from the command which our Saviour gave his apostles to commemorate him in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, which he this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> instituted; or from the new commandment which he gave them to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> one another, after he had washed their feet as a token of his love to them.

MAUPERTUIS

Pages 28-29
PETER LOUIS MORCEAU DE, a celebrated French academician, was born at St Malo in 1698; and was there privately educated till he arrived at his 16th year, when he was placed under the celebrated professor of philosophy M. le Blond, in the college of La Marche, at Paris. He soon discovered a passion for mathematical studies, and particularly for geometry. He likewise practised instrumental music in his early years with great success, but fixed on no profession till he was 20, when he entered into the army. He first served in the Grey musqueteers; but in the year 1720, his father purchased for him a company of cavalry in the regiment of La Rochequoyon. He remained but five years in the army, during which time he pursued his mathematical studies with great vigour; and it was soon remarked by M. Freret and other academicians, that nothing but geometry could satisfy his active soul and unbounded thirst for knowledge. In the year 1723, he was received into the Royal Academy of Sciences, and read his first performance, which was a memoir upon the construction and form of musical instruments, November 15, 1724. During the first years of his admission, he did not wholly confine his attention to mathematics; he dived into ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy, and discovered great knowledge and dexterity in observations and experiments upon animals. If the custom of travelling into remote climates, like the sages of antiquity, in order to be initiated into the learned mysteries of those times had still subsisted, no one would have conformed to it with greater eagerness than M. de Maupertuis. His first gratification of this passion was to visit the country which had given birth to Newton; and during his residence at London he became as zealous an admirer and follower of that philosopher as any one of his own countrymen. His next excursion was to Basil in Switzerland, where he formed a friendship with the famous John Bernouilli and his family, which continued to his death. At his return to Paris, he applied himself to his favourite studies with greater zeal than ever:—And how well he fulfilled the duties of an academician, may be gathered by running over the memoirs of the academy from the year 1724 to 1736; where it appears that he was neither idle nor occupied by objects of small importance. The most sublime questions in geometry and the relative sciences received from his hands that elegance, clearness, and precision, so remarkable in all his writings. In the year 1736, he was sent by the king of France to the polar circle to measure a degree, in order to ascertain the figure of the earth, accompanied by Messrs Clairault, Camus, Le Monnier, l'Abbe Outhier, and Celsius the celebrated professor of astronomy at Upsal. This distinction rendered him so famous, that at his return he was admitted a member of almost every academy in Europe. In the year 1740 Maupertuis had an invitation from the king of Prussia to go to Berlin; which was too flattering to be refused. His rank among men of letters had not wholly effaced his love for his first profession, namely that of arms. He followed his Prussian majesty into the field, and was a witness of the dispositions and operations that preceded the battle of Molwitz; but was deprived of the glory of being present, when victory declared in favour of his royal patron, by a singular kind of adventure. His horse, during the heat of the action, running away with him, he fell into the hands of the enemy; and was at first but roughly treated by the Austrian soldiers, to whom he could not make himself known for want of language; but being carried prisoner to Vienna, he received such honours from their Imperial Majesties as were never effaced from his memory. From Vienna he returned to Berlin; but as the reform of the academy which the king of Prussia then meditated was not yet mature, he went again to Paris, where his affairs called him, and was chosen in 1742 director of the Academy of Sciences. In 1753 he was received into the French academy; which was the first instance of the same person being a member of both the academies at Paris at the same time. M. de Maupertuis again assumed the soldier at the siege of Fribourg, and was pitched upon by Marshal Cogny and the Count d'Argenson to carry the news to the French king of the surrender of that citadel. He returned to Berlin in the year 1744, when a marriage was negotiated and brought about by the good offices of the queen-mother, between our author and Mademoiselle de Boreck, a lady of great beauty and merit, and nearly related to M. de Boreck, at that time minister of state. This determined him to settle at Berlin, as he was extremely attached to his new spouse, and regarded this alliance as the most fortunate circumstance of his life. In the year 1746, M. de Maupertuis was declared by his Prussian majesty president of the Royal Academy of Sciences at Berlin, and soon after by the same prince was honoured with the order of Merit: However, all these accumulated honours and advantages, so far from lessening his ardour for the sciences, seemed to furnish new allurements to labour and application. Not a day passed but he produced some new project or essay for the advancement of knowledge. Nor did he confine himself to mathematical studies only: metaphysics, chemistry, botany, polite literature, all shared his attention, and contributed to his fame. At the same time, he had, it seems, a strange inquietude of spirit, with a morose temper, which rendered him miserable amidst honours and pleasures.—Such a temperament did not promise a very pacific life, and he was engaged in several quarrels. He had... Maupertuis, a quarrel with Koenig the professor of philosophy at Franeker, and another more terrible with Voltaire. Maupertuis had inserted into the volume of Memoirs of the Academy of Berlin for 1746, a discourse upon the laws of motion; which Koenig was not content with attacking, but attributed to Leibnitz. Maupertuis, stung with the imputation of plagiarism, engaged the academy of Berlin to call upon him for his proof; which Koenig failing to produce, he was struck out of the academy, of which he was a member. Several pamphlets were the consequence of this; and Voltaire, for some reason or other, engaged against Maupertuis. We say, for some reason or other; because Maupertuis and Voltaire were apparently upon the most amicable terms; and the latter respected the former as his master in the mathematics. Voltaire, however, exerted all his wit and satire against him; and on the whole was so much transported beyond what was thought right, that he found it expedient in 1753 to quit the court of Prussia. Our philosopher's constitution had long been considerably impaired by the great fatigues of various kinds in which his active mind had involved him; though from the amazing hardships he had undergone in his northern expedition, most of his future bodily sufferings may be traced. The intense sharpness of the air could only be supported by means of strong liquors, which served to increase his disorder, and bring on a spitting of blood, which began at least 12 years before he died. Yet still his mind seemed to enjoy the greatest vigour; for the best of his writings were produced, and most sublime ideas developed, during the time of his confinement by sickness, when he was unable to occupy his presidial chair at the academy. He took several journeys to St Malo, during the last years of his life, for the recovery of his health: And though he always received benefit by breathing his native air, yet still, upon his return to Berlin, his disorder likewise returned with greater violence.—His last journey into France was undertaken in the year 1757; when he was obliged, soon after his arrival there, to quit his favourite retreat at St Malo, on account of the danger, and confusion which that town was thrown into by the arrival of the English in its neighbourhood. From thence he went to Bordeaux, hoping there to meet with a neutral ship to carry him to Hamburg, in his way back to Berlin; but being disappointed in that hope, he went to Thoulouse, where he remained seven months. He had then thoughts of going to Italy, in hopes a milder climate would restore him to health; but finding himself grow worse, he rather inclined towards Germany, and went to Neufchatel, where for three months he enjoyed the conversation of Lord Marischal, with whom he had formerly been much connected. At length he arrived at Basil, October 16, 1758, where he was received by his friend Bernouilli and his family with the utmost tenderness and affection. He at first found himself much better here than he had been at Neufchatel: but this amendment was of short duration; for as the winter approached, his disorder returned, accompanied by new and more alarming symptoms. He languished here many months during which he was attended by M. de la Condamine; and died in 1759. He wrote in French, 1. The figure of the earth determined. 2. The measure of a degree of the meridian. Maupertuis 3. A discourse on the parallax of the moon. 4. A dis- course on the figure of the stars. 5. The elements of geography. 6. Nautical astronomy. 7. Elements of astronomy. 8. A physical dissertation on a white inhabitant of Africa. 9. An essay on cosmography. 10. Reflections on the origin of languages. 11. An essay on moral philosophy. 12. A letter on the progress of the sciences. 13. An essay on the formation of bodies. 14. An elegium on M. de Montesquieu. 15. Letters, and other works.

MAUR

Pages 29-29

Sr., was a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of St Benedict. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we can believe a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of St Maur ascribed to Faustus his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, he was sent by Benedict on a mission to France. But this life is considered as apocryphal. In rejecting it, however, as well as the circumstances of the mission, we must beware of denying the mission itself. It is certain that it was believed in France as early as the 9th century; and notwithstanding the silence of Bede, Gregory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, and others, there are several documents which prove this, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least render it extremely probable. A celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>, took the name of St Maur in the beginning of the last century, and received the sanction of Pope Gregory XV. in 1621. This society was early distinguished by the virtue and the knowledge of its members, and it still supports the character. There are, perhaps, fewer eminent men in it than formerly; but this may be ascribed to the levity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and partly to the little encouragement for the researches of learned men. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> persons of ingenuity which this society has produced are, the Fathers Menard, d'Acheri, Mabillon, Ruinart, Germain, Lami, Montfaucon, Martin, Vaissette, le Nouvri, Martianay, Martenne, Massuet, &c. &c. See L'Histoire Litteraire de la <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">Congregation</a> de St Maur, published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, in 4to, 1770, by Dom. Tassin.

MAURICE

Pages 29-31

St., commander of the Theban legion, was a Christian, together with the officers and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of that legion, amounting to 6600 men.—This legion received its name from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, where it was raised. It was sent by Dionysius to check the Bagaudae, who had excited some disturbances in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. Maurice having carried his troops over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian commanded him to employ his utmost exertions to extirpate Christianity. This proposal was received with horror both by the commander and by the soldiers. The emperor, enraged at their opposition, commanded the legion to be decimated; and when they still declared Maurice, declared that they would sooner die than do anything prejudicial to the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, every tenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of those who remained was put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Their perseverance excited the emperor to still greater cruelty; for when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that nothing could make them relinquish their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he commanded his troops to surround them, and cut them to pieces. Maurice, the commander of these Christian heroes, and Exuperus and Candidus, officers of the legion, who had chiefly instigated the soldiers to this noble resistance, signalized themselves by their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the doctrines of the Christian religion. They were massacred, it is believed, at Agaune, in Chablais, the 22d of September, 286. Notwithstanding many proofs which support this transaction, Dubordier, Hottinger, Moyle, Burnet, and Mosheim, are disposed to deny the fact. It is defended, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, by Hicks an English writer, and by Dom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISLE">Lisle</a> a Benedictine monk de la <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> de Saint <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VANNES">Vannes</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of his, entitled Defense de la Verite du Martyre de la Legion Thebienne, 1737. In defense of the same fact, the reader may consult Historia de S. Mauritio, by P. Rosignole Jesuit, and the Acta Sanctorum for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September. The martyrdom of this legion, written by St Eucherius bishop of Lyons, was transmitted to posterity in a very imperfect manner by Surius. P. Chiflet a Jesuit, discovered, and gave to the public, an exact copy of this work. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Rainart maintains, that it has every mark of authenticity. St Maurice is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of a celebrated order in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>'s dominions, created by Emmanuel Philibert <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, to reward <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> merit, and approved by Gregory XIII. in 1572. The commander of the Theban legion must not be confounded with another St Maurice, mentioned by Theodoret, who suffered martyrdom at Apamea in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. Maurice (Mauritius Tiberius), was born at Arasissus in Cappadocia, A.D. 539. He was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Roman family. After he had filled several offices in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Tiberius Constantine, he obtained the command of his armies against the Persians. His gallantry was so conspicuous that the emperor gave him his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Constantina in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and invested him with the purple the 13th August 582. The Persians still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make inroads on the Roman territories, and Maurice sent Philippicus, his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, against them. This general conducted the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with various success. At first he gained several splendid victories, but he did not continue to have a decided superiority. As there was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for soldiers in these unfortunate times, the emperor issued a mandate in 592, forbidding any soldier to become a monk till he had accomplished the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of his military <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Maurice acquired much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in restoring Chosroes II. king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, to the throne, after he had been deposed by his subjects. The empire was in his reign harassed by the frequent inroads of the Arabian tribes. He purchased peace from them, by granting them a pension nearly equal to 100,000 crowns; but these barbarians took frequent opportunities to renew the war. In different engagements the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> destroyed 50,000, and took 17,000 prisoners. These were restored, on condition that the king of the Abari should return all the Roman captives in his dominions. Maurice, regardless of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, he demanded a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of 10,000 crowns. Maurice, full of indignation, refused the sum: and the barbarian, equally enraged, put the captives to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. While the emperor, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> this cruelty, was making preparations against the Abari, Phocas, who from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CENTURION">centurion</a> had attained the highest military preferment, assumed the purple, and was declared emperor. He pursued Maurice to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>, took him prisoner, and condemned him to die. The five sons of this unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> were massacred before his eyes, and Maurice, humbling himself under the hand of God, was heard to exclaim, Thou art <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, O <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, and thy judgments are without partiality. He was beheaded on the 26th November 602, in the 63rd year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> and 20th of his reign. Many writers have estimated the character of this prince by his misfortunes instead of his actions. They believed him guilty without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, and condemned him without reason. It cannot be denied, however, that he allowed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to be harassed; but he was a father to the rest of the empire. He restored the military <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, humbled the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of his enemies, supported the Christian religion by his laws, and piety by his example. He loved the sciences, and was the patron of learned men. Maurice, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, son of Henry le Pieux, was born A.D. 1521. He was early remarkable for his courage, and during his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he was engaged in warlike pursuits. He served under the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of 1544 against France; and in the year following against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of Smalkalde; with which, although a Protestant, he would have no manner of connexion. The emperor, as a reward for his services, in the year 1547, made him elector of Saxony, having deprived his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> John Frederick of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a>. Ambition had led him to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the views of Charles, in the hope of being elector, and ambition again detached him from that prince. In 1551 he entered into a league against the emperor, together with the elector of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Palatine, the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>, and many other princes. This league, encouraged by the young and enterprising Henry II. of France, was more dangerous than that of Smalkalde. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> was the deliverance of the landgrave of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, whom the emperor kept prisoner. Maurice and the confederates marched, in 1552, to the defiles of Tyrol, and put to flight the Imperial troops who guarded them. The emperor and his brother Ferdinand narrowly escaped, and fled from the conquerors in great disorder. Charles having retired into Passau, where he had collected an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, brought the princes of the league to terms of accommodation. By the famous peace of Passau, which was finally ratified the 12th of August 1552, the emperor granted an amnesty without exception to all those who had carried arms against him from the year 1546. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> not only obtained the free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their religion, but they were admitted into the imperial chamber, from which they had been excluded since the victory of Mulberg. Maurice soon after united himself with the emperor against the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> of Brandenburg, who laid waste the German provinces. He engaged him in 1553, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>- Maurice, ed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Sivershausen, and died of the wounds he had received in the engagement two days after. He was one of the greatest protectors of the Lutherans in Germany, and a prince equally brave and politic. After he had profited by the spoils of John Frederick, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Protestants, he became himself the leader of the party, and by these means maintained the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of power against the emperor in Germany. Maurice de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, Prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Low Countries after the death of his father William, who was killed in 1584 by the fanatic Gerard. The young prince was then only eighteen years of age, but his courage and abilities were above his years. He was appointed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> general of the United Provinces, and he reared that edifice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of which his father had laid the foundation. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a> submitted to him in 1590; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVENTER">Deventer</a>, Hulst, Nimeguen, in 1591. He gained several important advantages in 1592, and in the year following he made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Gertrudenburg. When he had performed these splendid services, he returned to the Low Countries by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>. His fleet was attacked by a dreadful tempest, in which he lost forty vessels, and he himself had very nearly perished. His death would have been considered by the Hollanders as a much greater calamity than the loss of their vessels. They watched over his safety with exceeding care. In 1594, one of his guards was accused of an intention to take away his life; and it was generally believed that he was bribed to this service by the enemies of the republic. He fell a sacrifice at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, either to his own fanaticism <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the jealous anxiety of the friends of Maurice. The prince of Orange, increasing in reputation, defeated the troops of the archduke Albert in 1597, and drove the Spaniards entirely out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. In 1600 he was obliged to raise the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>; but he took ample vengeance on Albert, whom he again defeated in a pitched battle near Nieuport. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, this great general sent back the ships which had brought his troops into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>: My brethren (said he to his army), we must conquer the enemy or drink up the waters of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Determine for yourselves; I have determined I shall either conquer by your bravery, or I shall never survive the disgrace of being conquered by men in every respect our inferiors. This speech elevated the soldiers to the highest pitch of enthusiasm, and the victory was complete. Rhinberg, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">Grave</a>, and Ecluse, cities in Flanders, submitted to the conqueror the following year. Maurice, however, not only laboured for the commonwealth, but also for himself. He coveted the sovereignty of Holland, and was opposed in the prosecution of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> by the pensioner Barneveldt. The zeal and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of this wise republican cost him his life. He was an Arminian; and at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Maurice defended Gomar against Arminius. Taking advantage of the general odium under which the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMINIANS">Arminians</a> lay, he found means to get Barneveldt condemned in 1619. His death, wholly owing to the cruel ambition of the Prince of Orange, made a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the minds of the Hollanders. The truce with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> being expired, Spinola laid siege to Breda in 1624, and in six months, by the proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of his great talents, though with great slaughter of his troops, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The prince of Maurice, Orange, unsuccessful in every attempt to raise the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a> siege, died of vexation in 1625, aged 55 years, with the reputation of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> of his time. "The life of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> (says the able Raynal) was almost an uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of battles, of sieges, and of victories. Of moderate abilities in every thing else, he shone conspicuous in his military capacity. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> was the school of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and those who received their military <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in his armies augmented, perhaps, the glory of their master. Like Montecucculi, he discovered inimitable skill in his marches and encampments; like Vauban, he possessed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> of fortifying places, and of rendering them impregnable; like Eugene, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of finding subsistence for great armies in countries barren by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, or ravaged by war; like Vendome, the happy talent of calling forth, in the moment they became necessary, greater exertions from his soldiers than could reasonably be expected; like Condé, that infallible quickness of eye which decides the fortune of battles; like Charles XII., the art of rendering his troops almost invincible to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, and fatigue; like Turenne, the secret of making war with the least possible expense of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood." The Chevalier Folard maintains, that Maurice was the greatest commander of infantry since the time of the Romans. He studied the military art of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and applied their rules with great exactness in the various occurrences of war. He not only took advantage of the inventions of others, but he enriched the science of war with several improvements. Telescopes were first used by him for a military purpose; and, besides a kind of gallery in conducting a siege, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of blockading a strong place, which were of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, he greatly improved the whole art by his method of pushing an attack with great vigour, and of defending, for the greatest length of time, and in the best manner, a place besieged. In short, the many useful things which he practised or invented, placed him in the highest rank among men of a military character. On one occasion, a lady of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> asked him, Who was the first general of the age? Spinola (replied he) is the second. It was his constant practice, during <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, to have two guards placed by his bedside, not only to defend him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of danger, but to awake him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there should be the least occasion. The war betwixt Spain and Holland was never carried on with greater keenness and animosity than during his administration. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Signor, hearing of the vast torrents of blood shed in this contest, thought that a great empire must depend on the decision. The object of so many battles was pointed out to him on a map, and he said coldly, If it were my business, I would send my <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a>, and order them to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> this little corner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> into the sea. Maurice, like many great men, was impatient under <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>, and too much devoted to women. He was succeeded by Frederick Henry his brother.

MAURICEAU

Pages 29-29

Francis, a French surgeon, who applied himself with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success and reputation to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of his art for several years at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>.
