Afterwards he confined himself to the disorders of pregnant and lying-in-women, and was at the head of all the operators in this way. His Observations sur la grossesse et sur l'accouchement des femmes, sur leurs maladies, et celles des enfans nouveaux, 1694, in 4to, is reckoned an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and has been translated into several languages, German, Flemish, Italian, English: and the author himself translated it into Latin. It is illustrated with cuts. He translated another piece <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two, by way of supplement, on the same subject; and died at Paris in 1759.

MAURITANIA

Pages 31-33

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, on the south by Getulia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a> Interior, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean; comprehending the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>. Its ancient limits are not exactly mentioned by any historian; neither Mauritania, neither can they now be ascertained by any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> observations, these kingdoms being but little known to Europeans. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was originally inhabited by a people called Mauri, concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of which name authors are not agreed. It is probable, however, that this country, or at least <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of it, was first called Phut, since it appears from Pliny, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, and St Jerome, that a river and territory not far from Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a> went by that name. From the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> Targum it likewise appears, that part of the Mauri may be deemed the offspring of Laud the son of Misraim, since his descendants, mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> x., are there called מִצְרָיִם Mauri, or Mauritani. It is certain, that this region, as well as the others to the eastward of it, had many colonies planted in it by the Phoenicians. Procopius tells us, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> two pillars of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> were to be seen there, with the following inscription in the Phoenician <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and character upon them: "We are the Canaanites, that fled from Joshua the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">Nun</a>, that notorious robber." Ibn Rachic, or Ibn Roquiz, an African writer cited by Leo, together with Evagrius and Nicephorus Callistus, assert the same thing. The Mauritians, according to Ptolemy, were divided into several cantons or tribes. The Metagonitae were seated near the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, now those of Gibraltar. The Succosii, or Cocossii, occupied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Iberian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Under these two petty nations the Massaces, Veruces, and Verbice or Vercices, were settled. The Salise or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALINES">Salines</a>, were situated lower, towards the ocean; and, still more to the south, the Volubiliani. The Mauritani and Herpiditani possessed the eastern part of this country, which was terminated by the Mulucha. The Angacauani, or Jangacauani, Neetiberes, Zagrenzii, Banibae, and Faeculer, extended themselves from the southern foot of Ptolemy's Atlas <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> to his Atlas <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>. Pliny mentions the Banibae, whom Father Hardouin takes to be Ptolemy's Banibae; and Mela, the Atlantes, whom he represents as possessed of the western part of this district. The earliest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Mauritania mentioned in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>; and next to him were Atlas and Anteus his two sons, both famous in the Grecian fables on account of their wars with Hercules. Anteus, in his contention with that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, seems to have behaved with great bravery and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. Having received <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> reinforcements of Libyan troops, he cut off great numbers of Hercules's men. But that celebrated commander, having at last intercepted a strong body of Libyans sent to the relief of Anteus, gave him a total overthrow, wherein both he and the best part of his forces were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. This decisive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> put Hercules in possession of Libya and Mauritania, and consequently of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of all these kingdoms. Hence came the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, that Hercules, finding Anteus, a giant of an enormous size with whom he was engaged in single <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, to receive fresh strength as often as he touched his mother <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> when thrown upon her, at last lifted him up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and squeezed him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Hence likewise may be deduced the fable intimating that Hercules took the globe from Atlas upon his own shoulders, overcame the dragon that guarded the orchards of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESPERIDES">Hesperides</a>, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> Mauritians en fruit there. Bochart thinks that the fable alluded chiefly to naval engagements, wherein Hercules, for the most part, was victorious; though Anteus from time to time received succours by sea. But at last Hercules, coming up with one of his squadrons which had a strong reinforcement on board, made himself master of it, and thus rendered Anteus incapable for the future of making head against him. The same author likewise insinuates, that the notion of Anteus's gigantic stature prevailing for so many centuries amongst the Tingitanians, pointed out the size of the vessels of which his fleets and squadrons were composed. As for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> apples so frequently mentioned by the old mythologists, they were the treasures that fell into Hercules's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> upon the defeat of Anteus; the Greeks giving the oriental word ἀργυροί riches, the signification affixed to their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> χρυσοί, apples. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which Atlas and Anteus lived, the most probable supposition seems to be that of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton. According to that illustrious author, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a> the father of Sesac was the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Libya, or that vast tract extending from the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to the Atlantic ocean; the conquest of which country was effected by Sesac in his father's lifetime. Neptune afterwards excited the Libyans to a rebellion against Sesac, and slew him; and then invaded Egypt under the command of Atlas or Anteus, the son of Neptune, Sesac's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>. Not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, Hercules, the general of Thebais and Ethiopia for the gods or great men of Egypt, reduced a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time the whole continent of Libya, having overthrown and slain Anteus near a town in the Thebais, from that event called Antea or Anteopolis: this, we say, is the notion advanced by Sir Isaac Newton, who endeavours to prove, that the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Libya, by Sesac, happened a little above a thousand years before the birth of Christ, as the last, by Hercules, did some few years after. Now, though we do not pretend to adopt every particular circumstance of Sir Isaac Newton's system, yet we cannot forbear observing, that it appears undeniably plain from Scripture, that neither the western extremity of Libya, nor even the other parts of that region, could possibly have been so well peopled before the time of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, as to have sent a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to invade Egypt. For Egypt and Phoenicia, from whence the greatest part of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of the Libyans came, and which were much nearer the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from whence the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of mankind was made, could not themselves have been greatly overstocked with inhabitants any considerable time before the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>. And that such an invasion happened in the reign of Neptune, or at least of his son Anteus, has been most fully evinced by this most excellent chronologer. From the defeat of Anteus, nothing remarkable occurs in the history of Mauritania till the times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who at last brought the whole kingdom under their jurisdiction; for which see the article ROME. 1. With regard to the customs, &c. of this people, it would seem, from what Hyginus insinuates, that they fought only with clubs, till one Belus, the son of Neptune, as that author calls him, taught them Sir Issac Newton makes this Belus to have been the same person with Sesostris king of Egypt, who overran a great part of the then known world. 2. All persons of distinction in Mauritania went richly attired, wearing much gold and silver in their clothes. They took great pains in cleansing their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and curled their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> in a curious and elegant manner. They combed their beards, which were very long, and always had their nails pared extremely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. When they walked out in any numbers, they never touched one another, for fear of disconcerting the curls into which their hair had been formed. 3. The Mauritanian infantry, in time of action, used shields made of elephants skins, being clad in these of lions, leopards, and bears, which they kept on both night and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. 4. The cavalry of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> was armed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> short lances, and carried targets or bucklers, made likewise of the skins of wild beasts. They used no saddles. Their horses were small and swift, had wooden collars about their necks, and were so much under the command of their riders, that they would follow them like dogs. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of these horsemen was not much different from that of the foot above mentioned, they constantly wearing a large tunic of the skins of wild beasts. The Phutaei, of whom the Mauritanians were a branch, were eminent for their shields, and the excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> they made of them, as we learn from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Xenophon, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, and Scripture. Nay, Herodotus seems to intimate, that the shield and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> came from them to the Greeks. 5. Notwithstanding the fertility of their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, the poorer sort of the Mauritanians never took care to manure the ground, being strangers to the art of husbandry; but roved about the country in a wild <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> manner, like the ancient Scythians or Arabes Scenite. They had tents, or mapalia, so extremely small, that they could scarce breathe in them. Their food was corn, herbage, &c. which they frequently did eat green, without any manner of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, being destitute of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and all the elegancies as well as many necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Their habit was the same both in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter, consisting chiefly of an old tattered, though thick garment, and over it a coarse rough tunic; which answered probably to that of their neighbours the Numidians. Most of them lay every night upon the bare ground; though some of them strewed their garments thereon, not unlike the present African Kabyles and Arabs, who, according to Dr Shaw, use their hykes for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> and covering in the night. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the most approved <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of Horace may be admitted, the Mauritanians <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> poisoned arrows; which clearly intimates, that they had some skill in the art of preparing poisons, and were excellent dartmen. This last observation is contemnanced by Herodian and Athen, who entirely come into it, affirming them to have been in such continual danger of being devoured by wild beasts, that they durst not stir out of their tents or mapalia without their darts. Such perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> must render them exceedingly skilful in hurling that weapon. 7. The Mauritanians sacrificed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> victims to their deities, as the Phoenicians, Carthaginians, &c. did. The country people were extremely rude and barbarous; but those inhabiting cities must undoubtedly have had at least some smattering in the literature of the several nations they deduced their origin from. That Mauritania the Mauritanians had some knowledge in naval affairs, seems probable, not only from the intercourse they had with the Phoenicians and Carthaginians, as well as the situation of their country; but likewise from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, or Onomacritus, who asserts them to have made a settlement at the entrance into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>, to which place they came by sea. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>, sorcery, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, &c. they appear to have applied themselves to in very early times. Cicero and Pliny say, that Atlas was the inventor of astrology, and the doctrine of the sphere, i.e. he first introduced them into Mauritania. This, according to Diodorus Siculus, gave rise to the fable of Atlas <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the heavens upon his shoulders. The same author relates that Atlas instructed Hercules in the doctrine of the sphere and astrology, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, who afterwards brought those sciences into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>.

MAURITIA

Pages 33-33

the Ginkgo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Maidenhair Tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of palms. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MAURITIUS

Pages 33-35
or Maurice, an island of Africa, about 400 miles east of Madagascar, lying in the latitude of 20 and 21 degrees south. It is about 150 miles in circumference. In the beginning of the 16th century it was discovered by the Portuguese, who knowing that Pliny and other ancient writers had mentioned the island of Cerne in these seas, took it for granted that this must be it; and accordingly we find it styled Cerne or Sirne, in their maps; but, notwithstanding this, they did not think fit to settle it; and indeed their force was so small, in comparison of the vast dominions they grasped, that it was very excusable. However, according to their laudable custom, they put some hogs, goats, and other cattle, upon it, that in case any of their ships either going to the Indies or returning to Portugal should be obliged to touch there, they might meet with refreshments. The Dutch, in the second voyage they made to the East Indies under their admiral James Cornelius Vanneck, came together with five ships on the 15th of September 1668; anchored in a commodious port, to which they gave the name of Warwick Haven; and gave a very good account of the place in their journals. Captain Samuel Castleton, in the Pearl, an English East India ship, arrived there on the 27th of March 1612; and taking it to be an island undiscovered before, bestowed upon it the name of England's Forest, though others of his crew called it Pearl Island; and in the account of their voyage, written by John Tatton the master of the ship, celebrated it as a place very convenient for shipping, either outward or homeward bound, to refresh at. This they sometimes accordingly did, and brought some cargoes of ebony, and rich wood from thence; but without fixing any settlement. At length, in 1638, the Dutch seated themselves here; and it is highly remarkable, that at the very time they were employed in making their first settlement, the French sent a vessel to take possession of it, who found the Dutch beforehand with them, and refused the assistance of an English Indiaman, wooing and watering in another part of the island, who very frankly offered it, to drive the Dutch from their half settled posts. They continued for some time in quiet possession. Mauritius, possession of the places they fortified in this island, to which they gave the name of Mauritius, in honour of Prince Maurice their stadtholder. But having engaged the French, who were settled on Madagascar, to steal 50 of the natives, and sell them for slaves, for the improvement of the Dutch settlements here, this proved the ruin of both colonies; for the negroes surprised and massacred the French in Madagascar; and the slaves in Mauritius fled into the centre of the island; from whence they so much and so incessantly molested those who had been formerly their masters, that they chose to quit a country where they could no longer remain in any tolerable degree of safety. The East India Company, however, from motives of convenience, and a very imperfect notion of its value, disapproved this measure, and therefore ordered it to be resettled; which was accordingly done, and three forts erected at the principal havens. Things now went on somewhat better than they did before; but they were still very much disturbed by the revolted negroes in the heart of the isle, whom they could never subdue. One principal use that the company made of this place, was to send thither state prisoners, who, as they were not men of the best morals, quickly corrupted the rest of the inhabitants, and rendered them such a race of outrageous smugglers, the situation of the place concurred with their bad disposition, that after various ineffectual attempts made to reform them, orders were at length given to abandon Mauritius a second time, which after some delays, were put in execution in the year 1710. Two years after this, the French took possession of it, and named it the isle de France. This name has obtained among themselves, but the Europeans in general continue to call it Mauritius. It lies in 8° Lat. 20° 13' E. Long. 6° 15'. The inconveniences arising from the want of a port at the island of Bourbon, induced the French to take possession of Mauritius, it having two very good harbours, to fortify which no expense has been spared. That on the north-west is called Port ass="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis, that on the south-east side of the island is called Port Bourbon. The trade-wind from the south-east in these latitudes blows all the year round, excepting for a few days at the summer solstice, when it is interrupted by hard gales and hurricanes from the north. The ease with which this wind enables ships to enter the port of Bourbon, caused the French, when they first took possession of this spot, to esteem it the best port in the island; but experience pointing out to them, that the same wind often rendered the passage out of the harbour so difficult, that a ship was sometimes obliged to wait a considerable time before the weather admitted of her putting to sea, this harbour is in a great measure abandoned, and the principal town and seat of government is now fixed at Port Louis, which is nearly in the middle of the north side of the island, and its entrance is through a channel formed by two shoals, which advance about two miles into the sea. When a ship arrives opposite to this channel, the south-east wind hinders her from entering the port under sail, and she must either warp in with cables or be towed in with boats. The necessity of this operation, joined to the extreme narrowness of the channel, which does not admit of two ships abreast of each other entering at the same time, is one of the best defences the harbour has against an attack by sea; for, from these obstacles, an enemy would find it a matter of the greatest difficulty to force the port; and in addition to this natural strength, they have built two forts and as many batteries, which are mounted with heavy cannon, and entirely command the approach to the harbour, should ships presume to force an entry under sail. This port is capable of containing 100 sail of ships, and is well provided with every requisite for repairing and even building of ships. This port has proved of the greatest advantage to France in the several wars which have been carried on between Great Britain and her; and has proved of great utility to the French East India Company's commerce; for here their ships and crews were sure to meet with all necessary refreshment after a long voyage. The port of Bourbon is also fortified; and an army landed here would find it an extremely difficult task to pass the mountains to the different parts of the island. There are several places between the north-east extremity and Port Louis where boats may land, but all these are defended by batteries; and the country behind them is a continued thicket: The rest of the coast is inaccessible. In the north-eastern quarter is a plain extending about 10 miles from east to west, and in some places five miles inland from the northern coast. All the rest of the island is full of high and steep mountains, lying so near to one another, and the intervals between them so narrow, that, instead of valleys, they rather resemble the beds of torrents; and these are choked with huge fragments of rocks which have fallen from the steep sides of the impending mountains. On the summits of the mountains ice is frequently to be found, and they are covered with forests of ebony and other large trees. The ground they shade produces herbage, shrubs, and plants of various sorts, from the common grass to the strongest thorn, and that in such profusion, that they form a thicket so closely interwoven, that no progress can be made but by means of a hatchet. Notwithstanding these difficulties, plantations have been formed on these mountains, and very considerable progress has been made in the plains; but the productions, although mostly of the same kind, are not only in less quantity, but of an inferior quality to those produced at Bourbon island. In a course of years, however, the settlement cost so much, and was considered in every light worth so little, that it had been more than once under deliberation, whether, after the example of the Dutch, they should not leave it again to its old negro inhabitants; which sooner or later in all likelihood would have been its fate; if, in 1735, the famous M. de la Bourdonnais had not been sent thither with the title of governor-general of the French islands. He found this isle in the worst state possible, thinly inhabited by a set of lazy people, who equally hated industry and peace, and who were continually flattering this man to his face, and betraying him wherever and as far as they durst. He gave himself no trouble about this, having once found the means to make himself obeyed; he saw the vast importance of the island; he conceived that it might be settled to great advantage; and, without so much as expecting the thanks of those for whom he laboured, he began to execute this great design. His first step was to bring over black Mauritius, black boys from Madagascar, whom he carefully trained up in good principles, and in continual exercise; by which he rendered them so good soldiers, that he very quickly obliged the Marones, or wild negroes, either to submit or to quit the island: he taught the planters to cultivate their lands to advantage; he, by an aqueduct, brought fresh water to the sea side; and whereas they had not so much as a boat at his coming thither, he made a very fine dock, where he not only built sloops and large vessels, but even a ship of the burden of 500 tons. However incredible it may seem, yet it is certainly fact, that in the space of five years he converted this country into a paradise, that had been a mere wilderness for 5000; and this in spite of the inhabitants, and of the company, who being originally prejudiced by them, behaved ill to him at his return. He soon made the cardinal de Fleury, however, sensible of the true state of things; and compelled the company to acknowledge, though they did not reward, his services. He afterwards returned into the Indies, and perfected the work he had begun, and to him it is owing that the isle of France was rendered one of the finest and most important spots upon the globe. Here no coffee is raised; but by the indefatigable industry of M. de Bourdonnais, sugar, indigo, pepper, and cotton (which are not at Bourbon), came to be cultivated with success. Since the departure of that most excellent governor, the plantations have been neglected, and are fallen off; but if a proper spirit of activity was raised among the inhabitants, they might soon be made to resume their flourishing appearance. Mines of iron have been discovered in the mountains near the great plain, in the north-east part of the island; and these mountains affording in great abundance the necessary fuel, forges have been erected: but the iron produced is of a very inferior quality, it being brittle, and only fit for making cannon-balls and bomb-shells. Black cattle, sheep, and goats, are preserved with difficulty; the first generally die before they have been a year in the island, and this occasions frequent importations of them from Madagascar and other parts. Common domestic poultry breed in great plenty; and, with fish and turtle, furnish a great part of the food of the European inhabitants. The approach to the island is extremely dangerous, it being surrounded with ledges of rocks, and many of them covered by the sea. The shore abounds with coral and shells. This island is said to contain 60 rivers; some are considerable streams, and most of them have their sources from lakes, of which there are several in the middle part of the island. The rivers afford plenty of various kinds of fish, particularly eels. These are of an enormous size, some having been found that were six feet long, and six inches in circumference, and so extremely voracious, that it is dangerous to bathe in those parts of the river where they lie, as they will seize a man without fear, and have strength sufficient to keep him under water till he is drowned. Here is a great variety of birds, and bats as large as a young kitten: the inhabitants esteem them a delicate morsel. The air is both hot and moist, but not unwholesome. The place abounds with insects, which are very troublesome; but there are no serpents. It has been discovered, that off Port Louis the south-west wind generally blows with least strength about Mauritius sunrise; and it also happens, on four or five days at intervals, in the course of a month, that early in the morning the wind ceases in the northern part of the island for an hour or two, when a breeze rises, although but faintly, from the north-west; during which, a ship stationed at the entrance of the channel to avail herself of this breeze, may enter the harbour and attack the forts. This island, during the period of the French revolution, did not entirely escape from the storm which then agitated the parent country. In the year 1799, a conspiracy was formed, and broke out, for the purpose of resisting the government which had been established under the authority of the republic. It was, however, soon suppressed by the activity of the civil authorities, supported by the majority of the inhabitants. The population of this island in 1799 amounted to 65,000, viz. 55,000 slaves, and 10,000 whites and mulattoes. The following is a state of the produce of this island in 1800: viz. coffee, 6000 bales, of 100 lbs. French; indigo, 300,000 lbs. from 2s. to 8s. per lb.; cotton, 2000 bales, of 250 lbs.; raw sugar, 20,000,000 lbs.; cloves, 20,000 lbs. The island of Mauritius, as well as the other French islands in the Indian ocean, were taken by the British in 1811; and their possession was confirmed to Britain by the treaty of Paris in 1814.

MAURUA

Pages 35-35

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, entirely surrounded with a ridge of rocks, and without any harbour for shipping. It is inhabited; and its productions are the same with those of the neighbouring islands. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> round hill rises in the middle of it, which may be seen at the distance of 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 leagues. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 152° 32' S. Lat. 16° 25'.

MAUSOLEUM

Pages 35-35

a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sepulchral monument. The word is derived from Mausolus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, to whom <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> his widow erected a most stately monument, esteemed one of the wonders of the world, and called it, from his own name, Mausoleum. Sr MAWES, a town of Cornwall, in England, seated on the east side of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a> haven, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 56' N. Lat. 50° 6'. Though but a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, two miles off, without a minister, or either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, chapel, or meeting-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, it has sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> ever since 1562, who are returned by its mayor or portreeve. It consists but of one street, under a hill, and fronting the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and its inhabitants subsist purely by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. K. Henry VIII. built a castle here, opposite to Pendennis, for the better security of Falmouth haven. It has a governor, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, and two gunners, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of guns. Here is a fair the Friday after St Luke's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>.

MAXENTIUS

Pages 35-36

Marcus Aurelius Valerius, a son of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximianus <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, was, by the voluntary abdication of Diocletian, and of his father, raised to the empire A.D. 306. He afterwards invited his father to reassume his imperial authority; and in a perfidious manner destroyed Severus, who had delivered himself into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and relied upon his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> for the safety of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. His victories and successes were impeded by Galerius Maximianus, who opposed him with a powerful force. The defeat Maxentius and voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Galerius soon restored peace to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and Maxentius passed into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, where Maximus rendered himself odious by his cruelty and oppression. He soon after returned to Rome, and was informed that Constantine was come to dethrone him. He gave his adversary <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> near Rome, and, after he had lost the victory, he fled back to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over which he crossed the Tiber was in a decayed situation, and he fell into the river, and was drowned, A.D. 312. The cowardice and luxuries of Maxentius were as conspicuous as his cruelties. He oppressed his subjects with heavy taxes, to gratify the cravings of his pleasures, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the avarice of his favourites. He was debauched in his manners, and neither virtue nor innocence were safe whenever he was inclined to voluptuous pursuits. His body was deformed and unwieldy. To visit a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> ground, or to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> himself under a marble portico, or walk on a shady terrace, was to him a Herculean labour, which required the greatest exertions of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>.

MAXIM

Pages 36-36

an established proposition <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> principle: in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it denotes much the same with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-AXIOM">axiom</a>. MAXIMILIAN I., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany, signalled himself against the French while he was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and after he was emperor entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Henry VIII. of England as a volunteer against that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>: he was a protector of learned men, and abolished an iniquitous tribunal, styled Judicium occultum Westphaliae; he composed some poems, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He died in 1519, aged 62.

MAXIMUM

Pages 36-36

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, denotes the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> attainable in any given <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a quantity conceived to be <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> increases <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> decreases till it arrives at a certain magnitude or position, and then, on the contrary, grows greater or lesser, and it be required to determine the said magnitude or position, the question is called a problem de maximis et minimis.

MAXIMUS

Pages 36-36

a celebrated Cynic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and magician, of Ephesus. He instructed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>; and, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some historians, it was in the conversation and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of Maximus that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOSTASY">apostasy</a> of Julian originated. The emperor not only visited the philosopher, but he even submitted his writings to his inspection and censure. Maximus refused to live in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Julian; and the emperor, not dissatisfied with the refusal, appointed him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> pontiff in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lydia, an office which he discharged with the greatest moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. When Julian went into the east, the philosopher promised him success, and even said that his conquests would be more numerous and extensive than those of the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>. He persuaded his imperial pupil, that, according to the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a>, his body was animated by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> which once animated the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> whose greatness and victories he was going to eclipse. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Julian, Maximus was almost sacrificed to the fury of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; but the intercession of his friends saved his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and he retired to Constantinople. He was soon after accused of magical practices, before the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>, and beheaded at Ephesus, A.D. 356. Maximus wrote some philosophical and rhetorical treatises, some of which were dedicated to Julian. They are all now lost. MAXIMUS of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosopher, went to Rome in 146, and acquired such reputation there, that the emperor Marcus Aurelius became his scholar, and gave him frequent proofs of his esteem. This philosopher is thought to have lived till the reign of the emperor Commodus. There are still extant 41 of his dissertations; a good edition of which was printed by Daniel Heinsius, in 1624, in Greek and Latin, with notes. MAXIMUS MARIUS. See MARILS.

MAY

Pages 36-38

the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> in the year, reckoning from our first, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; and the third, counting the year to begin with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> anciently did. It was called Maius by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, in respect to the senators and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, who were named magores; as the following month was called Junius, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the youth of Rome, in honorem juniorum, who served him in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; though some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to have been thus called from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAIA">Maia</a>, the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, to whom they offered sacrifice on the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of it; and Papius derives it from Madius, eo quod tune terra medeat. In this month the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> enters Gemini, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in general begin to flower.—The month of May has ever been esteemed favourable to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>; and yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as well as many of the moderns, look on it as an unhappy month for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The original reason may perhaps be referred to the feast of the Lemures, which was held in it. Ovid alludes to this in the fifth of his Fasti, when he says, Nec vidua tardis cadem, nec virginis opta Tempora; qua auspit, non diuturna fuit; Hac quoque de causa, si te proverbia tangunt, Mense malum Maio nubere vulgus ait. May-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>. See Dew. May-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cherry. See PRUNUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of, a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at the mouth of the frith of Forth, in Scotland, about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circumference, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Fife, almost opposite to the rock called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">Bass</a>. It formerly belonged to the priory of Pittenweem; and was dedicated to St Adrian, supposed to have been martyred in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by the Danes; and hither, in times of Popish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, barren women used to come and worship at his shrine, in hopes of being cured of their sterility. Here is a tower and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> built by Mr Cunningham of Barns, to whom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. granted the island in fee, with power to exact twopence per ton from every ship that passes, for the maintenance of a lighthouse. In the middle of it there is a fresh-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and a small lake. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> produces pasturage for 100 sheep and 20 <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. On the west side the steep rocks render it inaccessible; but to the east there are four landing places and good riding. It was here that the French squadron, having the chevalier de St George on board, anchored in the year 1708, when the vigilance of Sir George Byng obliged him to relinquish his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and bear away for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>. The shores all round round the island abound with fish, and the cliffs with water fowl. May, Thomas, an eminent English poet and historian in the 17th century, was born of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> but decayed family in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and afterwards removed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. While he resided at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he wrote the five plays now extant under his name. In 1622, he published a translation of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Georgics, with annotations; and in 1635 a poem on King Edward III. and a translation of Lucan's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>; which poem he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Julius Caesar, both in Latin and English <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. Upon the breaking out of the civil wars he adhered to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and in 1647, he published, "The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the parliament of England, which began November the third, MDCXL." With a short and necessary view of some precedent years." In 1649, he published, Historiae Parliamenti Anglici Breviarium, in three parts; which he afterwards translated into English. He wrote the History of Henry II. in English verse. He died in 1642. He went well to rest over night, after a cheerful bottle as usual, and died in his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> before morning: upon which his death was imputed to his tying his nightcap too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> under his fat <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> and chin, which caused his suffocation; but the factious Andrew Marvel has written a poem of 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, to make him a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and die by the force of good wine. He was interred near Camden in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>; which caused Dr Fuller to say, that "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were a biased and partial writer, yet <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> lieth buried near a good and true historian indeed." Soon after the Restoration, his body, with those of several others, was dug up, and buried in a pit in St Margaret's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>; and his monument, which was erected by the appointment of parliament, was taken down and thrown aside. Mayer, Tobias, one of the greatest astronomers and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> the 18th century produced, was born at Masbach, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Württemberg, 1723. He taught himself <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fourteen designed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> and instruments with the greatest dexterity and justness. These pursuits did not hinder him from cultivating the belles lettres. He acquired the Latin tongue, and wrote it with elegance. In 1750, the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a> chose him for their mathematical professor; and every year of his short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was thenceforward marked with some considerable discoveries in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He published several works in this way, which are all reckoned excellent; and some are inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the university of Gottingen." His labours seem to have exhausted him; for he died worn out in 1762. Mayerne, Sir Theodore de, baron of Aubone, was the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> de Mayerne, the celebrated author of the General History of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and of the Monarchie aristocrate-démocratique, dedicated to the states-general. He was born in 1573, and had for his godfather Theodore Beza. He studied physic at Montpelier, and was made physician in ordinary to Henry IV. who promised to do <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> things for him, provided he would change his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. James I. of England invited him over, and made him first physician to himself and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, in which office he served the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAYENNE">Mayenne</a> whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his death in 1655. His works were printed at London in 1700, and make a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> folio, divided into two books; the first containing his Consilia, Epistolae, et Observationes; the second his Pharmacopoeia variaeque medicamentorum formule. Mayhem. See Maim. Mayne, Jasper, an eminent English poet and divine in the 17th century, who was bred at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and entered into holy orders. While his majesty resided at Oxford, he was one of the divines appointed to preach before him. He published in 1647 a piece entitled Oxaomaxia, or The people's war examined according to the principles of reason and scripture, by Jasper Mayne. In 1648 he was deprived of his studentship at Christ <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and two livings he had; but was restored with the king, who made him his chaplain and archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>; all which he held till he died. Dr Mayne was held in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem both for his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> parts and his acquired accomplishments. He was an orthodox preacher, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of severe virtue and exemplary behaviour; yet of a ready and factious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and a very singular turn of humour. From some stories that are related of him, he seems to have borne some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of resemblance in his manner to the celebrated Dr Swift; but if he did not possess those very brilliant parts that distinguished the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a>, he probably was less subject to that capricious and those unaccountable whimsies which at times so greatly eclipsed the abilities of the latter. Yet there is one anecdote related of him, which, although it reflects no great honour on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, as it seems to carry some degree of cruelty with it, yet it is a strong mark of his resemblance to the Dean, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that his propensity for drollery and joke did not quit him even in his latest moments. The story is this: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> had an old <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, who had lived with him some years, to whom he had bequeathed an old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, in which he told him he would find something that would make him drink after his death. The servant, full of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> that his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, under this familiar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, had left him somewhat that would be a reward for the assiduity of his past services, as soon as decency would permit, flew to the trunk; when, behold, to his great disappointment, the boasted legacy proved to be a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>. The doctor, however, bequeathed many legacies by will to pious uses; particularly 50 pounds towards the rebuilding of St Paul's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and 200 pounds to be distributed to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of the parishes of Cassington and Pyrton, near <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WATLINGTON">Watlington</a>, of both which places he had been <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. In his younger years he had an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and wrote two plays, the latter of which may be seen in the tenth volume of Dodsley's Collection, viz. 1. Amorous war, a tragi-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. 2. The city-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, a comedy. He published a poem upon the naval victory by the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> over the Dutch, printed in 1665. He also translated into English from the Greek, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Lucian's Dialogues. Maynooth, or Manoath, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> town in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, 12 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. At this place there is a catholic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, established by Maynooth the Irish parliament in 1795. Young men destined for the catholic church had formerly gone to the continent for their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. This had now become nearly impossible, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the war with France and Spain; and for this reason, as well as to prevent those foreign attachments which grow out of a foreign education, it was thought prudent to provide the means of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> instruction for the catholics. They had only petitioned for leave to establish a seminary; but the parliament also granted 800l. per annum for its support, which was afterwards enlarged to 13,000l.; but has since been diminished. There were in 1808, eight professorships and three lectureships; and there was accommodation for 200 students, to whom the establishment afforded commons and instruction.

MAYNWARING

Pages 38-38
ARTHUR, an eminent political writer in the beginning of the 18th century, staid several years at Oxford, and then went to Cheshire, where he lived some time with his uncle Mr Francis Cholmondeley, a very honest gentleman, but extremely averse to the government of King William III., to whom he refused the oaths. Here he prosecuted his studies in polite literature with great vigour; and coming up to London, applied to the study of the law. He was hitherto very zealous in anti-revolutionary principles, and wrote several pieces in favour of King James II.; but upon being introduced to the duke of Somerset and the earls of Dorset and Burlington, began to entertain very different notions in politics. His father left him an estate of near 800l. a-year, but so encumbered, that the interest money amounted to almost as much as the revenue. Upon the conclusion of the peace he went to Paris, where he became acquainted with Mr Boileau. After his return he was made one of the commissioners of the customs, in which post he distinguished himself by his skill and industry. He was a member of the Kit-cat club, and was looked upon as one of the chief supports of it by his pleasantry and wit. In the beginning of Queen Anne's reign, the lord treasurer Godolphin engaged Mr Donne to quit the office of auditor of the imprests, and made Maynwaring a present of a patent for that office worth about 2000l. a-year in a time of business. He had a considerable share in the Medley, and was author of several other pieces. The Examiner, his antagonist in politics, allowed that he wrote with tolerable spirit, and in a masterly style. Sir Richard Steele dedicated the first volume of the Tatler to him.

MAYO

Pages 38-38

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Connaught, having <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLIGO">Sligo</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; Roscommon on the south, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEITRIM">Leitrim</a> and Roscommon on the east, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> on the west. It contains 724,640 Irish plantation acres, 68 parishes, and 140,000 inhabitants. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Bourke. This county takes its name from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, built in 664; the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, and some traces of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls which encompassed the city, yet remain on the plains of Mayo. It was a university, founded for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of such of the Saxon youths as were converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>: it was situated a little to the south of Lough Conn; and is to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> frequently called Mayo of the Saxons, being celebrated for giving education to Alfred the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England. As this town has gone to decay, Balmroke is reckoned the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town. The county by the sea is mountainous; but inland has good pastures, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. It is about 62 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 32 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASTLEBAR">Castlebar</a> is the assizes town.—Mayo was formerly a bishop's see, which is now united to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TUAM">Tuam</a>.

MAYOR

Pages 38-39

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> town, chosen annually out of the aldermen. The word, anciently wrote meyr, comes from the British mirret, i.e. custodire, or from the old English maier, viz. potestas, and not from the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Richard I. in 1189, changed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> into a mayor, and from that example King John made the bailiff of King's Lynn a mayor anno 1204: Though the famous city of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a> obtained not this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> for its chief magistrates till the seventh year of King Henry V. anno 1419; since which there are few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> but have had a mayor appointed for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Mayors of corporations are justices of peace pro tempore, and are mentioned in several statutes; but no person shall bear any office of magistracy concerning the government of any town, corporation, &c. who hath not received the sacrament according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England within one year before his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, and who shall not take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of supremacy, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any person intrudes into the office of mayor, a quo warranto lies against him, upon which he shall not only be ousted, but fined. And no mayor, or person holding an annual office in a corporation for one year, is to be elected into the same office for the next; in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, persons obstructing the choice of a successor are subject to 100l. penalty. Where the mayor of a corporation is not chosen on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> appointed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, the next officer in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> shall the day after hold a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> and elect one; and if there be a default or omission that way, the electors may be compelled to choose a mayor, by a writ of mandamus out of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. Mayors, or other magistrates of a corporation, who shall voluntarily absent themselves on the day of election, are liable to be imprisoned, and disqualified from holding any office in the corporation. Mayor's Courts. To the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor and city of London belong several courts of judicature. The highest and most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> is that called the hustings, destined to secure the laws, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, franchises, and customs of the city. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is a court of request, or of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>; of which before. The third is the court of the lord mayor and aldermen, where also the sheriffs sit; sit; to which may be added two courts of sheriffs, and the court of the city orphans, whereof the lord mayor and aldermen have the custody. Also the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, which is a court or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, wherein are made all by-laws which bind the citizens of London. It consists, like the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, of two houses: an upper, consisting of the lord mayor and aldermen; and a lower, of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of common council men, chosen by the several wards as represen- tatives of the body of the citizens. In the court of common council are made laws for the advancement of trade, and committees yearly appointed, &c. But acts made by them are to have the assent of the lord mayor and aldermen by stat. 11 Geo. I. Also the chamberlain's court, where every thing relating to the rents and re- venues of the city, as also the affairs of servants, &c. are transacted. Lastly, to the lord mayor belong the courts of coroner and of escheator; another court for the conservation of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>; another of gaol delivery; held usually eight times a year, at the Old Bailey, for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of criminals, whereof the lord mayor is himself the chief judge. There are other courts called wardmotes or meetings of the wards; and courts of halymote or assemblies of the several guilds and fraternities.

MAZAGAN

Pages 39-39

a strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>- dom of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, and on the frontiers of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Duguela. It was fortified by the Portuguese, and besieged by the king of Morocco with 200,000 men in 1562, but to no purpose. It is situated near the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 15'. N. Lat. 33° 12'.

MAZARA

Pages 39-39

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a considerable valley of the same name, which is very fertile, and watered with several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The town is a bishop's see, and has a good harbour; is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 30'. N. Lat. 37° 53'.

MAZARINE

Pages 39-39

Julius a famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> and prime minister of France, was born at Piseina in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Abruzzo, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in 1602. After having finished his studies in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, he en- tered into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Cardinal Sachets, and became well skilled in politics, and in the interests of the princes at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in Italy; by which means he was enabled to bring affairs to an accommodation, and the peace of Queiras was shortly concluded. Cardinal Richelieu being taken with his conduct, did from thenceforward highly esteem him; as did also Cardinal Antonio, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII., who procured him a car- dinal's hat in 1641. Richelieu made him one of the executors of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>; and during the minority of Louis XIV. he had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of affairs. At last he became the envy of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, which occasioned a civil war; whereupon Mazarine was forced to re- tire, a price was set on his head, and his library sold. Notwithstanding, he afterwards returned to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> in more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> than ever; concluded a peace with Spain, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and the in- fanta. This treaty of peace passes for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>- piece of Cardinal de Mazarine's politics, and procured him the French king's most intimate confidence: but at last his continual application to business threw him Mazarine into a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, of which he died at Vincennes in 1661.—Cardinal Mazarine was of a mild and affable temper. One of his greatest talents was his knowing mankind, and his being able to adapt himself, and to assume a character conformable to the circumstances of affairs. He possessed at one and the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>, and the abbeys of St Arnauld, St Clement, and St Vincent, in the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; that of St Dennis, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLUNY">Cluny</a>, and Victor, of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>; of St Michel at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of others. He founded Mazarine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; which is also called the college of the four nations. There has been published a collection of his letters, the most copi- ous edition of which is that of 1745, in 2 vols. duo- decimo. MAZZUOLI. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARMIGIANO">Parmigiano</a>.

MEAD

Pages 39-40

Dr Richard, a celebrated English physi- cian, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol20.html#article-STEPNEY">Stepney</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where his father, the Reverend Mr Matthew Mead, had been one of the two ministers of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>; but in 1662 was ejected for nonconformity, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to preach at Stepney till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. As Mr Mead had a handsome fortune, he bestowed a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> upon 13 children, of whom Richard was the eleventh; and for that purpose kept a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, who taught him the Latin tongue. At 16 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> Richard was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, where he studied three years under the famous Grevius; and then choosing the profession of physic, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he attended the lectures of the famous Pitcairn on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of medicine, and Herman's botanical courses. Having also spent three years in these studies, he went with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and two other gentlemen to visit <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and physic in 1695. Afterwards he spent some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and at Rome; and returning home the next year, settled at Stepney, where he married, and practised physic with a success that laid the foundation of his future greatness. In 1703, Dr Mead having communicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of Dr Bonomo's discoveries relating to the cutaneous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> the itch, which they inserted in the Philosophical Transactions; this, with his account of poisons, procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the Royal Society, of which Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton was then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. The same year he was elected physician of St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and was also employed by the surgeons to read anatomical lectures in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, which obliged him to remove into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In 1707 his Paduan diploma for doctor of physic was confirmed by the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and being patronized by Dr Radcliffe, on the death of that famous physician he succeeded him in his house at Bloomsbury-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his business. In 1727 he was made physician to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> George II. whom he had also served in that capacity while he was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; and he had afterwards the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of seeing his two sons-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, Dr Nichols and Dr Wilmot, his coadjutors in that eminent station. Dr Mead was not more to be admired for the qualities of the head than he was to be loved for those of his heart. Though he was himself a hearty whig, yet, uninfluenced by party principles, he was a friend to all men of merit, by whatever denomination they might happen to be distinguished. Thus he was intimate with Garth, with Arbuthnot, and with Freind; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> kept up a constant correspondence with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Boerhaave, who had been his fellow student at Leyden: they communicated to each other their observations and projects, and never loved each other the less for being of different sentiments. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, intent as Dr Mead was on the duties of his profession, he had a greatness of mind that extended itself to all kinds of literature, which he spared neither pains nor <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to promote. He caused the beautiful and splendid edition of Thuanus's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> to be published in 1713, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes folio: and by his interposition and assiduity, Mr Sutton's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> foul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> from ships and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> places was carried into execution, and all the ships in his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> provided with this useful machine. Nothing pleased him more than to call hidden talents into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; to give encouragement to the greatest projects; and to see them executed under his own eye. During almost half a century he was at the head of his business, which brought him one year about seven thousand pounds, and for several years between five and six thousand; yet clergymen, and in general all men of learning, were welcome to his advice. His library consisted of 10,000 volumes, of which his Latin, Greek, and oriental <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, made no inconsiderable part. He had a gallery for his pictures and antiquities, which cost him great sums. His reputation, not only as a physician, but as a scholar, was so universally established, that he corresponded with all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> literati in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>: even the king of Naples sent to desire a complete collection of his works; and in return made him a present of the two first volumes of Signior Bajardi, which may be considered as an introduction to the collection of the antiquities of Herculaneum. At the same time that prince invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, that he might have an opportunity of showing him those valuable monuments of antiquity; and nothing but his great age prevented his undertaking a journey so suited to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. No foreigner of learning ever came to London without being introduced to Dr Mead; and on these occasions his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> was always open, and the magnificence of princes was united with the pleasures of philosophers.
