Cosmo soon after received from Pope Pius IV. the title of grand duke, and had it not been opposed by all the princes of Italy, this pontiff, who was entirely devoted to Cosmo, because he had thought proper to acknowledge him to be of his house, would have conferred on him the title of king. There never was a more zealous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learning. Ambitious of imitating the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Caesar, he like him, was fond of learned men, kept them near his person, and founded for them the university of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>. He died in 1574, at the age of 55, after governing with equal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and glory. In 1562 he instituted the military order of St Stephen. His son, Francis <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> who died in 1587, was the father of Mary of Medicis, the wife of Henry the Great and of Ferdinand I. who died in 1608. Medietas linguae, in Law, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, or inquest impanelled, of which the one half are natives of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and the other foreigners. This jury is never used except where one of the parties in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> is a stranger and the other a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a>. In petit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, murder,

MEDINA

Pages 535-535

Sir John, an eminent painter, was son of Medina de l'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, a Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, who settled at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, where the son was born in 1660. He was instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> by Du Chatel; under whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> he made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress; and applying himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of Rubens, made that eminent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>. He painted both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>; and was held in extraordinary esteem by most of the princes of Germany, who distinguished his merit by several marks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He married young, and came into England in 1686, where he drew portraits for several years with great reputation; as he painted those subjects with remarkable freedom of touch, a delicate management of tints, and strong resemblance of the persons. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Leven encouraged him to go to Scotland, and procured him a subscription of 300l. worth of business. He went, carrying a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bodies and postures, to which he painted heads. He returned to England for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but went back to Scotland, where he died, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of the Grayfriars at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, in 1711, aged 52. He painted most of the Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Two small history pieces, and the portraits of the professors, in the Surgeons <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> at Edinburgh, were also painted by him. At Wentworth castle is a large piece containing the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyll and his sons, the two late dukes John and Archibald, in Roman habits; the style Italian, and superior to most <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> performers. The duke of Gordon presented Sir John Medina's head to the great duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> for his collection of portraits done by the painters themselves; the duke of Gordon too was drawn by him, with his son the marquis of Huntly and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Lady Jane, in one piece. Medina was knighted by the duke of Queensberry, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>; and was the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> made in Scotland before the union. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> in the octavo edition of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> were designed by him: and he composed another set for Ovid's Metamorphoses, but they were never engraved.

MEDINA TALNARI

Pages 534-535

a famous town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, between Arabia Deserta and Arabia the Happy; celebrated for being the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Mahomet. It stands at a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from the port of Tambo. It is of moderate size, surrounded by wretched walls, and situated in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain. It belongs to the sherif of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, although it had of late times a particular sovereign of the family of Dacii Barkad. At present the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is confided by the sherif to a vizir, who must be taken from the family of the sovereign. Before Mahomet, this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was called Iathreb; but it got the name of Medinah en Nebbi, "the City of the Prophet," after Mahomet, being driven from Mecca by the Koreischites, had taken refuge there, and passed in it the rest of his days. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Mahomet at Medina is respected by Mussulmans, but they are under no obligation to visit it for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> alone, which on their return from Mecca <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> near Medina, go a little out of their way to see the tomb. It stands in a corner of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, whereas the Kaba is situated in the middle of that at Mecca. That the people may not perform some superstitious worship to the relics of the prophet, they are prevented from approaching the tomb by gates, through which they may look at it. It consists of a piece of plain mason <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, without any other monument. The tomb is placed between two others, where the ashes of the two first caliphs repose. Although it is not more magnificent than the tombs of the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the founders of mosques, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> that covers it is decorated with a piece of green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuff embroidered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which the pacha of Damascus renews every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. It is guarded by 40 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>, who watch the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> said to be deposited there. It is seated in a plain abounding with palm trees, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 57° 10', N. Lat. 25°. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) ARABIA. MEDINA Celi, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Old Castile, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name; seated near the river Xalon, in W. Long. 2° 9', N. Lat. 41° 13'. MEDINA de-las-Torres, a very ancient town of Spain, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, with an old castle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a duchy. It is seated on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, at the foot of a mountain near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADAJOZ">Badajoz</a>. MEDINA-del-Campo, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and ancient town of Spain, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon. The great square is very fine, and adorned with a superb fountain. It is a trading place, enjoys great privileges, and is seated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with corn and wine. W. Long. 4° 20', N. Lat. 41° 22'. MEDINA-del-rio-Secco, an ancient and rich town of Spain, in the kingdom of Leon, with the title of a duchy: seated on a plain, remarkable for its fine pastures. E. Long. 4° 33', N. Lat. 42° 8'.

MEDINE

Pages 535-535

an Egyptian piece of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> silvered over, and about the size of a silver threepence.

MEDIOLANUM

Pages 535-536

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Insubres, built by the Gauls on their settlement in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; a municipium, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength; and a seat of the liberal arts; whence it had the name of Novae Athenae. Now <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, capital of the Milanese, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Olana and Lombo. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 30', N. Lat. 45° 25'. MEDIOLANUM Aulercorum, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Gallia Celtica, which afterwards took the name of the Eburovicum Civitas (Antonine); corrupted to Civitas Ebroicorum, and this last to Elbroica; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> appellation <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, a city of Normandy. E. Long. 1° 12', N. Lat. 49° 41'. MEDIOLANUM Gugernorum, in Ancient Geography, a town of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>; now the village Moyland, not far from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>. MEDIOLANUM Ordovicum, in Ancient Geography, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, now Llan Vethlin, a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. MEDIOLANUM Santonum, in Ancient Geography, which afterwards taking the name of the people, was called called Santonica Urbs; also Santones and Santoni: A town of Aquitaine. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAINTES">Saintes</a>, capital of Saintonge in Guienne, on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>.

MEDIOMATRICI

Pages 536-536

anciently a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>.

MEDITATION

Pages 536-536

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> by which we consider anything closely, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wherein the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is employed in the search or consideration of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. In our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, it is used to signify a consideration of the objects and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> truths of the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Mystic divines make a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between meditation and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>: the former consists in discursive acts of the soul, considering methodically and with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of faith and the precepts of morality; and is performed by reflections and reasonings, which leave behind them manifest impressions on the brain. The pure contemplative have no need of meditation, as seeing all things in God at a glance, and without any reflection. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, therefore, has once quitted meditation, and is arrived at contemplation, he returns no more; and, according to Alvarez, never resumes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> of meditation, except when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> of contemplation is too weak to fill his sails.

MEDITERRANEAN

Pages 536-536

something enclosed within <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is remote from the ocean. MEDITERRANEAN is more particularly used to signify that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which flows between the continents of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, entering by the straits of Gibraltar, and reaching into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, as far as the Euxine sea and the Palus Maeotis. The Mediterranean was anciently called the Grecian sea and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> sea. It is now cantoned out in several divisions, which bear several names. To the west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> it is called the Ligustic or Tuscan sea; near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, the Adriatic; towards <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, the Ionic and Ægean; between the Hellespont and the Bosphorus, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> sea, as being very safe; and beyond, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea, its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> being dangerous.

MEDITRINALIA

Pages 536-536

a Roman festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Meditrina, kept on the 30th of September. Both the deity and the festival were so called à medendo, because on this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> they began to drink new wine mixed with old by way of medicine. The mixture of wines, on this festival, was drunk with much form and solemn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>.

MEDITULLIUM

Pages 536-536

is used by anatomists for that spongy substance between the two plates of the cranium, and in the interstices of all laminated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See ANATOMY, No. I. II.

MEDIUM

Pages 536-536

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, that space <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> region through which a body in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> passes to any point: thus <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> is supposed to be the medium through which the heavenly bodies move; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the medium wherein bodies move near our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the medium wherein fishes live and move; and glass is also a medium of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, as it affords it a free passage. That density or consistency in the parts of the medium, whereby the motion of bodies in it get retarded, is called the resistance of the medium; which, together with the force of gravity, is the cause of the cessation of the motion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>. Subtle or Æthereal MEDIUM. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton considers it probable, that, beside the particular aerial medium, wherein we live and breathe, there is another more universal one, which he calls an æthereal medium; vastly more rare, subtle, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, than air, and by that means freely permeating the pores and interstices of all other mediums, and diffusing itself through the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; and by the intervention hereof he thinks it is that most of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are affected. See ÆTHER, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>, FIRE, &c.

MEDLAR

Pages 536-536

see MESPILOUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEDULLA OSSIIUM

Pages 536-536
or MARROW of the bones. See ANATOMY, No. 5. MEDULLA cerebri and cerebelli, denotes the white soft part of the brain and cerebellum, covered on the outside with the cortical substance, which is of a more dark or ashy colour. See ANATOMY, No. 131—133. MEDULLA oblongata, is the medullary part of the brain and cerebellum, joined in one; the fore part of it coming from the brain, and the hind part from the cerebellum. See ANATOMY, No. 134. It lies on the basis of the skull, and is continued through the great perforation thereof into the hollow of the vertebrae of the neck, back, and loins; though only so much of it retains the name oblongata as is included within the skull. After its exit thence it is distinguished by the name of medulla spinalis. Ibid. No. 135.

MEDUSA

Pages 537-537

a genus of vermes, belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEDWAY

Pages 537-537

a river of England, rises in the Weald of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, and entering <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> near Ashurst, runs by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, and thence continues its course towards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAIDSTONE">Maidstone</a>. It is navigable for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and thence for vessels and barges to Maidstone, the tide flowing up to that town. The distance between the mouth of this river, where the fort at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> is erected, and Rochester bridge, is between 16 and 18 miles. In this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the river, the channel is so deep, the banks so soft, and the reaches so short, that it is one of the best and safest harbours in the world; and ships of 80 guns ride afloat at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, within musket <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of Rochester bridge. Nor is there a single instance upon record, that any of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> ever suffered here by storms, except in the dreadful tempest which happened in November 1793, when the Royal Catherine was sunk and lost. On the shore of this river are two castles, one at Upnor, which guards two reaches of the river, and is supposed to defend all the ships which ride above, between that and the bridge; on the other side of the river is Gillingham castle, built for the same purpose, and well furnished with cannon, which commands the river. Besides these, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of guns at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called the Swan, and another at Cockhamwood. But the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fortification on this river is the castle at Sheerness.

MEEREN

Pages 537-537
or MEER, John Vander, called De Jonghe, an eminent landscape painter, is supposed to have been the son of the old John Vander Meer, and of whom he learned the first rudiments of the art; but being in his youth deprived of his instructor before he had made any great progress, he became a disciple of Nicholas Berghem, and was accounted the best of those who were educated in the school of that admired master. In the manner of his master, he painted landscapes and cattle; and his usual subjects are cottages, with peasants at their rural occupations and diversions. It is observed of him, that he very rarely introduced cows, horses, or any other species of animals, except goats and sheep; the latter of which are so highly finished, that one would imagine the wool might be felt by the softness of its appearance. His touch is scarce perceptible, and yet the colours are admirably united. He died in 1688. The genuine works of this Vander Meer bear a very high price, and are esteemed even in Italy, where they are admitted into the best collections; but the scarcity of them has occasioned many moderate copies after his works to be passed on the undiscerning for real originals.

MEETRETES

Pages 793-794

a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, containing something more than <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> English gallons. See MEASURE.

MEGALESIA

Pages 537-537

and MEGALENSES LUDI, feasts and games in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Cybele <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Rhea the mother of the gods, kept on the 12th of April by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and famous for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rejoicings and diversions of various sorts. The Galli carried the image of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of drums and other music, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the noise they made to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> from hearing the cries of his infant son <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, when he was disposed to devour him.

MEGALOPOLEIS

Pages 537-537

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, dividedly (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Pausanias); <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conjunctly Megalopolis, (Strabo): A town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, built under the auspices of Epaminondas, after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEUCTRA">Leuctra</a>; many considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> being joined together in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the better to withstand the Spartans. It was the greatest city of Arcadia, according to Strabo.

MEGARA

Pages 537-539

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a noble <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Megaris, which for many years carried on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Corinthians and Athenians. It had for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a school of philosophers, called the Megarici, successors of Euclid the Socratic, a native of Megara. Their dialect was the Doric; changed from the Attic, which it formerly had been, because of Peloponnesian colonists who settled there. Megara was situated at a distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, about midway between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Corinth. Its port was called Nisera, from Nisus son of Pandon the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, who obtained Megaris for his portion, when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Athens was divided into four lots by his father. He founded the town, which was eighteen stadia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from the city, but united with it, as the Piraeus with Athens, by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> walls. It had a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>. "The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> (says Pausanias) may be supposed to have fallen through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>." The site (as Dr Chandler informs us*) is now covered with rubbish, among which are standing some ruinous churches. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has been named from them Dode Ecclesiis, "The Twelve Churches;" but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. The acropolis or citadel, called also Nisera, was on a rock by the sea side. Some pieces of the wall remain, and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> fortress has been erected on it, and also on a lesser rock near it. The village Megara (continues the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>) consists of low <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> cottages pleasantly situated on the slope of a brow or promontory indented in the middle. On each side of this vale was an acropolis or citadel; one named <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>; the other from Alcathous, the builder of the wall. They related, that he was assisted by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, who laid his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> aside on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which, as Pausanias testifies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> struck with a pebble returned a musical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the wall of one citadel is seen by a windmill. The masonry is of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> called Incertum. In 1676 the city wall was not entirely demolished, but comprehended the two summits, on which are some churches, with a portion of the plain toward the south. The whole site, except the hills, was now green with corn, and marked by many heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, the collected rubbish of buildings. A few <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> are found, with pedestals fixed in the walls and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>; and also some maimed or mutilated Megara, mutilated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. One of the former relates to Atticus Herodes, and is on a pedestal which supported a statue erected to him when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, A.D. 143, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and people of Megara, in return for his benefactions and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> toward the city. In the plain behind the summits, on one of which was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, with scattered fragments of marble, the remains of a bath or of a fountain, which is recorded as in the city, and remarkable for its size and ornaments, and for the number of its columns. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> was named from the local nymphs called Sithnides. The stone of Megara was of a kind not discovered anywhere else in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELLAS">Hellas</a>; very <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, uncommonly soft, and consisting entirely of cockle shells. This was chiefly used; and, not being durable, may be reckoned among the causes of the desolation at Megara, which is so complete, that one searches in vain for vestiges of the many public edifices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and sepulchres, which once adorned the city. Megara was engaged in various wars with Athens and Corinth, and experienced many vicissitudes of fortune. It was the only one of the Greek cities which did not flourish under their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> benefactor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>; and the reason assigned is, that the avenging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> of the gods pursued the people for their impiety in killing Anthemocritus, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALD">herald</a>, who had been sent to them in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>. The Athenian generals were sworn on his account to invade them twice a-year. Hadrian and Atticus were followed by another friend, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is preserved by an inscription on a stone lying near a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the village: "This too is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the most magnificent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> son of Archelaus, who regarding the Grecian cities as his own family, has bestowed on that of the Megarensians one hundred pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> towards the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of their towers, and also one hundred and fifty more, with two thousand two hundred feet of marble toward re-edifying the bath; deeming nothing more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> than to do good to the Greeks, and to restore their cities." This person is not quite unnoticed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He was one of the generals employed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Anastasius on a rebellion in Isauria. He surprised the capital Claudiopolis, and sustained a siege with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bravery, A.D. 494. Megara retains its original name. It has been much infested by corsairs; and in 1676 the inhabitants were accustomed, on seeing a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> approach in the daytime or hearing their dogs bark at night, immediately to secrete their effects and run away. The vauvode or Turkish governor, who resided in a forsaken tower above the village, was once carried off. It is no wonder, therefore, that Nissa has been long abandoned. The place was burned by the Venetians in 1687. Megara, in Ancient Geography, formerly called Hybla, a town towards the east <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; extinct in Strabo's time, though the name Hybla remained on account of the excellence of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. It was a colony of Megareans from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Risus Megaricus denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> laugh. Megaris, in Ancient Geography, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Megareans, is described as a rough region, like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>; the mountain called Oenian or the Asinine, now Macriplagi or "the long Mountain," extending through it towards <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> and Mount Cithaeron. It belonged to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a> or Attica, until it was taken by the Peloponnesians in the reign of Codrus, when a colony of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a> settled in it. This territory had Attica to the east, Boeotia to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west, and the isthmus of Corinth to the south. Megaris, a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Tuscan sea, joined to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, now called Castello dell'Ovo. Megasthenes, a Greek historian in the age of Seleucus Nicanor, about 300 years before Christ. He wrote about the oriental nations, and particularly the Indians. His history is often quoted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. What now passes as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is spurious. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEGIDDO">Megiddo</a>, in Ancient Geography, a town of Galilee, recited (Joshua xvii. 11.) among the cities of Massach, in the tribe of Issachar or Asser, on the west side of Jordan; famous for the defeat of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AHAZIAH">Ahaziah</a> and Josiah, who perished there (2 Kings xxiii. 29.) near it was an open plain, fit for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>. It was situated to the north, contrary to its position in the common maps. The Canaanites, being tributary to the Israelites, dwelt in it, Joshua xvii. It was rebuilt by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, 1 Kings ix. Meibomius, the name of several learned Germans.—John Henry Meibomius was professor of physic at Helmstadt, where he was born, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a>; he wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Mecenas, published at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 4to, 1653, with several other learned works. Henry, his son, was born at Lubeck in 1638; became professor of physic at Helmstadt; and, besides works in his own profession, published Scriptores rerum Germanicarum, 3 vols. folio, 1688; a very useful collection, first begun by his father.—Marcus Meibomius, of the same family, published a collection of seven Greek authors who had written upon ancient music, with a Latin version by himself, dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who invited him to her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. But she engaging him one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to sing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of ancient music, while somebody was ordered to dance to it, the immoderate noise which this occasioned in the spectators so disgusted him, that he immediately left the court of Sweden. His edition of the Greek mythologists, and notes upon Diogenes Laertius in Menage's edition, show him to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of learning; but he suffered no little railing for his attempt to correct the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, by a kind of metre he fancied he had found out in these ancient writings. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, a considerable town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and in the margravate of Misnia, with a castle. It formerly belonged to the bishop, but is now secularized, and the inhabitants are Lutherans. In this place is a famous manufactory of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>. E. Long. 13. 27. N. Lat. 51. 19. Meli, Honey, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>. See HONEY. Mela, Pomponius, an ancient Latin writer, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Baetica in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and flourished in the reign of the emperor Claudius. His three books of Cosmography, or De situ orbis, are written in a concise, perspicuous, and elegant manner; and have been thought worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and labours of the ablest critics. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius gave an edition of them in 1638, 4to, with very large and copious notes. To this edition is added, Julii Honorii oratoris excerptum cosmographicum, first published from the manuscript, and and *Ethici cosmographia*. Gronovius afterwards published another edition with illustrations by medals. In his last edition are added five books, *De Geographia*, written by some later author; by Jornandes, as Fabricius conjectures.

MELAMPODIUM

Pages 539-539

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELAMPUS

Pages 539-539

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated soothsayer and physician of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, son of Amythaon and Idomenea <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dorippe. He lived at Pylos in Peloponnese. His servants once killed two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> who had made their nests at the bottom of a large oak; and Melampus paid so much regard to their remains, that he raised a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> pile and burned them upon it. He also took particular care of their young ones, and fed them with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after this, the young serpents crept to Melampus as he slept on the grass near the oak; and, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> sensible of the favours of their benefactor, they wantonly played around him, and softly licked his ears. This awoke Melampus, who was astonished at the sudden change which his senses had undergone. He found himself acquainted with the chirping of the birds, and with all their rude notes, as they flew around him. He took advantage of this supernatural gift, and soon made himself perfect in the knowledge of futurity, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> also instructed him in the art of medicine. He had soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of curing the daughters of Pretus, by giving them hellebore, which from that circumstance has been called melampodium; and, as a reward for his trouble, he married the eldest of these princesses. The tyranny of his uncle Neleus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pylos, obliged him to leave his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and Pretus, to show himself more sensible of his services, gave him <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. About this time the personal charms of Pero, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Neleus, had gained many admirers; but the father promised his daughter only to him who brought into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the oxen of Iphiclus. This condition displeased many; but Bias, who was also one of her admirers, engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Melampus to steal the oxen and deliver them to him. Melampus was caught in the attempt, and imprisoned; and nothing but his services as a soothsayer and physician to Iphiclus would have saved him from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. All this pleaded in the favour of Melampus; but when he had taught the childless Iphiclus how to become a father, he not only obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but also the oxen; and with them he compelled Neleus to give Pero in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to Bias. A severe distemper, which had rendered the women of Argos insane, was totally removed by Melampus; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>, who then sat on the throne, rewarded his merit by giving him part of his kingdom, where he established himself; and where his posterity reigned during six successive generations. He received divine honours after death, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were raised to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.

MELAMPYRUM

Pages 539-539

Cow-wheat, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Personatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELANCHOLY

Pages 539-539

a kind of delirium attended with gloomy thoughts, heaviness, and sorrow. See Medicine, No. 327.

MELANCTHON

Pages 539-540
Philip, born at Bretten in the Palatinate in 1495, was one of the wisest and most able men of his age among the reformers, though of a mild temper, and disposed to accommodate rather than to inflame disputes. In his youth he made an admirable progress in learning, and was made Greek professor at Wittenberg in 1529. Here his lectures upon Homer and the Greek text of St Paul's Epistle to Titus, drew to him a great number of auditors, and entirely effaced the contempt to which his low stature and mean appearance had exposed him. Melancthon reduced the sciences to systems; and acquired such reputation, that he had sometimes 2500 auditors. He soon entered into an intimate friendship with Luther, who taught divinity in the same university; and in 1519 they went together to Leipzig, to dispute with Eccius. The following years he was continually engaged in various employments; he composed several books; he taught divinity; took several journeys, in order to found colleges and visit churches; and in 1530 drew up a confession of faith, which goes by the name of the Confession of Augsburg, because it was presented to the emperor at the diet held in that city. All Europe was convinced that he was not, like Luther, backward to accommodate the differences between the various sects of Christians. He hated religious disputes, and was drawn into them only through the necessity of the part he was called to act in the world; and therefore would have sacrificed many things to have produced an union among the Protestants. For this reason, Francis I., the French king, wrote to desire him to come and confer with the doctors of the Sorbonne, in order to agree with them about putting an end to all controversies; but though Luther endeavoured to persuade the elector of Saxony to consent to that journey, and though Melancthon himself desired it, that prince, whether he distrusted Melancthon's moderation, or was afraid of quarrelling with the emperor Charles V., would never grant his permission. The king of England also in vain desired to see him. Melancthon, in 1529, assisted at the conferences of Spires. In 1541, he was at the famous conferences at Ratisbon. In 1543, he went to meet the archbishop of Cologne to assist him in introducing the reformation into his diocese; but that project came to nothing; and in 1548, he assisted at seven conferences on the subject of the interim of Charles V., and wrote a censure on that interim, and all the writings presented at these conferences. He was extremely affected at the dissensions raised by Flaccus Illyricus. His last conference with those of the Roman communion was at Worms, in 1557. He died at Wittenberg in 1560, and was interred near Luther. Some days before he died, he wrote upon a piece of paper the reasons which made him look upon death as a happiness; that the chief of them was, that it "delivered him from theological persecutions." Nature had given Melancthon a peaceable temper, which was but ill suited to the time he was to live in. His moderation served only to be his cross. He was like a lamb in the midst of wolves. Nobody liked his mildness; it looked as if he was... was lukewarm; and even Luther himself was sometimes angry at it. Melancthon was a man in whom many good as well as great qualities were wonderfully united. He had great parts, great learning, great sweetness of temper, moderation, contentedness, and the like, which would have made him very happy in any other times but those in which he lived. He never affected dignities, or honours, or riches, but was rather negligent of all these things; too much so in the opinion of some, considering he had a family; and his son-in-law Sabinus, who was of a more ambitious temper, was actually at variance with him upon this very account. Learning was infinitely obliged to him on many accounts: on none more than this, that, as already observed, he reduced almost all the sciences which had been taught before in a vague irregular manner into systems. Considering the distractions of his life, and the infinity of disputes and tumults in which he was engaged, it is astonishing how he could find leisure to write so many books. Their number is prodigious, insomuch that it was thought necessary to publish a chronological catalogue of them in the year 1582. His works indeed are not correct, and he himself owned it: but as he found them useful, he chose rather to print a great number, than to finish only a few: "which however (as Bayle says), was postponing his own glory to the advantage of others." His constitution was very weak, and required great tenderness and management; which made Luther, as hot and zealous as he was, blame him for labouring too earnestly in the vineyard.

MELANIPPIDES

Pages 540-540

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Greek poet about 520 years before Christ. His grandson of the same name, flourished about 60 years after at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Perdiccas the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">Second</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>. Some fragments of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> are still extant.

MELANTERIA

Pages 540-540

an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, which seems to have been applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> pyrites. The Greeks used it externally as a gentle escharotic and a styptic, as an ingredient in their ointments for old ulcers, and also to sprinkle in the form of powder on fresh wounds, in order to stop the hemorrhage. MELASSES. See Molasses.

MELASTOMA

the American Gooseberry-tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Calycanthemae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELCHA

Pages 540-540

a small village of Barbary, situated about 30 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, built on the ruins of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, some of which are still visible.

MELCHISEDEC

Pages 540-541
or Melchizedek, king of Salem, and priest of the Most High. The scripture tells us nothing either of his father, or of his mother, or of Melchisedec's genealogy, or of his birth, or of his death. And yet in this sense he was a figure of Jesus Christ, as St Paul affirms, who is a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedec, and not according to the order of Aaron, whose original, life, and death, are known. When Abraham returned from pursuing the four confederate kings, who had defeated the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, and had taken away Lot, Abraham's nephew, along with them (Gen. xiv. 17, 18, 19, &c.), Melchisedec came to meet Abraham as far as the valley of Shaveh, who was afterwards named the King's valley, presented him with the refreshment of bread and wine (or he offered bread and wine in sacrifice to the Lord, for he was a priest of the most high God), and blessed him. Abraham being desirous to acknowledge in him the quality of priest of the Lord, offered him the tythes of all he had taken from the enemy. After this time, there is no mention made of the person of Melchisedec: only the Psalmist (cx. 4.) speaking of the Messiah, says, "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec." St Paul, in his epistle to the Hebrews, unfolds the mystery which is concealed in what is said of Melchisedec in the Old Testament. See Heb. v. 6—10. An infinite number of difficulties and scruples have been started on the subject of Melchisedec.—St Jerome thought that Salem, of which Melchisedec was king, was not Jerusalem, but the city of Salem near Scythopolis, where they still pretended to show the ruins of the palace of this prince. The greatness and extent of these ruins are a sufficient proof of the magnificence of this ancient building. He thinks it was at this city of Salem or Shalem, that Jacob arrived after his passage over Jordan, at his return from Mesopotamia (Gen. xxxiii. 18.). Some believe that Salem, where Melchisedec reigned, is the same as Salim spoken of in the gospel of St John, chap. iii. 23. From the time of Epiphanes, there were names invented for the father and mother of Melchisedec. To his father was given the name of Heracles or Hercules, and to his mother that of Ashtaroth or Astaria. It is generally agreed on by the learned, that when the apostle says, he was "without father and without mother," no more is meant, than that he is introduced into the history of Abraham without acquainting us who he was, or whence he came, where he lived or when he died. Nevertheless, some have taken St Paul's words literally, and contended that he was not of human but divine nature. Origen and Didymus took him to be an angel; and the author of the Questions upon the Old and New Testaments pretends, that he was the Holy Ghost, who appeared to Abraham in a human form. The Arabic Catena upon the ninth chapter of Genesis, makes Melchisedec to be descended from Shem by his father, and from Japheth by his mother. Heracles or Herachim his father, was, they say, son or grandson of Phaleg, and son of Heber; and his mother, named Salathiel, was daughter of Gomer son of Japheth. Cedrenus and others derive Melchisedec from an Egyptian stock. They say his father was called Sidon or Sida, and was the founder of the city of Sidon, the capital of Phoenicia. Snidas says he was of the cursed race of Canaan; for which reason the scripture does not mention his genealogy. The Jews and Samaritans believed Melchisedec to be the same same with the patriarch Shem; which opinion has been followed by a great number of modern writers. M. Jurius has undertaken to prove that he is the same as Cham or Ham. It would be endless to set down all the opinions upon this matter: therefore we shall only add, that Peter Cumeus and Peter du Moulin have asserted, that Melchisedec who appeared to Abraham was the Son of God, and that the patriarch worshipped him and acknowledged him for the Messiah. About the beginning of the third century arose the heresy of the Melchisedecians, who affirmed that Melchisedec was not a man, but a heavenly power, superior to Jesus Christ: for Melchisedec, they said, was the intercessor and mediator of the angels, but Jesus Christ was so only for men, and his priesthood only a copy of that of Melchisedec, who was the Holy Ghost. We shall only beg leave to add here one opinion more concerning Melchisedec, which is that of the learned Heidegger, who, as the author of the Hist. Patriar. thinks, has taken the right method of explaining the accounts of Moses and the apostle Paul relating to this extraordinary person. He supposes a twofold Melchisedec; the one historical, whereof Moses gives an account in the 14th chapter of Genesis, as that he was king as well as high priest of Jerusalem; the other allegorical, whom St Paul describes, and this allegorical person is Jesus Christ. As the history of this prince and priest is so little known, it is no wonder, as Selden observes, that many fabulous accounts have been invented of him; of which the following may suffice as a specimen. Eutychus patriarch of Alexandria relates, that the body of Adam having been embalmed according to his order, was deposited in a cave under a mountain of the children of Seth; but that Adam before his death had commanded that they should take away his remains from that place, and transport them to the middle of the earth: that Noah, to follow the orders of his ancestors, had preserved the bodies of Adam and all the patriarchs with him in the ark: that finding himself near his death, he ordered his son Shem to take the body of Adam, to furnish himself with bread and wine for his journey, to take with him Melchisedec the son of Phaleg, and to go to the place in which an angel would show them where to bury the first man: that Noah added this order, "Command Melchisedec to fix his residence in that place, and to live unmarried all his lifetime, because God has chosen him to do service in his presence; command him, that he build no temple, nor shed the blood of birds, nor four-footed beasts, or any other animal; and that he offer no other oblations to God but bread and wine." This is the reason, according to this author, why Melchisedec, when he met Abraham, brought forth only bread and wine. A Greek author, under the name of Athanasius, relates, that Melchisedec was the son of an idolatrous king called Melchi and of a queen called Salem.—Melchi, having resolved to offer a sacrifice to the gods, sent his son Melchisedec to fetch him seven calves. In the way the young prince was enlightened by God, and immediately returned to his father, to demonstrate to him the vanity of his idols. Melchi, in wrath, sent him back to fetch the victims. While he was absent, the king sacrificed his eldest son, and a great many other children, to his gods. Melchisedec returning, and conceiving great horror at this butchery, retired to Mount Tabor, where he lived seven years, without clothes, and fed only on wild fruits. At the end of seven years, God appeared to Abraham, bid him go up to Mount Tabor, where he should find Melchisedec. He ordered him to clothe him, and to ask his blessing; which Abraham having done, Melchisedec anointed him with oil, and they came down together from the mountain.

MELCHITES

Pages 540-540

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name given to the Syriac, Egyptian, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The Melchites, excepting some few <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> no importance, which relate only to ceremonies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, are in every respect professed Greeks; but they are governed by a particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, who resides at Damas, and assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of patriarch of Antioch. They celebrate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> in the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> among the Melchites follow the rule of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rule of all the Greek monks. They have four fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> distant about a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from Damas, and never go out of the cloister.

MELCOMB-REGIS

Pages 541-542

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, in England, 130 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is situated at the mouth of the river Wey, by which it is parted from Weymouth. It appears from the name to have been anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s demesne, and from the records to have paid quit-rent to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> all along after King Edward I. till it was bought off by the inhabitants before they were united to Weymouth. It lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the haven, on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> surrounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on all sides except on the north. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and well paved, and many of the houses <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. It sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the reign of King Edward I. before Weymouth had that privilege. It was by parliament appointed a staple in the reign of Edward III. In the next reign the French burnt it; and it was thereby rendered so desolate, that the remaining inhabitants prayed and obtained a discharge from customs. On account of its quarrels with Weymouth, in the reign of Henry VI. its privileges as a port were removed to Poole: but in that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> they were restored to it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, which was confirmed in the next reign, on condition that Melcomb and Weymouth should make but one corporation, and enjoy their privileges in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; and to this was owing the flourishing state of both. In the two reigns last mentioned, a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> with seventeen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> was built from hence to Weymouth; to which, as well as its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> contributors were certain citizens of London; and upon its decay it was rebuilt in 1770. Here is a good market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, to which the members of the corporation of Weymouth come to attend public business, as the inhabitants do to its church for public worship. For several years past the sea has retired from it on the east, the priory formerly being bounded by the sea; but there is now a street beyond it, from which it is several paces to the high <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mark. The priory was situated in the east <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town, in Maiden street, whose site occupied about an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, now covered with tenements. On the south side are the remains of the chapel, now converted into a malt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Near it are the remains of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, formerly a nunnery. Here are three meeting houses, and a workhouse for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The church, which is in the middle of the town, has a wooden turret for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, and had been an old chapel. It was rebuilt in 1605, and made parochial, and is a handsome fabric, with a beautiful altarpiece painted and given by Sir James Thornhill. The port, which generally goes by the name of Weymouth, is said to be the best frequented in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and is defended by Sandford and Portland castles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> for both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Tuesdays and Fridays, but there are no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. In 1811 Melcomb contained 2985 inhabitants, Weymouth They are now one corporation and borough, consisting of a mayor, recorder, two bailiffs, an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of aldermen, and twenty-four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses. Whoever has been a mayor is ever after an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. They send four burgesses to Parliament, who are elected by such as have freeholds, whether they are inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not; the number of voters is near 700. Every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>, as in London, has the privilege of voting for four persons, who, when chosen, are returned, in two distinct indentures, as the burgesses of Weymouth and the burgesses of Melcomb-regis.

MELDAE

Pages 542-542

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Gallia Celtica, (called Meldorum Civitas in the Notitia), on the Matrona. Now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Champagne, on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, in France.

MELEAGER

Pages 542-542

a Greek poet, the son of Eurrates, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and flourished under the reign of Seleucus VI. the last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Syria. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>; and died in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Coos, anciently called Merope. He there composed the Greek epigrams called by us the Anthologia. The disposition of the epigrams in this collection was often changed afterwards, and many additions have been made to them. The monk Planudes put them into the order they are in at present, in the 1380.

MELEAGRIS

Pages 542-542

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; a genus of birds belonging to the order of gallinae. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELES

Pages 542-542

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a fine river running by the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, with a cave at its head, where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> is said to have written his poems. And from it Homer takes his original name Melesigenes, given him by his mother Critheis, as being born on its banks. (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>).

MELETIANS

Pages 542-542

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a considerable party who adhered to the cause of Meletius bishop of Lycopolis, in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, after he was deposed, about the year 306, by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his having sacrificed to the gods, and having been guilty of other heinous crimes; though Epiphanius makes his only failing to have been an excessive severity against the lazed. This dispute, which was at first a personal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Meletius and Peter, became a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> controversy; and the Meletian party subsisted in the fifth century, but was condemned by the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice.

MELIA

Pages 542-542

Azaderach, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a> Tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23rd order, Trihilata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELIANTHUS

Pages 542-542
Honey-flower, a genus of plants belonging to the didynamia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 24th order, Corydaliae. See Botany Index.

MELIBOEA

Pages 542-542

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>; which before it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, forms a spreading lake round it. This island was famous for its purple dye. Thought to be a colony of Thessalians; and hence Lucretius's epithet, Thessalicus.

MELICA

Pages 542-542

Ropegrass, a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the triandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Gremineae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELICERTA

Pages 542-543

MELICERTE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Melicertus, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a son of Athamas and Ino. He was saved by his mother from the fury of his father, who prepared to dash him against a wall as he had done his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Learchus. The mother was so terrified that she threw herself into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with Melicerta in her arms. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> had compassion on the misfortunes of Ino and her son. He changed them both into sea deities. Ino was called Leucothoe or Matuta; and Melicerta was known among the Greeks by the name of Palaimon, and among the Latins by that of Portunus. Some suppose that the Isthmian games were instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Melicerta.

MELINDA

Pages 543-543

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on the east <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated, according to some, between the third and fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude; though there is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disagreement among geographers as to its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is allowed by all, however, that the coasts are very dangerous; being full of rocks and shelves, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at some seasons very liable to tempests. The kingdom of Melinda is for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> rich and fertile; producing almost all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> except wheat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, both which are brought thither from Cambaya and other parts; and those who cannot purchase them make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of potatoes in their stead, which are here fine, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and in great plenty. They likewise abound with great variety of fruit trees, roots, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and other escalents, and with melons of exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. They have also great plenty of venison, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>, oxen, sheep, hens, geese, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, &c. and one breed of sheep whose tails weigh between 30 and 40 pounds. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is also called Melinda.

MELINUM

Pages 543-543

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> famous in the earliest ages of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, being the only <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> painters of antiquity; and, according to Pliny's account, one of the three colours with which alone they performed all their works. From the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> given of this earth it seems to be aluminous, tolerably pure, and in a state of minute <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>.

MELISSA

Pages 543-543

Baum, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the didynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order Verticillatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELISSUS OF SAMOS

Pages 543-543

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the son of Rhagines and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Parmenides; and lived about 440 B.C. He pretended that the universe is infinite, immoveable, and without a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>. Themistocles was among his pupils.

MELITE

Pages 543-543

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, struck out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Ionian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on account of the arrogance of the people, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> admitted in lieu of it. The situation is not specified.

MELITENSIS TERRA

Pages 543-543

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>: an earth of which there are two very different kinds; the one of which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>, the other a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a>. The latter is that known by medical authors under this name; the former is the Malta earth now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but both being brought from the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, are confusedly called by the same name. The Maltese marl, which is the terra Mediterranea of medical authors, is a loose, crumbly, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> earth, of an unequal and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> texture; and, when exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, soon falls into fine soft powder: but when preserved and dried, it becomes a loose, light <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a greyish <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>: it is rough to the touch, adheres firmly to the tongue, is very easily crumbled to powder between the fingers, and stains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it swells, and afterwards moulders away into a fine powder. It ferments very violently with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. Both kinds are found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Malta, and the latter has been much esteemed as a remedy against the bites of venomous animals. The other has supplied its place in the German shops; and is used there as a cordial, sudorific, and astringent.

MELITO

Pages 543-543

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a> in Lydia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century; remarkable for the apology he presented to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Aurelius, in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; on which Eusebius and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers bestow <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> praises: but that apology and all Melito's other works are lost.

MELITUS

Pages 543-543

a Greek orator and poet, the accuser of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. The Athenians, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Socrates, discovering the iniquity of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> they had passed against that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, put Melitus to death, 420 B.C.

MELLER

Pages 543-543
