a lake of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, 80 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; on which stands the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>.

MELLI

Pages 543-544

with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Mundingoes, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The country formerly called Melli, now chiefly inhabited by the Mundingoes, who still retain pretty much of the character ascribed to the people of Melli, lies to the south of the river <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>; on the west it borders on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Kabo; on the south it has Melli, properly so called, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> it from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; and on the east it extends to the kingdom of Gago. With a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of this country we are little acquainted, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to most of the inland territories of Africa; but towards the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> this country is a little better known. The first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> we meet with is Kachao, a Portuguese colony, situated on the river of St Domingo, which falls into the sea about 26 leagues below this town.—About 26 leagues above Kachao, on the same side of the river, is another trading town called Farini, where, in the months of October and November, there is some trade in wax and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>.—Bot is a village near the mouth of the river Gesves, where most of the traders buy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>; which is in great plenty there, and very good.—Gesves is a village on a river of the same name, on which the Portuguese have a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>. At Gesves one may trade yearly for 250 slaves, 80 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 100 quintals of wax, and as many of ivory. Near the mouth of the river of Gesves is a village called Kurballi, where there is a considerable trade for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; here are also some slaves and ivory. Rio Grande, or the Great River, runs about 10 or 12 leagues to the south of the river of Gesves. About 80 leagues from the mouth of it is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, who are considerable traders in ivory, rice, millet, and some slaves. They are called Anadons. Over against the mouth of Rio Grande is a cluster of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Bisogo Isles; the most considerable of which is Cassagat, being about six leagues <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very good, and produces millet, rice, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, besides <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and palm trees, and many others. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, with those of Carache, Canabae, and La Gallina, are the only ones where the Europeans may trade with some security. They trade, however, sometimes at the other islands, but they must be extremely cautious; and yet after all their precautions, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be robbed and murdered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they venture to go ashore. The river Nunho runs 16 leagues to the south of Rio Grande; it is very considerable, and comes from a vast distance inland. One may buy here 300 quintals of ivory and 100 slaves a-year. Rice grows here admirably well, and is very cheap. There are everywhere <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes which grow naturally; and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, which might turn to good account. The trade is carried on here from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> till August. In the river of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIERRA_LEONE">Sierra Leone</a>, the late <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> African <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of England had, in the year 1728, two islands; the one, called Tasso, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat island, near three leagues in circumference, on which the company's slaves had a good plantation; the rest of the island is covered with wood, among which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> cotton trees of an unaccountable size. The other island is Bense, whereon stood a regular fort. It was formerly the residence of one of the English chiefs.

MELLILLA

Pages 543-543

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Garret. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1469, but returned back to the Moors. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 9. N. Lat. 35. 20. MELILLOT. See TRIFOLIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELLITE

Pages 544-544
or HONEY-STONE, a mineral substance, composed of a peculiar acid and alumina. See MELLITE, MINERALOGY Index.

MELMOTH

Pages 544-544

WILLIAM, Esq. a learned member of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn, was born in 1666. In conjunction with Mr Peere Williams, Mr Melmoth was the publisher of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>'s Reports, under an order of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. He had once an intention of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> his own Reports; and a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> advertised them at the end of those of his coadjutor Peere Williams, as then actually preparing for the press. They have, however, not yet made their appearance. But the performance for which he justly deserves to be held in perpetual <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> is, "The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Importance of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>;" concerning which it may be mentioned to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that notwithstanding many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> editions had before been circulated, 42,000 copies of this useful treatise have been sold in the last 18 years. It is a somewhat singular circumstance, that the real author of this most admirable treatise should never before have been publicly known (it having been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> attributed to the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Egmont, and particularly by Mr Walpole in his Melo Catalogue); which is the more surprising, as the author is plainly pointed out in the following short character prefixed to the book itself: It may add <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, perhaps, to the reflections contained in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, to inform the reader, that the author's life was one uniform exemplar of those precepts which, with so generous a zeal, and such an elegant and affecting simplicity of style, he endeavours to recommend to general practice. He left others to contend for modes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and inflame themselves and the world with endless controversy: it was the wiser purpose of his more enabled aim, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> up to those clear rules of conduct which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> hath graciously prescribed. He possessed by temper every moral virtue; by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> every Christian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> that melted at every distress; a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> which not only thought no evil, but suspected none. He exercised his profession with a skill and integrity which nothing could equal but the disinterested <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> that animated his labours, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the amiable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> which accompanied all his virtues. He employed his industry, not to gratify his own desires; no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> indulged himself less; not to accumulate useless wealth; no man more disdained so unworthy a pursuit: it was for the decent advancement of his family, for the generous assistance of his friends, for the ready relief of the indigent. How often did he exert his distinguished abilities, yet refuse the reward of them, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the widow, the fatherless, and him that had none to help him! In a word, few have ever passed a more useful, nor one a more blameless life; and his whole time was employed either in doing good, or in meditating it. He died on the 6th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of April 1743, and lies buried under the cloister of Lincoln's Inn Chapel. MEM. PAT. OFF. MER. FIL. DIC." The son, by whom this character is drawn, is William Melmoth, Esq. the celebrated translator of Pliny and of Cicero's Letters; and author of those which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under the name of Sir Thomas Fitzosborne.

MELOCHIA

Pages 544-544

JEW'S MALLOW, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Columniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELODUNUM

Pages 544-544

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Cenones in Gallia Celtica, above Lutetia; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>.

MELODY

Pages 544-545

in music, a succession of sounds ranged in such a manner, according to the laws of rhythmus and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, that it may form a sentiment agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. Vocal melody is called singing; and that which is performed upon instruments may be termed symphonic melody. The idea of rhythmus necessarily enters into that of melody. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is not an air but in proportion as the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> are observed. The same succession of sounds is susceptible of as many different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, as many different kinds of melody, as the various ways by which its emphatic notes, and the quantities of those which intervene, may be diversified; and the change in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the notes alone, may <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> that very succession in such a manner that it cannot be known. Thus, melody in itself is nothing; it is the rhythmus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> measure which determines it, and there can be no air without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> then we <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> measure, measure from both, we cannot compare melody with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; for to the former it is essential, but not at all to the latter. Melody, according to the manner in which it is considered, has a relation to two different principles. When regarded only as agreeable to the proportions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and the rules of modulation, it has its principle in harmony; since it is a harmonical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, which exhibits the different gradations of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, the chords peculiar to each <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, and the laws of modulation, which are the sole elements that compose an air. According to this principle, the whole power of melody is limited to that of pleasing the ear by agreeable sounds, as the eye may be pleased with an agreeable assemblage of suitable colours. But when considered as an imitative art, by which we may affect the mind with various images, excite different emotions in the heart, inflame or soothe the passions; by which, in a word, we produce different effects upon our moral faculties, which are not to be effectuated by the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> alone, we must explore another principle for melody: for in our whole internal frame there appears to be no power upon which either harmony alone, or its necessary results, can <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a>, to affect us in such a manner. What then is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> principle? It is as much founded on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as the first; but, in order to discover its foundation in nature, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> require a more accurate though simpler observation, and a more exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> in the observer. This principle is the same which varies the tone of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, when we speak, according as we are interested in what we say, and according to the different emotions which we feel in expressing it. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> of languages which determines the melody of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; it is the accent which determines us to employ the emphasis of speaking while we sing, and to speak with more or less energy according as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is more or less accented. That language whose accents are the most sensible, ought to produce a more passionate and more lively melody; that which has little accentuation, or none at all, can only produce a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and languid melody, without character and without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. These are the true principles: in proportion as we depart from them, when we speak of the power of music upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart, we shall become unintelligible to ourselves and others: our words will be without meaning. If music does not impress the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> with images but by melody, if from thence it obtains its whole power, it must follow, that all musical sounds which are not pleasing by themselves alone, however agreeable to harmony they may be, is not an imitative music; and, being incapable, even with its most beautiful chords, either to present the images of things, or to excite the finer feelings, very soon cloy the ear, and leaves always the heart in cold indifference. It follows likewise, that notwithstanding the parts which harmony has introduced, and which the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of music so wantonly abuses, wherever two different melodies are heard at the same time, they counteract each other, and destroy the effects of both, however beautiful each may be when performed alone: from whence it may be judged with what degree of taste the French composers have introduced in their operas the miserable practice of accompanying one air with another, as well in singing, which is the native expression of pathos and sentiment, as in instrumental performances; which is the same thing as if whimsical orators should take it in their heads to recite two orations at the same time, that the elegance of each might derive more force from the other. So much for Rousseau. The translator, however, has reason to fear, that the causes by which national melody is diversified and characterized, are more profound and permanent than the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accentuation of language. This indeed may have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence in determining the nature of the rhythmus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of emphatic notes; but very little in regulating the nature of the emphasis and expression themselves. If Rousseau's principle be true in its full <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, he must of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> acknowledge, that an air which was never set or intended for words, however melodious, cannot be imitative; he must likewise confess, that what is imitative in one nation cannot be such in another: nor can it be denied, upon his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, that the recitative, which is formed upon the mode of speaking, is the most forcible of all melodies; which is absurd. His other observations are at once judicious and profound. Though it is impossible to exhibit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and variety of harmony by playing the same melody at the same time upon different keys, admitting those keys to form among themselves a perfect chord, which will of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> preserve all the subsequent notes in the same intervals; yet this perfect harmony would by no means be uniformly pleasing to the ear. We must therefore of necessity introduce less perfect chords to vary and increase the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and these chords in any complex system of music must of necessity produce dissonances. It then becomes the business of the composer to be careful that these discords may arise as naturally from, and return as naturally to perfect harmony as possible. All these causes must inevitably vary the melody of the different parts; but still, amidst all these difficulties, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> ought to be zealous in preserving the melody of each as homogeneous with the others as possible, that the result of the whole may be in some measure uniform. Otherwise, by counteracting each other, the parts will reciprocally destroy the effects one of another.

MELOE

Pages 545-545

a genus of insects of the order of coleoptera. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELON

Pages 545-545

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Cucumis, in the Linnean system. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">GARDENING</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> Melon. See ANGURIA, BOTANY Index.

MELOS

Pages 545-545

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> between <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, about 24 miles from Scylleum. It is about 60 miles in circumference, and of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. It enjoyed its independence for about 700 years before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This island was originally peopled by a Lacedaemonian colony, 1116 years before the Christian era. For this reason the inhabitants refused to join the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and the Athenians against the Peloponnesians. This refusal was severely punished. The Athenians took Melos, and put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> all such as were able to bear arms. The women and children were made slaves, and the island left desolate. An Athenian co-

MELOTHRIA

Pages 545-546

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Cucurbitaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELPOMENE

Pages 546-546

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Mnemosyne. She presided over tragedy. Horace has addressed the finest of his odes to her, as to the patroness of lyric <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. She was generally represented as a young woman with a serious countenance. Her garments were splendid; she wore a buskin, and held a dagger in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and in the other a sceptre and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.

MELROSE

Pages 546-546

a town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Selkirk, and on the confines of Tweedale, seated on the south side of the river Tweed; with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, now in ruins. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 32. N. Lat. 55. 32. This abbey was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. in 1136. He peopled it with Cistercians brought from Rivale abbey in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and dedicated it to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. At the Reformation James Douglas was appointed commendator, who took <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> much of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, in order to furnish materials for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to himself, which still remains, and is dated 1592. Nothing is left of the abbey excepting a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cloister wall elegantly carved; but the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> are of most uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> is excellent, and the figures generally in good preservation. A few years ago the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church was removed from the abbey, and a new church built at some distance from it. The rents of this abbey at the Reformation were, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> £144l. 15s. 4d. wheat, 19 ch. 9 bolls, bear 77 ch. 3 bolls, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> 14 ch., oats 47 ch. 1 boll, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> 105 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> 8 ch., capons 104, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> 520, peats 340 load. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> are one-third more than the standard. Alexander II. was buried beneath the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> altar, and it is also the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of the Douglasses and other potent families.—Its situation is extremely pleasant. MELT OF FISHES. In the melt of a living cod there are such numbers of those animalculæ said to be found in the semen of all <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> animals, that in a drop of its juice no larger than a grain of sand, there are contained more than 10,000 of them; and considering how many such quantities there are in the whole melt of one such fish, it is not incredible, that there are more animals in one melt of it than there are living men at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.

MELTING CONE

Pages 546-546

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a>, an hollow cone of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, into which melted metalline substances are thrown, in order to free them from their scorie. When a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is melted, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to rub the inside of the cone with grease; but when the quantity is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it contains any thing sulphureous, this caution of tallowing the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> is not sufficient. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the assayer has recourse to a lute reduced to thin pap with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which effectually prevents any injury to the cone.

MELTON MOWBRAY

Pages 546-546

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, 108 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> well-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; with a market on Tuesday, the most considerable for cattle of any in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. It is almost encompassed with a little river called the Melton Eyc, over which it has two fine bridges; and has a large handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with a free school. Here are frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races, and three <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year.

MELVIL

Pages 546-546

Sir James, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Scots family, being the third son of the laird of Kaeth, was born about the middle of the 16th century. He went to France very young, in the capacity of page to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, then married to the dauphin; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of her husband, followed her to Scotland, where he was made <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of her chamber, and admitted a privy counsellor. She employed him in her most important concerns, till her unhappy confinement in Lochleven, all which he discharged with the utmost fidelity; and, from his own accounts, there is reason to conclude, that, had she taken his advice, she might have avoided many of her misfortunes. When she was prisoner in England, she recommended him strongly to her son James; with whom he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in favour and employment until the death of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>: James would then have taken him to England; but Melvil, now grown old, was desirous of retiring from business, and in his retirement he drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his past <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his son. These Memoirs were accidentally found in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> castle in the year 1660, though nobody knew how they came to be deposited there; and were published in folio in 1683.

MEMBER

Pages 546-546

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, is applied to the parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. MEMBER is also used to denote some particular order or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in a state or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: thus we say, "member of a corporation, member of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>," &c.

MEMBERS

Pages 546-546

in Anatomy, the exterior parts, arising from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body of an animal like the boughs from the trunk of a tree.

MEMBRANE

Pages 546-546

Membrana, in Anatomy, a similar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an animal body; being a thin, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, expanded skin, formed of several sorts of fibres interwoven together, and serving to cover <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wrap up certain parts of the body. See Anatomy passim.

MEMEL

Pages 546-546
or Memmel; a town of Prussia, situated on the northern extremity of the Curische Haf, an inlet of the sea about 70 miles in length, which is here joined to the Baltic by a narrow strait.—It is an ill-built town, with narrow dirty streets; but remarkable for its extensive commerce, being provided with the finest harbour in the Baltic. In 1784, 996 ships, amongst which were 500 English, arrived here. The imports chiefly are, salt, iron, and salted herrings; the exports, which greatly exceed the imports, are amber, corn, hemp, flax, and particularly timber. An English consul resides here. The trade increased greatly on account of the high duties laid on the imports of Riga. F. Long. 21. 25. N. Lat. 55. 50.

MEMNON

Pages 546-549

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ethiopia, son of Tithonus and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>. He came with a body of 10,000 men to assist his uncle Priam, during the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He behaved with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> courage, and killed Antilochus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NESTOR">Nestor</a>'s son. The aged father challenged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">Memory</a>. When we remember with little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> no effort, it is called <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> simply, or memory, and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> memory*. When we endeavour to remember* Beattie's what does not immediately (and as it were) of itself Elements occur, it is called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> memory or recollection. A ready recollection of our knowledge, at the moment when we have occasion for it, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> of the greatest importance. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> possessed of it seldom fails to distinguish himself in whatever sort of business he may be engaged." It is indeed evident, that when the power of retention is weak, all attempts at eminence of knowledge must be vain; for "memory is the primary and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> power†, without which there could be no other intellectual operation. Judgment and ratiocination suppose something already known, and draw their decisions only from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Imagination selects <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> from the treasures of remembrance, and produces <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> only by varied <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>. We do not even form conjectures of distant, or anticipations of future events, but by concluding what is possible from what is past." Of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> so important, many rules have been given for the regulation and improvement; of which the first is, that he who wishes to have a clear and distinct remembrance, should be temperate with respect to eating, drinking, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. The memory depends very much upon the state of the brain; and therefore whatever is hurtful to the latter, must be prejudicial to the former. Too much sleep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> the brain, and too little overheats it; therefore either of these extremes must of course hurt the memory, and ought carefully to be avoided. Intemperance of all kinds, and excess of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, have the same ill effects; so that we rarely meet with an intemperate person whose memory is at once clear and tenacious. "The liveliest remembrance is not so vivid as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> that produced it‡; and ideas of memory do often, but not always, decay more and more, as the original sensation becomes more and more remote in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Those sensations and those thoughts have a chance to be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> remembered which are lively at first; and those are likely to be most lively which are most attended to, or which are accompanied with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or pain, with wonder, surprise, curiosity, merriment, and other lively passions. The art of memory, therefore, is little more than the art of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. What we wish to remember we should attend to, so as to understand it perfectly, fixing our view particularly upon its importance or singular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that it may raise within us some of the passions above mentioned. We should also disengage our minds from all other things, that we may attend more effectually to the object which we wish to remember. No man <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> read with much advantage who is not able at pleasure to evacuate his mind, or who brings not to his author an intellect defeated and pure, neither turbid with care, nor agitated with pleasure. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the repositories of thought are already full, what can they receive? If the mind is employed on the past or the future, the book will be held before the eyes in vain. "It is the practice of many readers, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the margin of their books the most important <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Moral Science." Memory, the strongest arguments, or the brightest sentiments. Thus they <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> their minds with superfluous attention, repress the vehemence of curiosity by useless deliberation, and by frequent interruption <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the current of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> or the chain of reason, and at last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the volume and forget the passages and the marks together. Others are firmly persuaded, that nothing is certainly remembered but what is transcribed; and they, therefore, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> weeks and months in transferring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quotations to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>-book. Yet, why any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a book which can be consulted at pleasure should be copied, we are not able to discover. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> has no closer correspondence with the memory than the eye. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> itself distracts the thoughts; and what is read twice, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> better remembered than what is transcribed. This method, therefore, consumes time, without assisting the memory. But to write an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of a good book may sometimes be a very profitable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. In general, when we would preserve the doctrines, sentiments, or facts, that occur in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, it will be prudent to lay the book aside, and put them in writing in our own words. This practice will give accuracy to our knowledge, accustom us to recollection, improve us in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and enable us so thoroughly to comprehend the thoughts of other men, as to make them in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> our own. "Our thoughts have for the most part a connection; so that the thought which is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now in the mind, depends partly upon that which went before, and partly serves to introduce that which follows.—Hence we remember best those things of which the parts are methodically disposed and mutually connected. A regular discourse makes a more lasting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon the hearer than a parcel of detached sentences, and gives to his rational powers a more salutary exercise: and this may show us the propriety of conducting our studies, and all our affairs, according to a regular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> or method. When this is not done, our thoughts and our business, especially if in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> complex, soon run into confusion." As the mind is not at all times equally disposed for the exercise of this faculty, such seasons should be made choice of as are most proper for it. The mind is seldom fit for attention presently after meals; and to call off the spirits at such times from their proper employment in digestion, is apt to cloud the brain, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Both the mind and body should be easy and undisturbed when we engage in this exercise, and therefore retirement is most fit for it: and the evening, just before we go to rest, is generally recommended as a very convenient season, both from the stillness of the night, and because the impressions will then have a longer time to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> before they come to be disturbed by the accession of others proceeding from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects; and to call over in the morning what has been committed to the memory overnight, must, for the same reason, be very serviceable. For, to review those ideas while they continue fresh upon the mind, and unmixed with any others, must necessarily imprint them more deeply. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers speak of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> memory, and lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> rules for attaining it. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a> the poet is said first to have discovered this, or at least to have given the occasion for it. The story they tell of him is this: Being once at a feast, he recited a poem which he had made in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the person who gave the entertainment. But having (as is usual in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>) made a large digression in praise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>; when he had repeated the whole poem, his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> would give him but half the sum he had promised, telling him he must get the other part from those deities who had an equal share in the honour of his performance. Immediately after, Simonides was told that two young men were without, and must needs speak with him. He had scarcely got out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, when the room where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was fell down, killed all the persons in it, and so mashed the bodies, that, when the rubbish was thrown off, they could not be known one from another: upon which Simonides recollecting the place where every one had sat, by that means distinguished them. Hence it came to be observed, that to fix a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of places in the mind in a certain order, was a help to the memory: As we find by experience, that, upon returning to places once familiar to us, we not only remember them, but likewise many things we both said and did in them. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> therefore of Simonides was afterwards improved into an art; and the nature of it is this: They bid you form in your mind the idea of some large place or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which you may divide into a great number of distinct parts, ranged and disposed in a certain order. These you are frequently to revolve in your thoughts, till you are able to run them over one after another without hesitation, beginning at any part. Then you are to impress upon your mind as many images of living creatures, or any other insensible objects which are most likely to affect you, and be soonest revived in your memory. These, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in shorthand, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, must stand to denote an equal number of other words, which cannot so easily be remembered. When therefore you have a number of things to commit to memory in a certain order, all that you have to do is, to place these images regularly in the several parts of your building. And thus they tell you, that, by going over several parts of the building, the images placed in them will be revived in the mind; which of course will give you the things or words themselves in the order you desire to remember them. The advantage of the images seems to be this; that, as they are more like to affect the imagination than the words for which they stand, they will for that reason be more easily remembered. Thus, for instance, if the image of a lion be made to signify strength, and this word strength be one of those I am to remember, and is placed in the porch; when, in going over the several parts of the building, I come to the porch, I shall sooner be reminded of that image than of the word strength. Of this artificial memory, both Cicero and Quintilian speak; but we know not of any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> orator that has ever made use of it. It seems indeed to have been a laborious way of improving the memory, if it serves that end at all, and fitter for assisting us to remember any number of unconnected words than a continual discourse, unless so far as the remembrance of one word may enable us to recollect more. It is, however, in allusion to it, that we still call the parts of a discourse places. But, doubtless, the most effectual way to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a good memory, is by constant and moderate exercise of it; for the memory, like other habits, is strengthened and improved by daily use. It is indeed hardly credible, to what a degree both active and passive remembrance may be improved by long practice. Scaliger reports of himself, that in his youth he could repeat above 100 verses, having once read them; and Berthecus declares, that he wrote his Comment upon Claudian without consulting the text. To hope, however, for such degrees of memory as these, would be equally vain as to hope for the strength of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, or the swiftness of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. "But there are clergymen who can get a sermon by heart* in two hours, though their memory, when they began to exercise it, was rather weak than strong: And pleaders, with other orators who speak in public and extempore, often discover, in calling instantly to mind all the knowledge necessary on the present occasion, and every thing of importance that may have been advanced in the course of a long debate, such powers of retention and recollection as, to the man who has never been obliged to exert himself in the same manner, are altogether astonishing. As habits, in order to be strong, must be formed in early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the memories of children should, therefore, be constantly exercised; but to oblige them to commit to memory what they do not understand, perverts their faculties, and gives them a dislike to learning." In a word, those who have most occasion for memory, as orators and public speakers, should not suffer it to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> idle, but constantly employ it in treasuring up and frequently reviving such things as may be of most importance to them; for by these means it will be more at their command, and they may place greater confidence in it upon any emergency." "Men complain of nothing more frequently than of deficient memory†: and indeed every one finds, that after all his efforts, many of the ideas which he desired to retain have slipped irretrievably away; that acquisitions of the mind are sometimes equally fugitive with the gifts of fortune; and that a short intermission of attention more certainly lessens knowledge than impairs an estate. To assist this weakness of our nature, many methods besides those which we have mentioned have been proposed; all of which may be justly suspected of being ineffectual: for no art of memory, however its effects may have been boasted or admired, has been ever adopted into general use; nor have those who possessed it appeared to excel others in readiness of recollection or multiplicity of attainments." The reader who is desirous to try the effect of these helps, may have recourse to a treatise entitled A new Method of Artificial Memory; but the true method of memory is attention and exercise.

MEMPHIS

Pages 549-550

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of the kings in the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; distant from the Delta to the south 15 miles, according to Pliny. Called also Moph, and Noph, in scripture. Though this city is now so completely ruined, that authors greatly disagree concerning its situation; yet Strabo informs us that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was the most magnificent in Egypt, next to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and there was an entire temple of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sacred ox was kept and worshipped. In the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was an apartment of the mother of the ox; a very magnificent temple of Vulcan; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> or space for fighting bulls; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> colossus in the middle of the city, which was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. There was likewise a temple of Venus, and a Scapium in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> place, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> heaps up hills of sand very dangerous to travellers; together with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sphinxes, the heads of some of them only being visible. In the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the city there were many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; and it contained a number of palaces, at that time in ruins. These buildings formerly stood upon an eminence: they lay along the side of the hill, stretching down to the lakes and groves, 40 stadia from the city. On a mountain in the neighbourhood, there was a great number of pyramids, with the sepulchres of the kings. From this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, Mr Bruce concludes that the celebrated capital of Egypt stood in the place where the villages of Metrahenny are now situated; in opposition to Dr Shaw's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, who thinks it was situated at Geeza or Gisa. M. Savary has also shown, that Gisa was not the situation of the ancient Memphis, which stood, he says, on the spot where the village of Memph now stands. Large heaps of rubbish are still to be seen there; but the Arabs have transported to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> the columns and remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which they have disposed, without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and without order, in their mosques and public buildings. This city extended as far as Saccara; and was almost wholly encompassed by lakes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which are still subsisting. It was necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> them to convey the dead to the sepulchres of their fathers. The tombs, hewn out of the rock, were closed up with stones of a proportionable size, and covered with sand. These bodies embalmed with so much care, preserved with so much respect, are torn from the monuments they repose in, and sold without decency to strangers by the inhabitants of Saccara. This place is called the plain of mummies. There too we find the well of the birds, into which one descends by means of a rope. It leads to subterraneous galleries, filled with earthen vases containing the sacred birds. They are rarely met with entire, because the Arabs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them in hopes of finding idols of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. They do not conduct travellers into the places where they have found more precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. They even <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> them up carefully, reserving to themselves some secret <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> by which they descend. In a journey into Egypt made by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Chaulnes, he advanced very far into these winding labyrinths, sometimes crawling, and sometimes scrambling on his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. Informed by Mr Edward Worley Montague, who has carefully visited Egypt, he arrived at one of those passages which had an opening shut up from without by branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> tree interwoven, and covered with sand. He remarked there some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> in relief, executed in the highest perfection. But the Arabs resisted every offer he made them to permit him to take drawings of them, or to mould them, in order to preserve their form. The duke de Chaulnes is of opinion that these hieroglyphics, sculptured with so much art that the objects they represent may be discovered at the first sight, might possibly furnish the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the others, whose contours are simply expressed, and form a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> of this unintelligible <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Several pyramids are distinguishable along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which bound Saccara on the west, the greatest part of which appear as lofty as those of Giza. See PYRAMIDS.

MENAGE

Pages 550-550

denotes a collection of animals; whence we have derived the word menagerie.

MENANDER

Pages 550-551

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in the same year with Epicurus, which was the third of the 109th Olympiad. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in introducing the new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, and refining an art which had been so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and licentious in former times, quickly spread his name over the world. Pliny informs us, that the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and Macedon gave a noble testimony of his merit, by sending ambassadors to invite him to their courts, and even fleets to bring him over; but that Menander was so much of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, as to prefer the free enjoyment of his studies to the promised favours of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. Of his works, which amounted to above 100 comedies, we have had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> loss, the originals being not only vanished, but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them, when copied by Terence, having unfortunately perished by shipwreck before they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Rome. Yet the four plays which Terence borrowed from him before that accident happened, are still preserved in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and it is chiefly from Terence that most people form their judgment of Menander, the fragments that remain of him not being sufficient to enable them to do it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> things of Menander; and we find the old masters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> recommending his works as the true patterns of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of public speaking. Quintilian declares, that a careful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Menander only, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> satisfy all the rules he has laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in his Institutions. It is in Menander that he would have his orator search for a copiousness of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, for a happy elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and especially for that universal genius which is able to accommodate itself to persons, things, and affections.—But Julius Caesar has left the loftiest as well as the justest praise of Menander's works, when he calls Terence only a Half-Menander. For while the virtues of the Latin poet are so deservedly admired, it is impossible we should raise a higher notion of excellency than to conceive the great original still shining with half its lustre unreflected, and preserving an equal part of its graces, above the power of the best copier in the world. Menander died in the 3d year of the 122d Olympiad. Menander Olympiad, as we are taught by the same old inscription from which we learn the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his birth. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, in Pausanias's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was to be seen at Athens, in the way from the Piraeus to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the honorary monument of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>. Quintilian, in his judgment of Afranius the Roman cenciarian, who imitated him, censures Menander's morals as much as he commends his writings; and his character, according to Suidas, is, that he was a very "mad fellow after women." Phaedrus has given him the gait and dress of a most affected fop: "Unguento delibutus, vestitu adluens, "Veniebat gressu delicatulo et languido." Lib. v. fab. 2.

MENANDRIANS

Pages 551-551

the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> branch of Gnostics; thus called from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, said by some, without sufficient foundation, to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Simon Magus, and himself a reputed magician. He taught, that no person could be saved, unless he were baptized in his name; and he conferred a peculiar sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, which would render those who received it immortal in the next world: exhibiting himself to the world, with the phrensy of a lunatic more than the founder of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, as a promised saviour. For it appears by the testimonies of Irenæus, Justin, and Tertullian, that he pretended to be one of the sons sent from the pleroma, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> regions, to succour the souls that lay groaning under bodily oppression and servitude; and to maintain them against the violence and stratagems of the demons that hold the reins of empire in this sublunary world. As this doctrine was built upon the same foundation with that of Simon Magus, the ancient writers looked upon him as the instructor of Menander. See Simonians.

MENASSEH BEN ISRAEL

Pages 551-551

a celebrated rabbi, born in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> about the year 1604, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Ben Israel, and followed his father into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Here he was educated by Rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Uziel, under whom he in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> made such progress in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue, that at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> he succeeded him in the synagogue of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years, and married Rachel of the family of the Abarbanels, whom the Jews imagine to be descended from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. He afterwards went to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Ephraim, a rich merchant, who had settled at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; by whose advice he entered into trade. Some time after, the hopes of a more agreeable settlement induced him to come into England, under the protectorship of Cromwell; who gave him a very favourable reception, and one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> entertained him at his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with several other learned divines. However, he soon after passed into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLEBURG">Middleburg</a> about the year 1657. The Jews at Amsterdam obtained his body, and interred it at their expense. He was of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; had a lively <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgment, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and all the virtues that can adorn private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote many works in Hebrew, Latin, Spanish, and English. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of those published in Latin, are, 1. His Commentarius; a learned and curious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in which he reconciles those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture which seem to contradict each other. 2. De resurrectione mortuorum. 3. De termino vitae. 4. Dissertatio de fragilitate humana, ex lapsu Adami, deque Divino in bono Menash operæ auxilio. 5. Spes Israel. Dr Thomas Pococke has written his life in English.

MENDELSON

Pages 551-551

MOSES, that is, Moses the son of Mendel, a Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and one of the most celebrated writers of Germany, died there in the year 1785 at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 57. His first attempt as an author was soon after 1767, by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; in which, besides other bold and unjustifiable opinions; he maintains, that the Jews have a revealed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> but not a revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; that opinions are not subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>; and that the only religion of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is that of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> by his Phædon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "Discourses on the Immateriality and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">Immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>," translated into the French 1773, 8vo; in which he unfolds this important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the great foundation of all morality, with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of an enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and the charms of an elegant writer. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this excellent work, he was styled the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> by some of the periodical writers; but he wanted the firmness and courage of the Grecian philosopher. His timidity, and even pusillanimity, defects too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> men, prevented him from being of any essential <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his nation; of which he might have become the benefactor by being the reformer. The pliancy of his character, his soft, modest, and obliging disposition, gained him the esteem alike of the superstitious and of the incredulous. After all, he could never procure admission to the Berlin <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, or to the conversation of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. At his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he received from his nation those honours which are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> paid to their first rabbins. Contrary to an imprudent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> prevalent among the Jews of burying their dead before sunset, his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> was delayed till 24 hours after he expired. Though Mendelshon was descended from a respectable family, he was very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. In early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he entered into a counting-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his own nation, wherein he greatly recommended himself by his capacity and integrity in business: But <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and literature soon became his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> occupation; and to the famous Lessing he was indebted for counsels which, without diverting his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> from those pursuits that were necessary to his subsistence, accelerated his progress in his literary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. Even after the death of his benefactor, Mendelshon retained for him the sincerest regard and the most lively <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. Notwithstanding the very strict regimen which he observed, he survived him only a few years; for his feeble frame and weak <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> were gradually and insensibly undermined by intense application to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>.

MENDEZ PINTO

Pages 551-552

FERDINAND, was born at Montemor-o-Velho in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and was at first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of making a fortune, he embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> in 1537. His vessel being taken by the Turks on his passage, he was carried to Mocká, and sold to a Greek renegade, and afterwards to a Jew, in whose possession he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till he was redeemed by the governor of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a>, a Portuguese fort. The governor procured him an opportunity of going out to India, agreeable to his first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. During a residence of twenty-one years in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he was witness to very important transactions, and experienced many singular adventures. He returned to Portugal in 1558, where he enjoyed the re- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> of his labours, after having been thirteen times a slave and sixteen times sold. A very curious account of his travels was written by himself, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, A.D. 1614, in folio. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was translated into French by Bernard Figueir, a Portuguese gentleman, and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1654, in 4to. It is written in a very interesting manner, and in a style more elegant than might have been expected from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was spent in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. It elucidates a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of particulars relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and manners of the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, Achem, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, &c. Many of his facts appeared fabulous, but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> has been since ascertained. M. de Surgi compiled an interesting history from the most singular facts in Mendez Pinto's relation, which he published in the Vicissitudes de la Fortune, Paris, 2 vols. 8vo.

MENDICANTS

Pages 552-553
or BEGGING FRIARS, several orders of religious in Popish countries, who having no settled revenues, are supported by the charitable contributions they receive from others. This sort of society began in the 13th century; and the members of it, by the tenor of their institution, were to remain entirely destitute of all fixed revenues and possessions; though in process of time their number became a heavy tax upon the people. Innocent III. was the first of the popes who perceived the necessity of instituting such an order; and accordingly he gave such monastic societies, as made a profession of poverty, the most distinguishing marks of his protection and favour. They were also encouraged and patronized by the succeeding pontiffs, when experience had demonstrated their public and extensive usefulness. But when it became generally known, that they had such a peculiar place in the esteem and protection of the rulers of the church, their number grew to such an enormous and unwieldy multitude, and swarmed so prodigiously in all the European provinces, that they became a burden, not only to the people, but to the church itself. The great inconvenience that arose from the excessive multiplication of the mendicant orders was remedied by Gregory X. in a general council, which he assembled at Lyons in 1272. For here all the religious orders that had sprung up after the council held at Rome in 1215, under the pontificate of Innocent III., were suppressed; and the extravagant multitude of mendicants, as Gregory called them, were reduced to a smaller number, and confined to the four following societies or denominations, viz. the Dominican, the Franciscan, the Carmelite, and the Augustinian or hermits of St. Augustine. As the pontiffs allowed these four mendicant orders the liberty of travelling wherever they thought proper, of conversing with persons of every rank, of instructing the youth and multitude wherever they went; and as those monks exhibited, in their outward appearance and manner of life, more striking marks of gravity and holiness than were observable in the other monastic societies, they arose all at once to the very summit of fame, and were regarded with the utmost esteem and veneration through all the countries of Europe. The enthusiastic attachment to these sanctimonious beggars went so far, that, as we learn from the most authentic records, several cities were divided or cantoned out into four parts, with a view to these four orders; the first part being assigned to the Dominicans, the second to the Franciscans, the third to the Carmelites, and the fourth to the Augustins. The people were unwilling to receive the sacraments from any other hands than those of the mendicants, to whose churches they crowded to perform their devotions, while living, and were extremely desirous to deposit there also their remains after death: nor did the influence and credit of the mendicants end here; for we find in the history of this and of the succeeding ages, that they were employed not only in spiritual matters, but also in temporal and political affairs of the greatest consequence, in composing the differences of princes, concluding treaties of peace, concerting alliances, presiding in cabinet councils, governing courts, levying taxes, and other occupations, not only remote from, but absolutely inconsistent with, the monastic character and profession. However, the power of the Dominicans and Franciscans greatly surpassed that of the other two orders: insomuch that these two orders were, before the Reformation, what the Jesuits have been since that happy and glorious period, the very soul of the hierarchy, the engines of the state, the secret springs of all the motions of the one and the other, and the authors and directors of every great and important event, both in the religious and political world. By very quick progression their pride and confidence arrived at such a pitch, that they had the presumption to declare publicly, that they had a divine impulse and commission to illustrate and maintain the religion of Jesus; they treated with the utmost insolence and contempt all the different orders of the priesthood; they affirmed, without a blush, that the true method of obtaining salvation was revealed to them alone; proclaimed, with ostentation, the superior efficacy and virtue of their indulgencies; and vaunted beyond measure their interest at the court of heaven, and their familiar connexions with the Supreme Being, the Virgin Mary, and the saints in glory. By these impious wiles, they so deluded and captivated the miserable, and blinded the multitude, that they would not entrust any other but the mendicants with the care of their souls. They retained their credit and influence to such a degree, towards the close of the 14th century, that great numbers of both sexes, some in health, others in a state of infirmity, and others at the point of death, earnestly desired to be admitted into the mendicant order, which they looked upon as a sure and infallible method of rendering heaven propitious. Many made it an essential part of their last wills, that their bodies after death should be wrapped in old ragged Dominican or Franciscan habits, and interred among the mendicants. For such was the barbarous superstition and wretched ignorance of this age, that people universally believed they should readily obtain mercy from Christ, at the day of judgment, if they appeared before his tribunal associated with the mendicant friars.
