About this time, however, they fell under an universal odium; but being resolutely protected against all opposition, whether open or secret, by the popes, who regarded them as their best friends and most effectual supports, they suffered little or nothing from the efforts of their numerous adversaries. In the 15th century, century, besides their arrogance, which was excessive, a quarrelsome and litigious spirit prevailed among them, and drew upon them justly the displeasure and indignation of many. By affording refuge at this time to the Beguins in their order, they became offensive to the bishops, and were hereby involved in difficulties and perplexities of various kinds. They lost their credit in the 16th century by their rustic impudence, their ridiculous superstitions, their ignorance, cruelty, and brutish manners. They discovered the most barbarous aversion to the arts and sciences, and expressed a like abhorrence of certain eminent and learned men, who endeavoured to open the paths of science to the pursuits of the studious youth, recommended the culture of the mind, and attacked the barbarism of the age in their writings and discourse. Their general character, together with other circumstances, concurred to render a reformation desirable, and to accomplish this happy event. Among the number of mendicants are also ranked the Capuchins, Recollets, Minims, and others, who are branches or derivations from the former. Buchanan tells us, the mendicants in Scotland, under an appearance of beggary, lived a very luxurious life; whence one wittily called them, not Mendicant but Manducant friars.

MENECRATES

Pages 553-553

a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, who flourished about 360 B.C. is famous for his skill in his profession, but much more for his vanity. He would always be followed by some of the patients he had cured, and with whom he previously stipulated that they should follow him wherever he went. One appeared with the attributes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, another with those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and others again with those of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Æsculapius; while he, clad in a purple robe, with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head, and a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, presented himself, to the admiration of the public, under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and travelled through different countries escorted by these counterfeit deities. He once wrote the following <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon: Menecrates Jupiter to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, greeting. Thou reignest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, and I in medicine; thou givest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to those who are in good <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, I restore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the sick; thy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> is composed of Macedonians; the gods themselves constitute mine." Philip answered him in a word, that he wished him restored to reason. Learning some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after that he was in Macedon, Philip sent for him, and invited him to an entertainment. Menecrates and his companions were placed on rich and lofty couches; before which was an altar, covered with the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>; and, whilst an excellent repast was served up to the other guests, perfumes and libations only were offered to these new gods, who, unable to endure the affront, hastily left the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, in which they never more made their appearance.

MENEDEMUS

Pages 553-553

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Erythreum, was the son of Calisthenes, and one of Phedo's followers. He was in the greatest esteem, and enjoyed several important posts, in his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He several times defended Erythreum with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bravery, and died of grief when Antigonus became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it. A person one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> saying to him, "It is a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to have what we desire," he replied: "It is a much greater to desire nothing but what we have." He flourished about 300 B.C.

MENELAUS

Pages 553-553

a mathematician in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, wrote three books on the Sphere, which have been published by Father Mersenne.

MENES

Pages 553-553

born at This, a town of Thebais in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, was the founder of the Egyptian empire. He had three sons, viz. Athotis, who ruled after him, at This and Thebes; Curudes, who in Lower Egypt founded the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, which afterward was the kingdom of Diospoli; and Necherophes, who reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>. It is thought this Menes reigned 117 years after the birth of Phaleg, son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, which was the very year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the people throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> Memphis, he stopped the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> near it, by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of a causeway 100 furlongs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and caused it to run through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>.

MENIALS

Pages 553-553
domestic or household servants, who live under their lord or master's roof.

MENINGES

Pages 553-553
or Menyges, in Anatomy, a name given to the dura and pia mater of the brain. See Anatomy, No. 129.

MENINX

Pages 553-553

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean, to the west of the Syrtis <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. Supposed by Strabo and Polybius to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTOPHAGI">Lotophagi</a>; and hence <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> and Eratosthenes denominate the island Lotophagitis, with a cognominal town Meninx. It was the country of Vibiusr <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and of Volusianus. Now called Gerhi and Zarbi.

MENIPPEAN

Pages 553-553

a kind of satire consisting of prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> intermixed. It is thus called from Menippus a cynic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> who delighted in composing satirical letters, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of him, Varro also wrote satires under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Satire Menippae: whence this sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is also denominated Varronian satire. Among the moderns there is a famous piece under this title first published in 1594, against the chiefs of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, called also the Catholicon of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is esteemed a masterpiece for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

MENIPPUS

Pages 553-553

a cynic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of Phoenicia. He was originally a slave, but obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> with a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and became one of the greatest usurers at Thebes. He grew so desperate from the continual reproaches and insults to which he was daily exposed on account of his meanness, that he destroyed himself. He wrote 13 books of satires, which have been lost.

MENISCUS

Pages 553-553

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, a glass <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENS">lens</a>, concave on one side and convex on the other; sometimes also called lunula. See Optics.

MENISPERMUM

Pages 553-553

Moonseed, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioica class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th order, Sarmentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MENNITH

Pages 553-555
or Minnith, Judges xi. 33. a town near Mennonites near Heshbon (Jerome), in Arabia Petraea; in a district named Eccepolis or twenty-towns, (Cellarius). There is also a Minnith mentioned Ezekiel xxvii. as being in a good wheat country: but whether the same with the foregoing is uncertain; though some think that the first Minnith lay in the country of Ammon, (Wells). Mennonites, a sect in the United Provinces, in most respects the same with those in other places called Anabaptists. They had their rise in 1536, when Menno Simon, a native of Friesland, who had been a Romish priest, and a notorious profligate, resigned his rank and office in the Romish church, and publicly embraced the communion of the Anabaptists. Menno was born at Witmarsum, a village in the neighbourhood of Bolswerp in Friesland, in the year 1505, and died in 1561 in the duchy of Holstein, at the country seat of a certain nobleman not far from the city of Oldesloe, who, moved with compassion by a view of the perils to which Menno was exposed, and the snares that were daily laid for his ruin, took him with certain of his associates into his protection, and gave him an asylum. The writings of Menno, which are almost all composed in the Dutch language, were published in folio at Amsterdam in the year 1651. About the year 1637, Menno was earnestly solicited by many of the sect with which he connected himself, to assume among them the rank and functions of a public teacher; and as he looked upon the persons who made this proposal to be exempt from the fanatical phrensy of their brethren at Munster, (though according to other accounts they were originally of the same stamp, only rendered somewhat wiser by their sufferings), he yielded to their entreaties. From this period to the end of his life, he travelled from one country to another with his wife and children, exercising his ministry, under pressures and calamities of various kinds, that succeeded each other without interruption, and constantly exposed to the danger of falling a victim to the severity of the laws. East and West Friesland, together with the province of Groningen, were first visited by this zealous apostle of the Anabaptists; from whence he directed his course into Holland, Guelderland, Brabant, and Westphalia, continued it through the German provinces that lie on the coasts of the Baltic sea, and penetrated as far as Livonia. In all these places his ministerial labours were attended with remarkable success, and added to his sect a prodigious number of followers. Hence he is deservedly considered as the common chief of almost all the Anabaptists, and the parent of the sect that still subsists under that denomination. Menno was a man of genius, undirected by a very sound judgment: he possessed a natural and persuasive eloquence, and such a degree of learning as made him pass for an oracle in the estimation of the multitude. He appears, moreover, to have been a man of probity, of a meek and tractable spirit, gentle in his manners, pliable and obsequious in his commerce with persons of all ranks and characters, and extremely zealous in promoting practical religion and virtue, which he recommended by his example as well as by his precepts. The plan of doctrine and discipline drawn up by Menno was of a much more mild and moderate nature than that of the furious and fanatical Anabaptists, whose tumultuous proceedings have been recited under that article, but somewhat more severe, though more clear and consistent than the doctrine of the wiser branches of that sect, who aimed at nothing more than the restoration of the Christian church to its primitive purity. Accordingly he condemned the plan of ecclesiastical discipline that was founded on the prospect of a new kingdom, to be miraculously established by Jesus Christ on the ruins of civil government and the destruction of human rulers, and which had been the fatal and pestilent source of such dreadful commotions, such execrable rebellions, and such enormous crimes. He declared publicly his dislike of that doctrine, which pointed out the approach of a marvellous reformation in the church by the means of a new and extraordinary effusion of the Holy Spirit. He expressed his abhorrence of the licentious tenets, which several of the Anabaptists had maintained, with respect to the lawfulness of polygamy and divorce; and finally, considered as unworthy of toleration those fanatics who were of opinion that the Holy Ghost continued to descend into the minds of many chosen believers, in an extraordinary manner as he did at the first establishment of the Christian church, and that he testified this peculiar presence to several of the faithful by miracles, predictions, dreams and visions of various kinds. He retained indeed the doctrines commonly received among the Anabaptists, in relation to the baptism of infants, the millennium, or 1000 years reign of Christ upon earth, the exclusion of magistrates from the Christian church, the abolition of war, and the prohibition of oaths enjoined by our Saviour, and the vanity as well as the pernicious effects of human science. But while Menno retained these doctrines in a general sense, he explained and modified them in such a manner as made them resemble the religious tenets that were universally received in the Protestant churches; and this rendered them agreeable to many, and made them appear inoffensive even to numbers who had no inclination to embrace them. It however so happened, that the nature of the doctrines considered in themselves, the eloquence of Menno which set them off to such advantage, and the circumstances of the times, gave a high degree of credit to the religious system of this famous teacher among the Anabaptists, so that it made a rapid progress in that sect. And thus it was in consequence of the ministry of Menno, that the different sorts of Anabaptists agreed together in excluding from their communion the fanatics that dishonoured it, and in renouncing all tenets that were detrimental to the authority of civil government, and by an unexpected coalition formed themselves into one community. Though the Mennonites usually pass for a sect of Anabaptists, yet M. Herman Schyn, a Mennonite minister, who has published their history and apology, maintains, that they are not Anabaptists either in principle or by origin. However, nothing can be more certain than this fact, viz. that the first Mennonite congregations were composed of the different sorts of Anabaptists, of those who had been always inoffensive and upright, and of those who, before their conversion by the ministry of Menno, had been seditious fanatics: besides, it is alleged that the Mennonites MENNONITES do actually retain, at this day, some of those opinions and doctrines, which led the sedulous and turbulent Anabaptists of old to the commission of so many and such enormous crimes: such particularly is the doctrine concerning the nature of Christ's kingdom, or of the church of the New Testament, though modified in such a manner as to have lost its noxious qualities, and to be no longer pernicious in its influence. The Mennonites are subdivided into several sects; whereof the two principal are the Flemings or Flemingsians, and the Waterlandians. The opinions, says Mosheim, that are held in common by the Mennonites, seem to be all derived from this fundamental principle, that the kingdom which Christ established upon earth is a visible church or community, into which the holy and just alone are to be admitted, and which is consequently exempt from all those constitutions and rules of discipline that have been invented by human wisdom, for the correction and reformation of the wicked. This principle, indeed, was avowed by the ancient Mennonites, but it is now almost wholly renounced: nevertheless, from this ancient doctrine, many of the religious opinions that distinguish the Mennonites from all other Christian communities, seem to be derived: in consequence of this doctrine, they admit none to the sacrament of baptism but persons that are come to the full use of their reason; they neither admit civil rulers into their communion, nor allow any of their members to perform the functions of magistracy; they deny the lawfulness of repelling force by force, and consider war, in all its shapes, as unchristian and unjust; they entertain the utmost aversion to the execution of justice, and more especially to capital punishments; and they also refuse to confirm their testimony by an oath. The particular sentiments that divided the more considerable societies of the Mennonites are the following: The rigid Mennonites, called the Flemingsians, maintain with various degrees of rigour, the opinions of their founder Menno, as to the human nature of Christ, alleging that it was produced in the womb of the Virgin by the creating power of the Holy Ghost; the obligation that binds us to wash the feet of strangers, in consequence of our Saviour's command; the necessity of excommunicating and avoiding, as one would do the plague, not only avowed sinners, but also all those who depart, even in some light instances pertaining to dress, &c., from the simplicity of their ancestors; the contempt due to human learning, and other matters of less moment. However this austere system declines, and the rigid Mennonites are gradually approaching towards the opinions and discipline of the more moderate or Waterlandians. The first settlement of the Mennonites, in the United Provinces, was granted them by William prince of Orange, towards the close of the 16th century; but it was not before the following century that their liberty and tranquillity were fixed upon solid foundations, when, by a confession of faith published in the year 1626, they cleared themselves from the imputations of those pernicious and detestable errors that had been laid to their charge. In order to appease their intestine discords, a considerable part of the Anabaptists of Flanders, Germany, and Friseland, concluded their debates in a conference held at Amsterdam, in the year 1630, and entered into the bonds of fraternal communion, each reserving to themselves a liberty of retaining certain opinions. This association was renewed and confirmed by new resolutions, in the year 1649; in consequence of which, the rigorous laws of Menno and his successors were, in various respects, mitigated and corrected.

MENOLOGY

Pages 555-555

MENOLOGIUM, (from μήν, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and λόγος, discourse), is much the same as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">martyrology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, in the Latin. The Greek menologium is divided into the several months in the year; and contains an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the lives of the saints, with a bare enumeration of the names of such whose lives were never written. The Greeks have various menologies; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> tax them with inserting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> heresies in their menologies as saints.—Baillet treats of them at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>.

MENSA

Pages 555-555

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> books, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> that includes in it all patrimony, and necessaries for livelihood.

MENSALS

Pages 555-555

MENSALIA, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, such livings as were formerly united to the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and hence called mensal benefices. See the article BENEFICE.

MENSES

Pages 555-555

CATAMENIA, in Medicine, the monthly evacuations from the uterus of women not with child <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not giving suck. They are so called from mensis "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>," the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> wherein they return. They are also called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, courses, &c. By the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> a woman was unclean while the menstrual blood flowed; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who touched her, and the moveables she had touched, were declared unclean.—Lev. xv. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">MIDWIFERY</a> and MEDICINE.

MENSORES

Pages 555-555

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, were harbingers, whose business it was to go before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and fix upon lodgings for him when he travelled into any of the provinces. They also marked out encampments, and assigned every regiment its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>. Mensores were also <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-surveyors, architects, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appraisers of houses and public buildings. The distributors of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were called mensores frumentarii. And mensores was also an appellation given to servants who waited at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>.

MENSTRUAL

Pages 574-574
or Menstruous, in Physiology, is applied to the blood which flows from women in their ordinary monthly purgations. See Midwifery and Medicine Index.

MENSTRUM

Pages 574-574

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, any body which in a fluid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subtilized state is capable of interposing its small parts betwixt the small parts of other bodies, so as to divide them subtly, and form a new uniform <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the two.

MENSURATION

Pages 573-574

ends, and the sum of these two gives after proper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> \((39B^2 + 26BH + 25H^2) \times \frac{L_n}{90}\), nearly, for the content in inches. And the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> \(n\) <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> \(\frac{7854}{90}\) being divided by 231 gives \(\frac{0.0034}{9}\) the multiplier for wine gallons; and since 231 is to 282 as 9 to 11 nearly, \(\frac{0.0034}{11}\) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the multiplier for ale gallons as in the rule. Ex. Suppose a cask to have the same dimensions as in the four former rules; required the content? Here \((39 \times 32^2 + 26 \times 32 \times 24 + 25 \times 24^2) \times 40 \times \frac{0.0034}{11} = 1010.53\), which being divided by 9 and by 11 we obtain 112.3 wine gallons or 91.9 ale gallons for the content required.

MENTHA

Pages 574-574

Mint, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MENTOR

Pages 574-574

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a faithful friend of Ulysses; a son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sidonia, who revolted against <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Osimus, and afterwards was restored to favour by his treachery to his allies, &c. Diod. 16. An excellent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> in polishing cups and engraving <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on them. Plin. 33. c. 11.—Mart. 9. ep. 65. v. 16.

MENTZ

Pages 580-581

a considerable town of Germany, in the circle of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of the same name, is situated on the Rhine near its confluence with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, 15 west of Francfort, and 75 east of Triers, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 20' N. Lat. 40° 51'. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> claims a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>: (see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Printing). Here is a very beautiful quay along the river, defended by several works well fortified with cannon. That <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city which extends towards the river is most populous. The best vineyards for Rhenish wine being in this neighbourhood, Mentz has a flourishing trade in that commodity more particularly; and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is the brisker, by reason that all the merchandise which passes up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Rhine stops in its harbour to change bottoms. The northern part of the city, in which the archbishop resides, is full of very regular buildings. Here are three regular streets, called the Bleichen, which run <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other from the banks of the Rhine to 600 yards within the city, and are cut almost regularly by very pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> streets. The archbishop's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> has a most commanding view of these streets, the Rhine, and the Rhinegau. There are also some good buildings in the old part of the city. The market of beasts is extremely well worth seeing; and you here and there meet with other agreeable spots. The market in the middle of the town, though not regular, is one of the prettiest places in Germany. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is well worth notice. It is an immense <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> old Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the spire of which was struck with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> many years ago, and entirely laid in ashes. As it contained much wood, it burned 14 hours before it was entirely consumed. To prevent these accidents for the future, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> had the present one built to the same height in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, an undertaking which cost them 40,000 guilders <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 4000l. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pity (Baron Riesbeck observes) that it is overloaded with small ornaments: and a still greater, that this wonderful edifice is so choked up with shops and houses as to be hardly more than half visible. As, however, houses and shops are very dear in this part of the town, one cannot be very angry with the chapter for choosing rather to make the most of its ground, than to show off the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to the best advantage. The rent of a shop and a single room to live in is 150 guilders or 15l. per annum in this part of the town. There is hardly another church in Germany of the height and length of this cathedral; and the inside of it is decorated with several magnificent monuments of princes and other great personages. Besides the cathedral, the city of Mentz contains several other churches in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> style, very well worth seeing. St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, and the Jesuits church, though both too much loaded with ornament, are among this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The church of the Augustins, of which the inhabitants of Mentz are so proud, is a masterpiece of bad <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but that of Ignatius, though little is said about it, would be a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the antique, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> here likewise there had not been too much ornament lavished. Upon the whole, the palaces of the noblesse want that noble simplicity which alone constitutes true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and magnificence. In another century the externals of the city <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be quite changed. The late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> built a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, and the present has a taste for the same sort of expense. The monks and governors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> also have been forced to rebuild their houses; so that when a few more streets are made broader and straighter, the whole will have no bad appearance. The inhabitants, who together with the garrison amount to 30,000, are a good kind of people, and, like all the catholics of Germany, make great account of a good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Their faces are interesting, and they are not deficient either in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. There are few cities in Germany besides <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> which contain so rich and numerous a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> as this does: there are some houses here which have estates of 100,000 guilders, or 10,000l. a-year. The counts of Bassenheim, Schonborn, Stadion, Ingelheim, Elz, Ostein, and Walderdorf, and the lords of Dahlberg, Breitenbach, with some others, have incomes of from 30,000 to 100,000 guilders. Sixteen or eighteen houses have from 15,000 to 30,000 guilders annual revenue. The nobility of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> are said to be some of the oldest and most untainted in Germany. There are amongst them many persons of extraordinary merit, who join uncommon knowledge to all the duties of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Upon the whole, they are far superior to the greater part of the German nobility. Their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, however, is still too stiff. The first minister of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> was refused admittance into their assemblies for not being sufficiently noble; and they think they degrade themselves by keeping <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with bourgeois. The clergy of this place are the richest in Germany. A canonry brings in 3500 Rhenish guilders in a moderate year. The canonry of the provost brings him in 40,000 guilders a-year; and each of the deaneries is worth 2600 guilders. The income of the chapter altogether amounts to 300,000 guilders. Though it is forbidden by the canons of the church for any one to have more than a single prebend, there is not an ecclesiastic in this place who has not three or four; so that there is hardly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> amongst them who has not at least 8000 guilders a-year. The last provost, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Elz, had prebends enough to procure him an income of 75,000 guilders. Exclusive of the cathedral, there are several other choirs in which the canonries bring in from 1200 to 1500 guilders a-year. To give an idea of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the monasteries of this place, Baron Riesbeck informs us, that at the destruction of the Jesuits, their wine, which was reckoned to sell extremely cheap, produced 120,000 rixdollars. A little while ago the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> abolished one Carthusian convent and two nunneries, in the holy cellars of which there was found wine for at least 500,000 rixdollars. "Notwithstanding this great wealth (continues our author), there is not a more regular clergy in all Germany. There is no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, in which the regulations made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> have been more strictly adhered to than they have here; the archbishops having made a particular point of it both at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the reformation and ever since. One thing which greatly contributes to keep up <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> is the not suffering any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> to remain in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> who has not fixed and stated duties, and a revenue annexed to them. Most of the irregularities in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and other countries, arise from abbés who are obliged to subsist by their daily industry and any masses which they can pick up. These creatures are entirely unknown here. The theological tenets of this court are also much purer than those of any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> prince in Germany. I was pleased to see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, especially in the country. I was told that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of it was not forbidden in any part of the diocese; only persons were enjoined not to read it through, without the advice of their confessors. For a long time <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> has been hunted through its utmost recesses; and though it is not quite possible to get entirely clear of pilgrimages and wonder-working images, you will meet with no priest bold enough to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> or to preach such nonsense as we hear in the pulpits of other German churches." Though the trade of this place has been constantly on the increase for these 18 or 20 years past, yet it is by no means what it ought to be from the situation and other advantages. The persons here who call themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and who make any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, are in fact only brokers. A few toy-shops, five or six druggists, and four or five manufacturers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, are all that can possibly be called traders. There is not a banker in the whole town; and yet this country enjoys the staple privilege, and commands by means of the Maine, Necker, and Rhine, all the exports and imports of Alsatia, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>, Franconia, and a part of Suabia and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. The port too is constantly filled with ships, but few of them contain any merchandise belonging to the inhabitants of the place. The French took it by surprise in October 1792; it surrendered to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> in 1793; but the French again got possession of it in October 1797; and it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> united to the French empire till 1814, when it passed into the hands of the allies. It now forms a part of Germany.

MENTZEL

Pages 581-581

CHRISTIAN, born at Frustenwall in the Mittel-mark, is celebrated for his skill in medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, in pursuit of which he travelled through many countries. He had correspondents in the most distant parts of the world. He died A.D. 1701 about the 79th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was a member of the academy des Curieux de la <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>. His works are, 1. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> nominum plantarum, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in folio, 1696; and reprinted with additions in 1715, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Lexicon plantarum polyglottum universale. 2. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in German, printed at Berlin 1696, in 4to. The following <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> are preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> library at Berlin. 1. Sur l'Histoire Naturelle du Brasil, in four volumes folio. 2. Sur les Fleurs et les Plantes du Japon, with coloured plates, two vols folio.

MENUS

Pages 581-581

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river of Germany; now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, rising in Franconia, and running from east to west into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>.

MENUTHIAS

Pages 581-581

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the promontory Prasum of Ethiopia beyond <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. Some take it to be Madagascar, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the island St Lawrence. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to be Zanzibar; Madagascar being at a greater distance from the continent than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> ever sailed to, whereas Menuthias was nearer: yet though Zanzibar be nearer the continent, it is however nearer the equator than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s Menuthias, placed in south latitude 12° degrees.

MENYANTHES

Pages 581-581

Marsh-trefoil, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bogbean; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 21st order, Precise. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MENZIKOFF

Pages 581-582

ALEXANDER, was originally an apprentice to a pastry-cook near the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>; but by a fortunate circumstance was drawn from that situation in early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. Having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of several languages, and being formed for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and for business, he first rendered himself agreeable, and afterwards became necessary to his master. He assisted Peter in all his projects; and was rewarded for his services with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Ingria, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general. He signalized himself in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> in 1708 and 1709; but in 1713 he was accused of embezzling the public <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and fined in 300,000 crowns. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> remitted the fine; and having restored him to favour, gave him the command of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the Ukraine in 1719, and sent him as his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> into Poland in 1722. Constantly employed about the means of preserving his influence after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his master, who was then evidently on the decline, Menzikoff discovered the person to whom the czar intended to leave the succession. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was highly offended, and his penetration cost him the principality of Plescoff. Under the czarina Catherine, however, he was higher in favour than ever; because, on the death of the czar in 1725, he was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in bringing different parties in Russia to agree to her succession. This princess was not ungrateful. In appointing her son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Peter II. to be her successor, she commanded him to marry the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Menzikoff, and gave the czar's sister to his son. The parties were actually betrothed: and Menzikoff was made <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cozel and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> to the czar. But this summit of elevation was the prelude to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The Dolgoroukis, favourites of the czar, had influence enough to procure his banishment, together with that of his family, to one of his own estates at the distance of 250 leagues from Moscow. He had the imprudence to leave the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> with the splendor and magnificence of a governor going to take possession of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. His enemies took advantage of this circumstance to inflame the indignation of the czar. At some distance from Moscow he was overtaken by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The officer who commanded them made him alight from his chariot, which he sent back to Moscow; and placed him and his whole family in covered waggons, to be conducted into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of peasants. When he arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his destination, he was presented with cows and sheep big with young, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, without knowing from whom he received the favour. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was a simple cottage; and his employment was to cultivate the ground, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to superintend its cultivation. New causes of sorrow were added to the severities of exile. His wife died in the journey; he had the misfortune to lose Menzikoff one of his daughters by the smallpox; and his other two children were seized with the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, but recovered. He sunk under his misfortunes, November 2, 1729; and was buried beside his daughter, in a little chapel which he had built. His misfortunes had inspired him with sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, which, amid the splendor of his former situation, he had altogether neglected. His two surviving children enjoyed greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> after the death of their father. The officer permitted them to attend public worship on Sundays by turns. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when his daughter was returning from the village, she heard herself accosted by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> from the window of a cottage, and, to her great surprise, recognised in this peasant the persecutor of her family, Dolgorouki; who, in his turn, had fallen a sacrifice to the intrigues of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. She communicated this intelligence to her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who could not behold, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, this new instance of the vanity and instability of honours and power. Young Menzikoff and his sister were soon after recalled to Moscow by the czarina <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a>; and left Dolgorouki in possession of their cottage. He was made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the guards, and received the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his father's possessions. His sister was appointed maid of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the empress, and afterwards married to great advantage.

MENZINI

Pages 582-582

BENEDICT, a celebrated Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, was professor of eloquence at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> Della Sapienza at Rome, where he died in 1704. He wrote, 1. The art of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. 2. Satires, elegies, hymns, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah. 3. Academia Tuscanana, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose, which passes for his masterpiece.

MEOTIS

Pages 582-582
or PALUS MEOTIS, a sea of Turkey, which divides Europe from Asia; extending from Crim Tartary to the mouth of the river Don or Tanaïs.

MEPHITIC

Pages 582-582

a name expressing any kind of noxious vapour; but generally applied to that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vapour called fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. See CARBONIC ACID, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEPHITIS FANUM

Pages 582-582

a temple erected to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Mephitis, near Lacus Amsacti; who was worshipped also at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a>. Figuratively, Mephitis denotes a noisome <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pestilential exhalation, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>).

MEQUINEZ

Pages 582-582
or MIQUINEZ, the northern capital of the Morocco empire, stands at the extremity of the province of Beni Hassen, 80 leagues north from the city of Morocco (which is the southern imperial city), and 20 to the east of Salice and the ocean. Maknassa, its founder, built it first at the bottom of a valley; but Muley Ismael extended it considerably over the plain that lies to the west of the valley. It is surrounded with well cultivated fields and hills, adorned with gardens and olive plantations, and abundantly watered with rivulets. Accordingly, fruits and kitchen stuffs thrive here exceedingly, and even the superior urbanity of the inhabitants announces the temperature of the climate. The winter indeed is very inconvenient, on account of the dirtiness of the town, the streets not being paved, and the soil being slimy. Mequinez is surrounded with walls; the palace itself is fortified with two bastions, on which formerly some small guns were mounted. Muley Ismael, and Muley Abdallah, often in this city resisted the efforts of the Brebes, the sworn enemies of their tyranny. To the west are seen some walls of circumvallation, six feet in height, which were probably mere intrenchments for the infantry; the attacks of the Brebes being only sudden and momentary inroads, which did not require a long defence. There is at Mequinez, as well as at Morocco, a walled and guarded suburb for the Jews. The houses are neater here than at Morocco. The Jews here are more numerous; and they can turn their industry to greater account, because the Moors in this city are more polished, and (being nearer to Europe) more visited, than those in the southern parts. Near the Jewry, there is another enclosed and separate quarter, called the Negro town. It was built by Muley Ismael, for the accommodation of those black families which composed his soldiery. This town is now uninhabited, as are all those destined for the same use through the rest of the empire. At the south-east extremity of the city stands the palace of the emperor, which was built by Muley Ismael. The space occupied by this palace is very great; it includes several gardens, elegantly disposed, and well watered. There is a large garden in the centre, surrounded by a vast and pretty regular gallery resting on columns, which communicates with the apartments. Those of the women are very spacious, and have a communication with a large chamber which looks into the garden. As you pass from one apartment to another, you find at intervals regular courts paved with square pieces of black and white marble; in the middle of these courts is a marble basin, from the centre of which rises a jet d'eau, and the water falls down into this basin. These fountains are numerous in the palace; they are useful for domestic purposes, and they serve for the ablutions, which the scruples of the Mahometans have exceedingly multiplied. The palaces of the Moorish kings are large, because they are composed only of one range of apartments; these are long and narrow, from 18 to 20 feet high; they have few ornaments, and receive the light by two large folding doors, which are opened more or less as occasion requires. The rooms are always lighted from a square court in the centre, which is generally encompassed with a colonnade. The Moors here are more courteous than those in the southern parts; they are civil to strangers, and invite them into their gardens, which are very neat. The women in this part of the empire are beautiful; they have a fair complexion, with fine black eyes, and white teeth. I have sometimes seen them taking the air on the terraces; they do not hide themselves from Europeans, but retire very quickly on the appearance of a Moor.

MERA-DE-ASTA

Pages 582-582

formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, seated on the river Guadaleta, between Arcos and Xeres de la Frontera; but now only a large heap of ruins. Here the Arabs conquered Roderick the last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, and by that victory became masters of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in 713.

MERCATOR

Pages 582-583

GERARD, one of the most celebrated geographers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at Ruremonde in 1512. He applied himself with such industry to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, that he is said to have frequently forget to eat and drink. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. had a particular esteem for him, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Juliers made him his cosmographer. He Mercator composed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, some geographical tables, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATLAS">atlas</a>, &c., engraving and colouring the maps himself. He died in 1594. His method of laying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> is still used, and bears the name of Mercator's charts. Mercator, Nicholas, an eminent mathematician in the 17th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>; and came to England about the time of the restoration, where he lived many years. He was fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and endeavoured to reduce astrology to rational principles, as appeared from a MS. of his in the possession of William Jones, Esq. He published several works, particularly Cosmographia. He gave the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a> by an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>; which was the first appearance in the learned world of a series of this sort drawn from the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the curve, and that in a manner very new and abstracted. Mercator's Sailing, that performed by Mercator's chart. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>.

MERCATORUM FESTUM

Pages 583-583

was a festival kept by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> on the 15th of May, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who presided over merchandise. A sow was sacrificed on the occasion, and the people present sprinkled themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fetched from the fountain called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> Mercurii; the whole concluding with prayers to the god for the prosperity of trade.

MERCHANT

Pages 583-584

a person who buys and sells commodities in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> deals in exchanges; or that traffics in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, either by importation or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Formerly every one who was a buyer or seller in the retail way was called a merchant, as they still are both in France and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; but here shopkeepers, or those who attend <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, have lost that appellation. Previous to a person's engaging in a general trade, and becoming an universal dealer, he ought to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> up such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of useful knowledge as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable him to carry it on with ease to himself; and without risking such losses as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ill-concerted undertakings would naturally expose him to. A merchant should therefore be acquainted with the following parts of commercial learning: 1. He should write properly and correctly. 2. Understand all the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> that have any relation to commerce. 3. Know how to keep books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and single entry, as journals, a leger, &c. 4. Be expert in the forms of invoices, accounts of sales, policies of insurances, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-parties, bills of lading, and bills of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. 5. Know the agreement between the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, weights, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of all parts. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, he ought to know the places where these different sorts of merchandises are manufactured, in what manner they are made, what are the materials of which they are composed; and from whence they come, the proportions of these materials before working up, and the places in which they are sent after their fabrication. 7. He ought to know the lengths and breadths which silk, woollen, or hair stuffs, linen, cottons, fustians, &c. ought to have according to the several statutes and regulations of the places where they are manufactured, with their different prices, according to the times and seasons; and if he can add to his knowledge the different dyes and ingredients which form the various colours, it will not be useless. Merchant. 8. If he confines his trade to that of oils, wines, &c., he ought to inform himself particularly of the appearances of the succeeding crops, in order to regulate his disposing of what he has on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and to learn as exactly as he can what they have produced when got in, for his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in making the necessary purchases and engagements. 9. He ought to be acquainted with the sorts of merchandise found more in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than another, those which are scarce, their different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> and qualities, and the properest method for bringing them to a good market either by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. 10. To know which are the merchandises permitted or prohibited, as well on entering as going out of the kingdoms or states where they are made. 11. To be acquainted with the price of exchange, according to the course of different places, and what is the cause of its rise and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. 12. To know the customs due on importation or exportation of merchandises, according to the usage, the tariffs, and regulations of the places to which he trades. 13. To know the best manner of folding up, embaling, or tumbling, the merchandises for their preservation. 14. To understand the price and condition of freighting and insuring ships and merchandise. 15. To be acquainted with the goodness and value of all necessaries for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and repairs of shipping, the different manner of their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; what the wood, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, cordage, cannons, sails, and all requisites, may cost. 16. To know the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, officers, and sailors, and the manner of engaging with them. 17. He ought to understand the foreign languages, or at least as many of them as he can attain to; these may be reduced to four, viz. the Spanish, which is used not only in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> but on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope; the Italian, which is understood on all the coasts of the Mediterranean, and in many parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>: the German, which is understood in almost all the northern countries; and the French, which is now become almost universally current. 18. He ought to be acquainted with the consular jurisdiction, with the laws, customs, and usages of the different countries he does or may trade to; and in general all the ordinances and regulations both at home and abroad that have any relation to commerce. 19. Though it is not necessary for a merchant to be very learned, it is proper that he should know something of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, particularly that of his own country; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, hydrography, or the science of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and that he be acquainted with the discoveries of the countries in which trade is established, in what manner it is settled, of the companies formed to support those establishments, and of the colonies they have sent out. All these branches of knowledge are of great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to a merchant who carries on an extensive commerce; but if his trade and his views are more limited, his learning and knowledge may be so too; but a material requisite for forming a merchant is, his having on all occasions a strict regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and his avoiding fraud and deceit as corroding cankers that must inevitably destroy his reputation and fortune. Trade is a thing of so universal a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that it is impossible for the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, or of any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, to determine all the affairs relating to it; there- Merchant fore all nations, as well as Great Britain, show a particular regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-merchant, which is a law made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> among themselves; however, merchants and other strangers are subject to the laws of the country in which they reside. Foreign merchants are to sell their merchandise at the port where they land, in gross, and not by retail: and they are allowed to be paid in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a>, in foreign <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a> or jewels, which may be exported. If a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arises between the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and any foreign state, the merchants of that state are allowed six months <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to sell their effects and leave the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; during which time they are to remain free and unmolested in their persons and goods. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Commerce and Mercantile Law.

MERCHE

Pages 584-584

a fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> paid by inferior tenants to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to dispose of their daughters in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. No baron, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tenant, could marry his sole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and heir, without such leave purchased from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> pro <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">maria</a> filia. And many of our servile tenants could neither send their sons to school, nor give their daughters in marriage, without express leave from the superior lord. See Kemnet's Glossary in Maritogium. See also Marchet, under which word it is stated, and very generally understood, that this was a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> claimed by the lord of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the feudal system of passing the first night after marriage with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> villain. According to Mr Astle, the mercheta was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> between the lord and his vassal for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> of an offence committed by the vassal's unmarried daughter; and also a fine paid by a sokeman or a villain to his lord for permission to marry his daughter to a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the vassal gave away his daughter without having obtained this license, he subjected himself to a heavier fine.

MERCIA

Pages 584-585

the name of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> kingdoms founded in England by the Saxons. Though the latest formed, it was the largest of them all, and grew by degrees to be by far the most powerful. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it was bounded by the Humber and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, which separated it from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>; on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and the territories of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a> and Saxons; on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>; and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>. It comprehended well nigh 17 of our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> counties, being equal in size to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in France; very little, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at all, less than the kingdom of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and superior in size to that of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in Germany. Penda is regarded as its first monarch; and the kingdom is thought to derive its name from the Saxon word merc, which signifies "a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, bound, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> limit," because the other kingdoms bordered upon it on every side; and not from the river Mersey, as some would persuade us. Penda assumed the regal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> A.D. 626, and was of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 50 at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his accession; after which he reigned near thirty years. He was of a most furious and turbulent temper, breaking at different times with almost all his neighbours, calling in the Britons to his assistance, and shedding more Saxon blood than had been hitherto spilled in all their intestine quarrels. He killed two kings of Northumberland, three of the East Angles, and compelled Kenwall <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the West Saxons to quit his dominions. He was at length slain, with most of the Mercian princes of his family, and a multitude of his subjects, in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought not far from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>, by Oswy king of Northumberland. This battle, which the Saxon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> tells us was fought at Winwidfield, A.D. 655, made a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> change in the Saxon affairs, which the unbridled fury of Penda had thrown into great confusion. He had the year before killed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> king of the East Angles in battle, whose <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a> notwithstanding took <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with Penda. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Penda, the eldest son of Penda, to whom his father had given the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kingdom of the Mid Angles, had two years before married the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of King Oswy, and had been baptized at his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. At that time it should seem that Oswy and Penda were upon good terms; but after the latter had conquered the East Angles, he resolved to turn his arms against the kingdom of Northumberland. Oswy by no means had provoked this rupture; on the contrary, Bede tells us that he offered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and jewels of great value, to purchase peace; these offers being rejected, he was reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of deciding the quarrel by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The river near which the battle was fought overflowing, there were more drowned than killed. Amongst these, as the Saxon chronicle says, there were thirty princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> line, some of whom bore the title of kings; and also Ethelred king of the East Angles, who fought on the side of Penda against his family and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His son Penda, who married the daughter of that conqueror became a Christian, and was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after murdered, as is said, by the malice of his mother. His brother Wolfher becoming king of Mercia, embraced in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of the gospel, and proved a very victorious and potent monarch; and is, with no fewer than seven of his immediate successors, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> styled king of the Anglo-Saxons, though none of them are owned in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> by the Saxon chronicle. But though possibly none of them might enjoy this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, they were undoubtedly very puissant princes, maintaining great wars, and obtaining many advantages over the sovereigns of other Saxon states, and especially the East Angles, whom they reduced. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the Mercian territories was so ample as to admit, and so situated as to require, the constituting subordinate rulers in several provinces; to whom, especially if they were of the royal line, they gave the title of kings; which occasions some confusion in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Besides the establishing episcopal sees and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the Saxon monarchs took other methods for improving and adorning their dominions; and as Mercia was the largest, so these methods were most conspicuous therein. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, as being situated in the centre, was usually, but not always, the royal residence. Penda, who was almost continually in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, lived as his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations directed, in some great town on the frontiers. Wolfher built a castle or fortified <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for his own residence, which bore his name.—Offa kept his court at Sutton Walls near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>. In each of the provinces there resided a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; and if he was of the royal blood, had usually the title of king. Penda, at the time he married Oswy's daughter, had the title of king of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>.—Ethelred Ethelred made his brother Merowald king of Hereford; who, dying without issue, bequeathed it to his younger brother Mercelm. The like honours were sometimes conferred upon the princesses; and hence, in Mercia especially, we occasionally read of vice-queens. By these means the laws were better executed, the obedience of the subjects more effectually secured, and the splendour of these residences constantly kept up and augmented. At length the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> devolving sometimes on minors and sometimes on weak princes, intestine factions also prevailing, the force of this hitherto mighty kingdom began sensibly to decline. This falling out in the days of Egbert, the most prudent as well as the most potent monarch of the West Saxons, he took advantage of these circumstances; and having encouraged the East Angles to make an attempt for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their independence, he, in a conjuncture every way favourable to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, broke with the Mercians, and after a short war obliged them to submit. But this was not an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> conquest, the kings of Mercia being allowed by him and his successors to retain their titles and dominions, till the invasion of the Danes put an end to their rule, when this kingdom had subsisted above 250 years; and when the Danes were afterwards expelled by the West Saxons, it sunk into a province, or rather was divided into many. **MERCURIAL,** something consisting of, or relating to, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>.

MERCURIALIS

Pages 585-586

DOGS <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">MERCURY</a>;** a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dicca class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricocce. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **MERCURIFICATION,** in metallurgic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, the obtaining the mercury from metallic minerals in its fluid form. See Chemistry and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index. **MERCURY,** <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Quicksilver.
