See Chemistry and Mineralogy Index. **MERCURY,** in the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. See Hermes. Most of the actions and inventions of the Egyptian Mercury have likewise been ascribed to the Grecian, who was said to be the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAIA">Maia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. No one of all the heathen divinities had so many functions allotted to him as this god: he had constant employment both <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night, having been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> minister and messenger of the whole Pantheon; particularly of his father Jupiter, whom he served with indefatigable labour, and sometimes, indeed, in a capacity of no very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> kind. Lucian is very pleasant upon the multitude of his avocations; and according to the confession of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, Mercury was no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, but rather one who inspired mankind with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, learning, and the ornamental arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, than with courage. The pious emperor, however, omits some of his attributes; for this god was not only the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of trade, but also of theft and fraud. Amphion is said, by Pausanias, to have been the first that erected an altar to this god; who, in return, invested him with such extraordinary powers of music (and masonry), as to enable him to fortify the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of his lyre. Horace gives us the best <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his character: Thou god of wit, from Atlas sprung, Who by persuasive pow'r of tongue, And graceful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, refin'd The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> kind, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">Hail</a>! winged messenger of Jove, And all th'immortal pow'rs above. Sweet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> lyre, Thy praise shall all its sounds inspire. Artful and cunning to conceal Whate'er in sportive theft you steal, When from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> who gilds the pole, E'en yet a boy, his herds you stole; With angry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> the threat'n'g power Bade thee thy fraudulent prey restore; But of his quiver too beguiled, Pleas'd with the theft, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> smil'd. You were the wealthy Priam's guide, When safe from Agamemnon's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, Through hostile <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, which round him spread Their watchful fires, his way he sped. Unspotted spirits you consign To blissful seats and joys divine; And, pow'rful, with thy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> wand, The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, unbodied crowd command; Thus grateful does thy office prove To gods below, and gods above. Francis. This ode contains the substance of a very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Mercury, attributed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. Almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets relate the manner in which the Grecian Mercury discovered the lyre; and tell us that it was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> strings; a circumstance which makes it essentially different from that said to have been invented by the Egyptian Mercury, which had but three. However, there have been many claimants besides Mercury to the seven-stringed lyre. See Lyre. His most magnificent temple was on Mount <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. He is described by the poets as a fair beardless youth, with flaxen <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, lively blue eyes, and a smiling countenance. He has wings fixed to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> and sandals, and holds the caduceus (or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, with two wings on the top), in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and is frequently represented with a purse, to show that he was the god of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>. The animals sacred to him, were the dog, the goat, and the cock. In all the sacrifices offered to him, the tongues of the victims were burnt; and those who escaped imminent danger sacrificed to him a calf with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. **MERCURY,** § in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>. See Astronomy Index. This planet is brightest between his elongations and superior conjunction, very near to which last he can generally be seen. He becomes invisible soon after he has found his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELONGATION">elongation</a>, going towards his inferior conjunction; and becomes visible again a few days before his next elongation. The brightness of this planet alters sometimes very considerably in 24 hours. It has been observed when less than three degrees distant from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and may, perhaps, sometimes be seen even in conjunction with it. Mercury and Venus appear brightest and most beautiful in the opposite parts of their orbits; the first, between... between his elongations and superior conjunction; and the other, between her elongations and inferior con- junction. Therefore, Venus is seen in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, particularly in her inferior conjunction, whilst Mercury is seldom seen in such perfect phases. Mercury should be always observed on or near the mer- idian. When farthest from the sun, he always appears with a very faint light; and when he has a great south declination, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is not perfectly clear, he seldom can be seen in those parts of his or- bit, where he only begins to recover his brightness, or where it is much diminished. He has frequently been seen on the meridian even with a small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> and small power; and it appears from the above statement that he may be obscured in a clear day rather more than half his orbit, or near one hundred and fourscore days in the year.

MERCURY

Pages 586-586

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, for the purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> used in the arms of so- vereign princes.

MERCY

Pages 586-586

a virtue that inspires us with compassion for our brethren, and which inclines us to give them assistance in their necessities. Mercy is also taken for those favours and benefits that we receive either from God <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, particularly in the way of forgiveness of injuries or of debts. Nothing can be more beautiful than the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of mercy given us by Shakespeare, in the pleading between Portia and the Jew: Por. Then must the Jew be merciful. Shy. On what compulsion must I? tell me that. Por. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of mercy is not strain'd; It droppeth as the gentle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> from heav'n Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> beneath. It is twice bless'd: It blesseth him that gives, and him that takes. 'Tis mightiest in the mightiest; it becomes The throned monarch better than his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>: The sceptre shows the force of temporal power, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to awe and majesty, Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings; But mercy is above this scepter'd sway, It is enthroned in the heart of kings; It is an attribute to God himself, And earthly power doth then show likest God's, When mercy seasons <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Therefore, Jew, Though justice be thy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, consider this, That in the course of justice none of us Should see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. We do pray for mercy; And that same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> doth teach us all to render The deeds of mercy. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> iv.

MERCY-SEAT

Pages 586-586
or PROPITIATORY, in Jewish an- tiquity, the covering of the ark of the covenant.—The Hebrew name of this cover, which we translate mercy- seat, is Kapporeth (Exod. xxv. 17. 22.), from Copper, which signifies to cover, to shut up, to expiate, to pay. This cover was of gold, and at its two ends were fixed the two cherubims of the same metal, which by their wings extended forwards, seemed to form a throne for the majesty of God, who in scripture is represented to us as sitting between the cherubims, and the ark it- self was as it were his footstool. It was from hence that God gave his oracles to Moses, or to the high priest that consulted him, (Exod. xxv. 22. Numb. vii. 89.).

MERETRIX

Pages 586-586

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, differed from the prostibula. The prostibulae were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> courte- sans, with bills over their doors, signifying their profes- <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a>, and were ready at all times to entertain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>- ers; whereas the meretrices entertained none but at night.—The meretrices differed in their dress from the matrons; the former wore the toga and short tunics, like those of the men; the latter wore the pallia and the stola of such a length as to reach to their feet. MERGANSER. See MERGUS.

MERGUS

Pages 586-586

a genus of birds of the order of anseres. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MERIAN

Pages 586-586
MARIA SIBYLLA, a celebrated paint- ress, born at Frankfort in 1647, was the daughter of Matthias Merian, a noted engraver and geographer.— As she showed a very great fondness for painting, she was instructed by Abraham Mignon; from whom she learned great neatness of handling and delicacy of co- lour. Her genius particularly led her to paint reptiles, flowers, and insects, which she designed after nature, and studied every object with a most curious and in- quisitive observation; so that her works rose every day more and more into reputation. Frequently she paint- ed her subjects in water colours on vellum, and finishe- d an astonishing number of designs, as she was equally indefatigable in her work and in her inquiries into the curiosities of nature. She drew the flies and caterpil- lars in all the variety of changes and forms in which they successively appear from their quiescent state till they become butterflies; and also drew frogs, toads, ser- pents, ants, and spiders, after nature, with extraordinary exactness and truth. She even undertook a voyage to Surinam, to paint those insects and reptiles which were peculiar to that climate; and at her return to her own country published two volumes of engravings after her designs, which are well known to the curious. She died in 1717. Her daughter Dorothea Henrietta Graff, who painted in the same style, and had accompanied her mother to Surinam, published a third volume col- lected from the designs of Sibylla; which complete work has been always admired by the learned, as well as by the professors of painting.

MERIDA

Pages 586-586

a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, seated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, 132 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Pampeluna. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 71. 9. N. Lat. 8. 30.

MERIDEN

Pages 586-587
or MIREDEN, a town of Warwick- shire, 97 miles from London on the London road, near Coventry. It is pleasantly situated, though in a wet clayey situation, and is not ill built. The church stands on an elevated spot, and contains some good monuments. There is an inn here, about half-way from St Clement's forest to Coventry, one of the finest in this part of England, being built like a nobleman's seat.

MERIDIAN

Pages 587-587

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle supposed to be drawn through any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>; and to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is always perpendicular at noon. See Geography. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, this circle is supposed to be in the heavens, and exactly perpendicular to the terrestrial one. See Astronomy.

MERIDIANI

Pages 587-587

in antiquity, a name which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gave to a kind of gladiators, who entered the arena about noon after the bestiarii (who fought in the morning against beasts) had finished. They were thus called from meridies, i.e., noon, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when they exhibited their shows. The meridiani were a sort of artless combatants, who fought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with man, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Hence Seneca takes occasion to observe, that the combats of the morning were full of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> compared with those which followed.

MERIDIONAL DISTANCE

Pages 587-587

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, the same with departure, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> casting and westing; being the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> between the meridian under which the ship now is, and any other meridian which she was under before. **MERIDIONAL parts**, miles, or minutes, in Navigation, are the parts by which the meridians in a Mercator's chart do increase, as the parallels of latitude decrease.

MERIONETHSHIRE

Pages 587-587

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, is bounded on the north by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a> and Denbighshire; on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>; on the west by St George's channel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and on the south by Cardiganshire; extending 40 miles in length and 36 in breadth. It is divided into six <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>; in which are four market <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 37 parishes, about 6137 houses, and 30,924 inhabitants, in 1811. It lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, and sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very sharp in winter, on account of its many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is as bad as any in Wales, it being very rocky and mountainous. However, this county feeds <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks of sheep, many goats, and large herds of horned cattle, which find pretty good pasture in the valleys. Besides these, among their other commodities may be reckoned Welch cotton, deer, fowl, fish, and especially herrings, which are often taken on this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty. See Merionethshire, Supplement.

MERIT

Pages 587-587

signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> is more particularly applied to signify the moral goodness of the actions of men, and the rewards to which those actions entitle them.

MERLIN

Pages 587-587
Ambrose**, a famous English poet and reputed prophet, flourished at the end of the 5th century. Many surprising and ridiculous things are related of him. Several English authors have represented him as the son of an incubus, and as transporting from Ireland to England the great stones which form Stonehenge on Salisbury plain. Extravagant prophecies and other works are also attributed to him, on which some authors have even written commentaries. **MERLIN.** See Falco, Ornithology Index.

MERLON

Pages 587-587

in Fortification, is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> which is terminated by two embrasures of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>.

MERMAID

Pages 587-587
or Merman**, a sea-creature frequently talked of, supposed half human and half a fish. However naturalists may doubt of the reality of mermen or mermaids, we have testimony enough to establish it; though, how far these testimonies may be authentic, we cannot take upon us to say. In the year 1187, as Lary informs us, such a monster was fished up in the county of Suffolk, and kept by the governor for six months. It bore so near a conformity with man, that nothing seemed wanting to it but speech. One day it took the opportunity of making its escape; and plunging into the sea, was never more heard of. Hist.de Angleterre, P. I. p. 403. In the year 1430, after a huge tempest, which broke down the dikes in Holland, and made way for the sea into the meadows, &c., some girls of the town of Edam in West Friesland, going in a boat to milk their cows, perceived a mermaid embarrassed in the mud, with a very little water. They took it into their boat, and brought it with them to Edam, dressed it in woman's apparel, and taught it to spin. It fed like one of them, but could never be brought to offer at speech. Some time afterwards it was brought to Haerlem, where it lived for some years, though still showing an inclination to the water. Parival relates, that they had given it some notion of a Deity, and that it made its reverences very devoutly whenever it passed by a crucifix. Delices de Hollande. In the year 1562, near the island of Manaar, on the western coast of the island of Ceylon, some fishermen brought up, at one draught of a net, seven mermen and mermaids; of which several Jesuits, and among the rest F. Hen. Henriques and Dimas Bosquez, physicians to the viceroy of Goa, were witnesses. The physician, who examined them with a great deal of care, and made dissection thereof, asserts, that all the parts both internal and external were found perfectly conformable to those of men. See the Hist. de la compagnie de Jesus, P. II. T. iv. No 276, where the relation is given at length. We have another account of a merman, seen near the great rock called Diamond, on the coast of Martinico. The persons who saw it, gave in a precise description of it before a notary. They affirmed that they saw it wipe its hand over its face, and even heard it blow its nose. Another creature of the same species was caught in the Baltic in the year 1531, and sent as a present to Sigismund king of Poland, with whom it lived three days, and was seen by all the court. Another very young one was taken near Rocca de Sintra, as related by Damian Goes. The king of Portugal and the grand master of the order of St James, are said to have had a suit at law to determine which party these monsters belong to. In Pontopidan's href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History of Norway, also, we have accounts of mermaids; but not more remarkable or any way better attested than the above, to which we have given a place, merely to shew how far the folly and extravagance of credulity have been carried by weak minds.

MEROE

Pages 588-588

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ethiopia beyond <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; with a cognominal town, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Ethiopians. The Jesuits have endeavoured to prove, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Gojam in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a> is the Meroe of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; but this is strongly contested by Mr Bruce, who is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it must be looked for somewhere between the source of the Nile and its union with the Atbara. The latter, he thinks, is very plainly the Astaboras of the ancients; and Pliny says, that this stream encloses the left side of Meroë as the Nile does the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> we must suppose him looking southward from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, otherwise the words would not apply. We are told by Diodorus Siculus, that Meroë had its name from a sister of Cambyses <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, who died there in the expedition undertaken by that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> against the Ethiopians. His <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> perished with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and thirst in the deserts beyond Meroë, which could not have happened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had reached Gojam, the latter being one of the most plentiful countries in the world. A further <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that Gojam cannot be the ancient Meroë is, that the latter was enclosed between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Nile and Astaboras, while Gojam is almost entirely surrounded by the Nile. If the ancients were acquainted with Gojam, they must also have been acquainted with the fountains of the Nile, which we certainly know they were not. Pliny says that Meroë, the most considerable of all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Nile, was called Astaboras, from the name of its left channel, which cannot be supposed any other than the junction of the Nile and Atbara. He informs us moreover, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> was vertical twice in the year, viz. when proceeding northward he entered the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Taurus, and when returning he came to the 14th degree of Leo; but this could never be the case with Gojam, which lies in about 10 degrees <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. Again, the poet Lucan describes Meroë by two circumstances which cannot apply to any other than the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Atbara. One is, that the inhabitants were <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; which was the case with the Gymnosophists and first inhabitants, and which has been the case with all the rest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the Saracen conquest: but the inhabitants of Gojam, as well as the other Abyssinians, are fair, at least greatly different in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> from the blacks; they are also <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>-haired, and nobody imagined that they ever had philosophers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> science among them, which was eminently the case with the ancient inhabitants of Meroë. The other circumstance is, that the ebony tree grew in the island of Meroë, which at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> grows plentifully in the peninsula of Atbara, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the province of Kuara, but not in Gojam, where the tree could not subsist on account of the violent rains which take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> during six months in the year. Mr Bruce mentions another circumstance quoted from the poet Lucan, which likewise tends to prove the identity of Meroë and Atbara; viz. that though there are many trees in it, they afford no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. This our traveller found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, when returning from Abyssinia through Atbara. "The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> (says he) is flat, and has very little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The forests, though thick, afforded no sort of shade, the hunters for the sake of their sport, and the Arabs for destroying the flies, having set fire to all the dry grass and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; which passing with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> from east to west, though it had not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to destroy the trees, did yet hinder, and occasion every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> that was upon them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, unless in those spaces where villages had been, and where water was. In such spots a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> spreading trees remained full of foliage; which, from their great height and being cleared of underwood, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in full verdure, loaded with large, projecting, and exuberant branches. But even here the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> that their shade afforded was very temporary, so as to allow us no time for enjoyment. The sun, so near the zenith, changed his azimuth so rapidly, that every few minutes I was obliged to change the carpet on which I lay, round the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the tree to which I had fled for shelter; and though I lay down to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> perfectly screened by the trunk or branches, I was presently awakened by the violent rays of a scorching sun, the shade having passed beyond me. In all other places, though we had travelled constantly in a forest, we never met with a tree that could shade us for a moment, the fire having deprived them of all their leaves." The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of Atbara is excessive, the thermometer having been observed at 119°: two of Mr Bruce's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> died of thirst, or at least of the consequences of drinking after <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> thirst. The inhabitants live in the greatest misery, and are continually in danger from the neighbouring Arabs, who, by destroying and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> their corn, are able to reduce them to a starving condition. Notwithstanding all their disadvantages, however, they have a manufacture of coarse cotton towels, of a size <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> sufficient to go round the waist, which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> current as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> throughout the whole country.

MEROFS

Pages 589-589

a genus of birds belonging to the order of picae. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEROM

Pages 588-589

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. The waters of Merom, at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Jabin and the other confederate kings met to fight (Joshua xi. 5.), are generally supposed by the learned to be the lake Semechon, which lies between the head of the river Jordan and the lake Gennesareth; since it is agreed on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> Hazor, where Jabin reigned, was situated upon this lake. But others think that the waters of Merom <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Merome were somewhere about the brook Kishon, since there is a place of that name mentioned in the account of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against Sisera (Judg. v. 21.). And it is more rational to think, that the confederate kings advanced advanced as far as the brook Kishon, and to a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> which led into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to hinder Joshua from penetrating it, or even to attack him in the country where he himself lay encamped, than to imagine that they waited for him in the midst of their own country; leaving all Galilee at his mercy, and the whole tract from the brook Kishon to the lake Semechon.

MEROPE

Pages 589-589

in *Fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, one of the Atlantides. She married <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SISYPHUS">Sisyphus</a> the son of Æolus, and like her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> was changed into a constellation after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. It is said that in the constellation of the Pleiades the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of Merope appears more dim and obscure than the rest, because she, as the poets observe, married a mortal, while her sisters married some of the gods <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> their descendants.

MEROPS

Pages 589-589

in *Fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cos, who married Clymene, one of the Oceanides. He was changed into an eagle, and placed among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>. Also a celebrated soothsayer of Percosus in Troas, who foretold the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his sons Adrastus and Amphius, who were engaged in the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. They slighted their father's advice, and were killed by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>.

MEROVINGIAN CHARACTER

Pages 589-589

derives its name from Merouée, the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, which reigned 333 years, from Pharamond to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CHARLES_MARTEL"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Martel. This race is said by some to have terminated in Childeric III. A.D. 751. There are many MSS. in the French <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> still extant in this character.

MEROZ

Pages 589-589

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the neighbourhood of the brook Kishon, whose inhabitants refusing to come to the assistance of their brethren when they fought with Sisera, were put under an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> (Judges v. 23.) "Curse ye Meroz, says the angel of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof: because," &c. Some have thought that Meroz is the same as Merus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Merom; and this F. Calmet thinks the most probable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, that Meroz was a mighty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who dwelt near the Kishon, and not caring to come to the assistance of Barak and Deborah, was excommunicated by the angel of the Lord by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of 400 trumpets. The angel of the Lord, according to some, was Barak, the general of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but according to others he was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> being, or a prophet.

MERS

Pages 589-589
or MERSE, a county of Scotland, called also Berwickshire. This last name it derives from the town of Berwick, which was the head of the shire before it fell into the hands of the English, and obtained the appellation of Mers or March, because it was one of the borders towards England. See BERWICK, County of.

MERSA

Pages 589-589

a town of Barbary, pleasantly situated about 11 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and two from Melcha the site of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. The bey has here two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> houses, one of them very costly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, built by Hassan Bey surnamed the Good. From these are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> gardens reaching almost to the seashore; on the edge of which is a famous well of sweet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, esteemed the best and lightest in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> to this is a coffeehouse, whither numbers of people from the neighbouring places <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to drink coffee, and a glass of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> so peculiarly enjoyed in the eastern countries. In the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> mulberry tree, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of which they sit and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and play at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>; inhaling the comfortable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> breeze that refreshes this delightful spot. The water is drawn up by a camel with the Persian wheel. There are the remains of an ancient port, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cothon, (supposed to be an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> one), built by the Carthaginians after Scipio had blocked up the old port, nothing but the turret or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> being left.

MERSENNE

Pages 589-589

MARIN, in Latin Mersenius, a learned French author, born at Oysé, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, anno 1588. He studied at La Flèche at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with Des Cartes; with whom he contracted a strict friendship, which lasted till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and studied at the Sorbonne; and in 1611 entered himself among the Minims. He became well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. He was of a tranquil, sincere, and engaging temper; and was universally esteemed by persons illustrious for their birth, their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and their learning. He taught philosophy and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in the convent of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and at length became superior of the convent; but being willing to apply himself to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> with more freedom, he resigned all the posts he enjoyed in his order, and travelled into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent works; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. *Questiones celeberrimae in Genesim.* 2. *Harmoniconum libri.* 3. *De sonorum natura, causis, et effectibus.* 4. *Cogitata physico-mathematica.* 5. *La vérité des Sciences.* 6. *Les questions inutiles.* He died at Paris in 1648. He had the reputation of being one of the best men of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. No person was more curious in penetrating into the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and carrying all the arts and sciences to their utmost perfection. He was in a manner the centre of all the men of learning, by the mutual correspondence which he managed between them. He omitted no means to engage them to publish their works; and the world is obliged to him for several excellent discoveries, which, had it not been for him, would perhaps have been lost.

MERSEY

Pages 589-589

a river of England, which runs through the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and empties itself into the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>. By means of inland <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, it has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Derwent, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c.; which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, York, Lancaster, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, Chester, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, &c. Mersey <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, an island of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, at the mouth of the Coln, south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>. It was seized by the Danes in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred, for their winter <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. It had eight parishes, now reduced to two, viz. East and West Mersey. There was formerly a blockhouse on the island.

MERUS

Pages 589-590

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a mountain of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, hanging over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> Nyssa, built by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Cophen and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>. The name, denoting the thigh, gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Bacchus being inserted into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s thigh, and... being born twice; because in this mountain he and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are said to have been preserved, when <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and pestilence raged in the plains below.

MESARAIC VESSELS

Pages 590-590

in the general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are the same with MESENTERIC. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, mesaraic is more frequently applied to the veins, and mesenteric to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, of the mesentery. See ANATOMY.

MESCHEDE

Pages 590-590

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Chorassan; fortified with several towers, and famous for the magnificent sepulchre of Iman Risa, of the family of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, to whom the Persians pay <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. It is seated on a mountain near this town, on which are fine turquoise <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 59° 25' N. Lat. 37° 0'.

MESEMBRYANTHEMUM

Pages 590-590

Fig-Marigold, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICOSANDRIA">icosandria</a> class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MESENTERIC

Pages 590-590
or MESARAIC, an epithet given to two arteries arising from the descending aorta, and proceeding to the mesentery. See MESENTERY.

MESENTERY

Pages 590-590

MESENTERIUM, (formed of mesos, middle, and enteron, intestine), in anatomy, a fatty membranous body, thus called as being placed in the middle of the intestines, which it connects to one another. See ANATOMY, No. 94.

MESN

Pages 590-590
or MESNE, a term in law, signifying him who is lord of a manor, and so hath tenants holding of him; yet he himself holds of a superior lord. The word is properly derived from maisne, quasi minor natu; because his tenure is derived from another, from whom he holds.

MESN ALSO

Pages 590-590

n also denotes a writ, which lieth where there is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mesn and tenant; and the tenant is distrained for services due from the mesn to the superior lord. This is in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the tenant shall have judgment to be acquitted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> indemnified by the mesne lord; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he makes default therein, or does not appear originally to the tenant's writ, he shall be prejudiced of his mesnalty, and the tenant shall hold immediately of the lord paramount himself.

MESOCHRI

Pages 590-590

were musicians among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who presided in concerts, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> a wooden desk regularly with their feet, directed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the music. For the purpose of beating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they wore wooden clogs, called by the ancients crupesia, which occasioned the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> to be better heard.

MESOCOLON

Pages 590-590

in Anatomy, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mesentery, which, having reached the extremity of the ileum, contracts and changes its names. See ANATOMY, No. 94.

MESOLOGARITHMS

Pages 590-590

according to Kepler, are the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> of the co-sines and co-tangents; the former of which were called by Baron Napier anti-logarithms, and the latter differentials.

MESOPORPHYRON

Pages 599-599

a name given by the Greeks to the Roman laticeave; because that garment being edged on each side, where it opened before, with purple, appeared when closed with two purple stripes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the middle. The same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> was also applied to the angusticlavae.

MESOPOTAMIA

Pages 590-590

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Diarbeck, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. It is situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and Tigris; having Asyria on the east, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> on the west, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deserta with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a> on the south. The Hebrews called it Padan-aram, Gen. xxviii. 2. &c.) and Aram Naharaim (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Psalm lx.) <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Aram of the two rivers, because it was first peopled by Aram father of the Syrians, and is situated between the two rivers already mentioned. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is much celebrated in Scripture, as being the first dwelling of men both before and after the deluge; and because it gave birth to Phaleg, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, Terah, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, Nahor, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah, and to the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> was in the ancient Mesopotamia, till, by vast labour and industry, the two rivers of the Tigris and Euphrates were united into one channel. The plains of Shinar were in the same country. Often they gave it the name of Mesopotamia (Deut. xxiii. 4. &c.) and sometimes that of Syria (Hosea xii. 12.). Balashan son of Beor was of Mesopotamia, Deut. xxiii. 4. Chu-shan-rishathaim <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Mesopotamia kept the Hebrews in subjection some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Joshua, Judg. iii. 8.

MESOPTERYGIUS

Pages 590-590

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to such fishes as have only one back-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>, which is situated in the middle of the back.

MESPILUS

Pages 590-590

the Medlar, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICOSANDRIA">icosandria</a> class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 36th order, Pomaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MESSALINA

Pages 590-590

VALERIA, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Messala Barbatus. She married the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius, and disgraced herself by her cruelties and incontinence. Her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was not the only seat of her lasciviousness, but she prostituted herself in the public streets, and few men there were at Rome who could not boast of having enjoyed the favours of the impure Messalina. Her extravagancies at last irritated her husband, who commanded her to appear and answer all the accusations which were brought against her: upon which she attempted to destroy herself; and when her courage failed, one of the tribunes who had been sent to her despatched her with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. It is in speaking of her debaucheries and lewdness that Juvenal says, Et lassata viris, necdum satiata, recessit. Her name has become a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> appellation to denote a woman of shameless and inordinate lust.

MESSANA

Pages 590-591

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the first town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> on crossing over from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the strait now called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, (Italicus). Anciently called Zancle, according to Diodorus Siculus, from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Zanclus; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, from the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> Zanclon, denoting a sickle, alluding to the curvity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; a name appropriated by the poets; and hence Zanclari, the people, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Pausanias). the other name Messana is from the Messenii of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, (Strabo). <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> ascribes its origin to Anaxilas the Messenian, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of Rhegium, who received all comers, calling the town after the name of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Greeks always call it Messene; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MESSENA">Messena</a> constantly, to distinguish it from Messene of Peloponnesus. Now Messina, lately ruined by earthquakes.

MESSENA

Pages 591-591
or MESSENE, an inland town, and the capital of Messenia, a country of Peloponnesus; erroneously placed by Ptolemy on the coast. It was built by Epaminondas, who recalled all the Messenian exiles, and gave the town the name of Messene. A place varying in point of strength and situation with Corinth, according to Strabo; and therefore Demetrius Phalereus advised Philip, father of Perseus, that if he wanted to have Peloponnesus in his power, he should make himself master of these two towns, as thus he would have the ox by both horns.

MESSENGERS

Pages 591-594

in Scotland. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">LAW</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. MESSENGERS of the Exchequer, are four officers who attend the exchequer, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of pursuivants, and carry the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>'s letters, precepts, &c. MESSENGER of the Press, a person, who, by order of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, searches <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-houses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a> shops, &c. in order to discover the printers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> publishers of seditious books, pamphlets, &c. Messenia, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, mostly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a> to the west, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a> to the east. Anciently a part of Laconia under Menelaus, and called Messene by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; interpreted by the scholiast, Messenea Regio. Messenii, the people, reduced to a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> and subjection by the Spartans; Messenins, the epithet. This country is famous in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, on account of the resistance made by the Messenians against the Spartans, and the exploits of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Aristomenes. The first hostilities commenced about the year 652 B.C. on what occasion is uncertain. Though the Messenians were inferior in the knowledge of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to the Spartans; yet, by keeping for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the defensive, they improved so much, that in three years time they found themselves in a capacity of giving <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to their enemies in the open field; Messenian nor did they appear to be in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> inferior either in courage or conduct: the war was therefore protracted, with various success, on both sides. At last, both consulted the oracle at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; and received for answer, "that whoever should first dedicate 100 tripods in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> at Ithome, a strong hold of the Messenians, should be masters of the country." The inhabitants of Messenia, on hearing this, having no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to make the tripods of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, fell to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them out in wood; but before this could be accomplished, a Spartan having got into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> by stratagem, dedicated 100 little tripods of clay: which threw the Messenians into such despair, that they at last submitted to the Spartans. The new subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> were treated with the utmost barbarity by these cruel tyrants: so that a new war commenced under Aristomenes, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of unconquerable valour, and enthusiastically fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. He perceived that the Argives and Arcadians, who were called the allies of the Lacedaemonians, adhered to them only through fear of their power; but that in reality they hated them, and wished to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injuries they had done them. To these Aristomenes applied; and receiving an answer conformable to his wishes, he engaged his countrymen unanimously to take up arms. About a year after the revolt began, and before either party had received any auxiliaries, the Spartans and Messenians met at a village called Dera, where an obstinate engagement ensued. Aristomenes was conceived to have performed more than mortal achievements: in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> therefore, respect being also had to his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, his countrymen unanimously saluted him <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> he modestly waved, alleging, that he took up arms to set them free, and not to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; he consented, however, to accept the title of general, with a power of doing whatsoever he thought requisite for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the public. Knowing well the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, he resolved to intimidate the Spartans, by showing them what he was sure they would take for an ill <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>. Disguising himself therefore, he went privately to the city, where, in the night, he hung up a shield on the wall of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, with this inscription: Aristomenes dedicates this, out of the spoils of the Spartans, to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. It was easily perceived that this war would be both <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and bloody: the Lacedaemonians therefore sent deputies to Delphi, to inquire of the oracle concerning its event: the answer they received was, That it behoved the Spartans to seek a leader from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. The Athenians naturally envious of the Spartans, granted their request indeed, but in such a manner as manifested their spite; for they sent them for a general Tyrteus, a schoolmaster and poet, lame of one foot, and who was suspected to be a little out of his wits. But here their skill failed them; for this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, notwithstanding his despicable appearance, proved of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to Sparta, teaching them how to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> good, and how to bear up under ill fortune. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Aristomenes had drawn together a mighty <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the Eleans, Argives, Sicyonians, and Arcadians, having sent troops to his assistance; the Spartans in this, as in the former war, having no ally but Corinth. The Spartan kings, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>... custom of their city, no sooner took the field, than, notwithstanding their inferiority in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, they offered the enemy battle, which Aristomenes readily accepted. It was long, obstinate, and bloody; but in the end the Messenians were victorious, and the Lacedemonians put to flight with a great slaughter. It is scarce to be conceived how much the Spartans were struck with this defeat: they grew weary of the war, dissatisfied with their kings, diffident of their own power, and in a word sunk into a state of general uneasiness and want of spirit. It was now that the Athenian general convinced them, that he was capable of fulfilling all the promises of the oracle; he encouraged them by his poems, directed them by his counsels, and recruited their broken armies with chosen men from among the Helotes. Aristomenes, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, acted with no less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and vigour. He thought it not enough to restore the reputation of the Messenians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he did not also restore their wealth and power: he therefore taught them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> offensively against their enemies; and, entering the territories of Sparta, he took and plundered Phara, a considerable borough in Laconia, putting all such as made any resistance to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, carrying off at the same time an immense booty. This, however, was an injury which the Spartans could not brook with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>; they therefore sent immediately a body of forces to overtake the Messenians, which accordingly they did: but Aristomenes routed these pursuers, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make a mighty slaughter of them, till such time as he was disabled by having a spear thrust in his side, which occasioned his being carried out of the battle. His cure, which took up some time, being finished, he resolved to carry the war even to the gates of Sparta; and to that purpose raised a very great army; but, whether he found his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> impracticable, or was really diverted by some dream, he gave out, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, with their sister Helena, had appeared to him, and commanded him to desist. A short time after this retreat, going with a small party to make an incursion, and attempting to take prisoners some women who were celebrating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> near Eghla, a village in Laconia, those zealous matrons fell upon him and his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> with such fury, that they put them to flight, and took him prisoner: however, he soon afterwards made his escape, and rejoined his forces. In the third year of the war, the Spartans with a great force entered Messenia, whither Aristocrates king of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> was come, with a great body of troops to the assistance of his allies: Aristomenes therefore made no difficulty of fighting when the Spartans approached; but they entering privately into a negociation with Aristocrates, engaged him with bribes and promises to betray his confederates. When the battle began, the deceitful Arcadian represented to the forces under his command the mighty danger they were in, and the great difficulty there would be of retreating into their own country, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the battle should be lost: he then pretended, that the sacrifices were ominous; and, having terrified his Arcadians into the disosition of mind fittest to serve his purpose, he not only drew them off from both wings, but, in his flight, forced through the Messenian ranks, and put them too in confusion. Aristomenes and his troops, however, drew themselves into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> order, that they might defend themselves the best they could: and indeed they had need of all their valour and skill; for the Lacedemonians, who expected this event, immediately attacked and surrounded them on all sides. Fortune was, on this occasion, too powerful either for the courage or the conduct of the Messenians; so that, notwithstanding their utmost efforts, most of their army were cut to pieces, and amongst them the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Aristomenes, with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains of his shattered forces, retired as well as he could; and, perceiving that it was now impossible to maintain the war against the Lacedemonians upon equal terms, he exhorted his countrymen to fortify Mount Era, and to make the best dispositions possible for a long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. He likewise placed garrisons in Pylus and Methone on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coasts; and to these three places he gathered all the inhabitants, leaving the rest of Messenia to the mercy of the Spartans. They, on the other hand, looked on the war as now in a manner finished; for which reason they divided the lands among their citizens, and caused them to be carefully cultivated, while they besieged Era. But Aristomenes quickly convinced them that the war was far from being over: he chose out of all the Messenians 300 men, with whom he ravaged all the adjacent country: carried off a prodigious booty; and, when Messenia could no longer supply the wants of his garrison, penetrated into Laconia, and bore away corn, wine, cattle, and whatever else was necessary to the subsistence of his countrymen shut up in Era: so that at last the Spartans were constrained to issue a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, forbidding the cultivation, not only of the Messenian territory in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, but also of Laconia in its vicinity; whereby they distressed themselves more than their enemies, inducing at last a famine in Sparta itself, which brought with it its usual attendant, sedition. Here again all things had gone wrong, if the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the poet Tyrtæus had not supported the Spartan courage; nor was it without much difficulty that he influenced them to continue the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of Era, and to maintain a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for the security of the country. Aristomenes, in spite of all these precautions, committed terrible depredations with his small corps of 300 men. Amongst other places which he plundered, the city of Amyclæ was one; from whence he carried not only a great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, but also many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> laden with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The kings of Sparta lying with their troops in its neighbourhood, as soon as they heard of this expedition, marched after Aristomenes with the utmost diligence; and, as the Messenians were encumbered with their booty, came up with them before they could reach Era. In this situation of things, Aristomenes, prompted rather by despair than prudence, disposed his troops in order of battle; and, notwithstanding they were so few, made a long and vigorous resistance against the whole Lacedemonian army. At length, however, numbers prevailed: the greatest part of the Messenians were slain on the spot; and Aristomenes, with about 50 of his men who survived the slaughter, were taken prisoners; that chief having received so many wounds, that he was senseless when they carried him away. The Lacedemonians expressed the loudest joy at the sight of this illustrious captive; who for so many years, by his single abilities, had enabled his exhausted country to defend itself against the whole force of Sparta. When he was recovered of his wounds, they decreed him and all his fellow prisoners to be thrown together into a deep cavern, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the lowest kind of offenders. This judgment was executed with the utmost severity, excepting that Aristomenes had leave to put on his armour. Three days he continued in this dismal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, lying upon and covered over with dead bodies. The third <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he was almost famished through want of food, and almost poisoned with the stench of corrupted carcases, when he heard a fox gnawing a body near him. Upon this he uncovered his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and perceiving the fox <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> by him, he with one hand seized one of its hind legs, and with the other defended his face, by catching hold of its jaw when it attempted to bite him. Following as well as he could his struggling guide, the fox at last thrust his head into a little hole; and Aristomenes then letting go his leg, he soon forced his way through and opened a passage to the welcome rays of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, from which the noble Messenian had been so long debarred. Feeble as he was, Aristomenes wrought himself an outlet with his nails; and travelling by night with all the expedition he could, at length arrived safe at Era, to the great joy and amazement of his countrymen. When this news was first blazed abroad, the Spartans would have had it <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for a fiction; but Aristomenes soon put the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of it out of doubt, by falling on the posts of the Corinthians, who, as allies of the Spartans, had a considerable body of troops before Era. Most of their officers, with a multitude of private men, he slew; pillaged their camp; and in short, did so much mischief, that the Spartans under the pretence of an approaching festival, agreed to a cessation of arms for 40 days, that they might have time to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead. On this occasion, Aristomenes for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time celebrated the *hecatomphonia*, or the sacrifice appointed for those who had killed 100 of the enemy with their own hands. He had performed the same before and after his second battle: and he lived to do it a third time: which must appear wonderful to the reader, when he is informed, that notwithstanding this truce, certain Cretan archers in the service of the Spartans seized Aristomenes as he was walking without the walls, and carried him away a prisoner. There were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of them in all: two of them immediately flew with the news to Sparta, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> remained to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, whom they bound, and conducted to a lone cottage inhabited only by a widow and her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. It so fell out that the young woman dreamt the night before that she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a lion without claws, bound, and dragged along by wolves; and that she having loosed his bonds, and given him claws, he immediately tore the wolves to pieces. As soon as Aristomenes came into the cottage, and her mother, who knew him, had told her who he was, she instantly concluded that her dream was fulfilled; and therefore plied the Cretans with drink, and when they were asleep, took a poniard from one of them, cut the thongs with which Aristomenes was bound, and then put it into his hands. He presently verified her vision, by putting all his guards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and then carried her and her mother to Era, where, as a reward for her service, he married the young woman to his son Gorgus, then about 18 years of age. When Era had held out near eleven years, it fell into the hands of Sparta by an accident: the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of one Empiramus, a Spartan commander, driving his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s cattle to drink at the river Neda, met frequently with the wife of a Messenian whom he engaged in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a>. This woman gave him notice, that her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was without the wall; so that he could come to it without danger, when the good man was abroad; and she likewise gave him intelligence when her husband was upon duty in the garrison. The Spartan failed not to come at the time appointed; but they had not been long in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> before the husband returned, which put the house into great confusion; the woman, however, secured her gallant; and then let in her husband, whom she received in appearance with great joy, inquiring again and again by what excess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> she was blessed with his return. The innocent Messenian told her, that Aristomenes being detained in his bed by a wound, the soldiers knowing that he could not walk the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>, had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to retire to their houses, to avoid the inclemency of the season. The Spartan no sooner heard this, than he crept softly out of doors, and hastened away to carry the news to his master. It so happened, that the kings were at this time absent from the camp, and Empiramus had the chief command of the army. As soon as he received this information, he ordered his army to begin its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, though it rained excessively, and there was no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> light. The fellow guided them to the ford, and managed matters so well that they seized all the Messenian posts; yet, after all, they were afraid to engage; darkness, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, heavy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, together with the dread of Aristomenes, keeping them quiet in the places they had seized. As soon as it was light the attack began; and Era had been quickly taken, if only the men had defended it; but the women fought with such fury, and by their mingling in the fray, brought such an accession of numbers, as made the event doubtful. Three days and two nights this desperate engagement lasted: at last, all hopes of preserving the city being lost, Aristomenes drew off his wearied troops. Early in the fourth morning, he disposed the women and children in the centre, the Messenian youth in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and rear, the less able men in the main body: himself commanded the van; the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-guard</a> was brought up by Gorgus and Manticius, the former the son of Aristomenes, the latter of Theocles, a Messenian of great merit, who fell with much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in this attack, fighting valiantly in the cause of his country.
