When all things were ready, Aristomenes caused the last <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to be thrown open; and, brandishing his spear, marched directly towards the Spartan troops, in order to force a passage. Empiramus, perceiving his intent, ordered his men to open to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, and fairly gave them a passage; so that Aristomenes marched off in triumph, as it were, to Arcadia. The Arcadians, when they heard that Era was taken, were very desirous of succouring their old confederates in this deep distress: they therefore entreated their king Aristocrates to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them into Messenia. But he, corrupted by the Lacedemonians, persuaded them that it was too late; that the Messenians were all cut off; and that such a step would only expose them to the fury of the conquerors. When the things appeared to be otherwise, and it was known that Aristomenes was on the frontiers of Arcadia, they went in crowds to carry him provisions, and to testify their readiness to afford him and those under his command all the assistance in their power. Aristomenes desired to be heard before a general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; which being accordingly convoked, he there opened one of the boldest and best laid schemes recorded in history; he said, that he had yet 500 undaunted soldiers, who, at his command, would undertake anything; that it was very probable most of the Spartans were employed in pillaging Era, and that therefore he determined to march and surprise Sparta; which appeared so sensible, that all the assembly loudly commended his great capacity and unshaken courage. Aristocrates, however, took care to betray him; having, by various pretences, retarded the execution of the project. The Arcadians, who began to suspect him, waited for and surprised the messengers as they came back. They took the letters from them, and read them openly in the assembly. The purport of them was, that they acknowledged his great kindness both now and in the battle; and promised, that the Lacedemonians would be grateful. As soon as the letters were read, the Arcadians fell to stoning their king, frequently calling upon the Messenians to assist them; which, however, they did not, waiting for Aristomenes's order; who, far from triumphing in this spectacle, stood still, with his eyes fixed on the ground, which he wet with his tears, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> pierced with sorrow to see a crowned head so shamefully and so deservedly put to death. The Arcadians afterwards erected a monument over him, with an inscription to perpetuate his infamy. As for the Messenians under the command of Gorgus and Manticles, they passed over into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; where they founded the city of Messene, one of the most famous in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Aristomenes remained, however, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; where he married all his daughters, except the youngest, to persons of great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, inquiring of the oracle at Delphi, whom he should espouse, that his subjects might be happy under his posterity, was directed to marry the daughter of the most worthy of the Greeks; which answer was immediately understood to point at the virgin daughter of Aristomenes. Her therefore he demanded, and received; Aristomenes accompanying him back to his dominions, where he formed a scheme of uniting the Lydians and Medes against the Spartans, resolving with this view to go into Media, and to the court of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>; but while he meditated those great things, death surprised him, and thereby freed Lacedemon from the most formidable enemy she ever had.

MESSIAH

Pages 594-595

a word signifying one anointed, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> installed into an office by unction. It was usual among the Jews to anoint kings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> priests, and sometimes prophets, at the designation or installment of them, to signify emblematically the mental qualifications necessary for discharging those offices. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, and Joash, kings of Judah, received the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> unction. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and his sons received the sacerdotal, and Elisha the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Elijah received the prophetic unction.—The name MESSIAH, Anointed, or Christ, (Χριστός), was given to the kings and high priests of the Jews. The patriarchs and prophets are also called by the name of Messiah, or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s anointed. See 1 Sam. xii. 3, 5. 1 Chron. xvi. 22. Ps. cv. 15. But this name MESSIAH was principally and by way of eminence given by the Jews to their expected <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> deliverer, whose coming they still vainly wait; and is a name the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> apply to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">JESUS</a> CHRIST, in whom the prophecies relating to the Messiah were accomplished. The sum of these prophecies is, That there should be a glorious person named Messiah, descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, who should be born at Bethlehem, of a virgin of the family of David, then in its decline, before the Jews ceased to be a people, while the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> temple was standing, and about 500 years after <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; who, though appearing in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> circumstances, should be introduced by a remarkable forerunner, whose business it should be to awaken the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the people. That this illustrious person called Messiah should himself be eminent for the piety, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and benevolence of his character, and the miraculous works he should perform: yet that, notwithstanding all this, he should be rejected and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the Jews; but should afterwards be raised from the dead, and exalted to a glorious throne, on which he should through all generations continue to rule, at the same time making intercession for sinners. That great calamities should for the present be brought on the Jews for rejecting him; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of God should by his means be erected among the Gentiles, and disperse itself even unto the ends of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; wherever it came, destroying idolatry, and establishing true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and righteousness. In a word, That this glorious person should be regarded by all who believed in him as a divine teacher, an atoning sacrifice, and a royal governor; by means of whom God would make a covenant with his people, very different from that made with Israel of old; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they should be restored to, and established in, the divine favour, and fixed in a state of perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. See JESUS CHRIST, and CHRISTIANITY. The Jews, as was already observed, still wait for the coming of the Messiah, being impressed with the notion of a temporal Messiah, who is to be a mighty conqueror, and to subdue all the world. Most of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> rabbins, according to Buxtorf, believe that the Messiah is already come, but that he keeps himself concealed, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not manifest himself because of the sins of the Jews. Some of the Jews, however, in order to reconcile those prophecies that seem to contradict each other as to the character and condition of the Messiah, have had recourse to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of two Messiahs, who are yet to succeed each other; one in a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> and suffering; the other of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, splendor, and power. The first, they say, is to proceed from the tribe of Ephraim, who is to fight against Gog, and to be slain by Amnillus, Zech. xii. 10. The second is to be of the tribe of Judah, and and lineage of David, who is to conquer and kill Antichrist, and restore the kingdom of Israel, reigning over it in the highest glory and felicity. Jesus Christ asserts himself the Messiah. In St John iv. 25, the Samaritan woman says to Jesus, "I know that when Messiah comes, who is called the Christ, he will tell us all things." Jesus answered her, "I that speak to thee am he." There are several impostors, who have endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for Messiahs, as Christ himself predicted. J. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, a Dutchman, has written a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> De Pseudomessiahs "Of false Messiahs." The first he mentions was one Barcochab, who appeared under the empire of Adrian. The last was Rabbi Mordecai, who began to be talked of in 1682. A little before him, viz. in 1666, appeared Sabbethai Sebi, who was taken by the Turks, and turned Mahometan.

MESSINA

Pages 595-599

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and in the Val di Demona, with a citadel, several forts, a fine spacious harbour, and an archbishop's see. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> side; 110 miles east of Palermo, 260 south by east of Rome, and 180 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 50' N. Lat. 38° 10'. The public buildings and the monasteries were numerous and magnificent, and it contained about 60,000 inhabitants; the harbour is one of the safest in the Mediterranean, and extremely deep; the viceroy of Sicily resides here six months in the year; and it was a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fruit, corn, and excellent wine, especially since it was declared a free port. This city in the beginning of the year 1783 suffered most dreadfully by the earthquakes which shook great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> and Sicily to their foundations, overturned many rich and populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and buried thousands in their ruins: (see CALABRIA, and EARTHQUAKE, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>).—The following account of Messina, as it stood before the above <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is extracted from Mr Swinburne's Travels in Sicily. A large chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> presses upon the shore, and part of the city stands upon elevated ground. The mountains are many of them nobly wooded; the hills before them finely chequered with groves and fields. As the town runs in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> along the edge of a declivity, every <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is seen to advantage, while the less noble parts are hidden by the Palazzata. This is a regular ornamental range of lofty houses, with 19 gates, answering to as many streets: it follows the semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the port for one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and five <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and would have been the handsomest line of buildings in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> been completed; but a considerable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is not finished, except merely in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> wall, and that seems to be in a very ruinous condition. Philibert Emmanuel de Savoy, viceroy of Sicily, in 1622, began this princely <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Before it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> quay, decorated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and fountains; ships of any burden can moor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> in great depth of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. At the west extremity is a small fort and a gate; the other end is closed by the governor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and the citadel, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> pentagonal fortress, built on the point where the isthmus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> braccio di San Raniero issues from the main <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. On this slip of low ground, which with the Palazzata forms the circular harbour of Messina, is placed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> (farsetto), and on the point the old castle of St Salvatore. The circumference of the port is four miles: it probably owes its formation to an earthquake, which opened an immense chasm, and then filled it with water. Near the lighthouse is a kind of whirlpool in the sea, shown as the Charybdis of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The inner part of Messina is dirty, though it contains a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of neat churches and large substantial dwellings. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is Gothic, enriched with Saracenic mosaics on the altars and shrines; the front of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altar is particularly splendid: Gagini has embellished the pulpit and some tombs with excellent specimens of his art.—In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is preserved the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALLADIUM">palladium</a> of Messina, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> to its citizens (a). This is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> upon which the Messinese build their pretensions. (a) The story is as follows: After St Paul had made some stay at Messina (a circumstance of his travels unnoticed by St Luke), the Messinese prevailed upon him to return to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> with an embassy of four persons sent by the city to the Virgin Mary. Their excellencies were graciously received by her, and brought back a letter written with her own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue, which St Paul translated into Greek. By the irruption of the Saracens this invaluable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> was lost, and utterly forgotten till the year 1467, when Constantine Lascaris, a refugee Greek, found a copy of it, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it into Latin, made it known to the citizens, and then to all the Catholic world. Its authenticity is now so well established at Messina, that Regna the historian candidly acknowledges, that whoever was to confess even a doubt on the subject in that city would be treated as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a>. This curious epistle is conceived in these terms:—<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Virgo, Joachim filia, Dei humillima Christi Jesu crucifixi mater, ex tribu Judæ, stirpe <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Messanensis omnibus salutem, et Dei Patris Omnipotentis benedictionem. Vos omnes fide magna legatos ac nuncios per publicum documentum <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> nos misisse constat. Filium nostrum Dei genitum Deum et hominem esse fatemini, et in celum <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> suam resurrectionem ascendisse, Pauli apostoli electi predicacione mediatanea viam veritatis agnoscentes. Ob quod vos et ipsam civitatem bene dicimus, cujus perpetuum protectricem nos esse volumus. Anno filii nostri XLII. Indict. I. III. Nonas Junii, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNA">luna</a> XXVII. feria V. ex Hyerosolymis. Thus translated:—"The Virgin Mary, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Joachim, most humble mother of God, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ crucified, of the tribe of Juda and the family of David, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and the blessing of God the Father Almighty to all the people of Messina. Out of the abundance of your <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, you have, in consequence of a public deliberation, sent a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> to me; and since you acknowledge that my son is both God and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and that he ascended into heaven after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, as you have learned from the preaching of St Paul the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, pretensions to pre-eminence over the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, nay over the whole world; to its virtues and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> every piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, and to their own unworthiness all sinister events that have befallen them. The authenticity of this epistle has been seriously impugned, and of course vigorously defended by many Sicilian divines and disputators. There is another church in this city that deserves particular notice, not so much on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> or ornaments, as for its being the last refuge of the Greek liturgy, which was once the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the island, but gradually abolished by different conquerors. It is dedicated to the Virgin Mary de Graphco, or of the Letter, which denomination may perhaps have furnished Lascaris with the idea of his letter. It is known at present by the name of la Cattolica. According to the Greek canons, the entrance of monastic churches was reciprocally forbidden to each <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and the cathedrals were the only places of worship where a daily sacrifice was offered up by the bishop and clergy, and where both men and women were present at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but in different parts of the church. From this general admittance the building acquired the title of Catholic or universal. Messina is all paved with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, cut into large flags of two feet <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>: a material which the vicinity of lavas renders it easy to procure, and which being very hard resists friction better than any other. During a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of ages, notwithstanding the various revolutions and calamities to which it has been exposed, this city has still maintained its original situation; while most other cities have shifted their ground more or less from the place where they were first founded. But its situation enjoys advantages which have still tempted such of its inhabitants as escaped from the ravages of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the desolation of earthquakes to prefer it to every other spot, however delightful or secure. It is of very ancient origin; it has been under many different races of monarchs, and its name has been repeatedly changed: It has been at different times called Zancle, Mamertina, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MESSANA">Messana</a>. Its first name Zancle, which in the old <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Sicily meant "a sickle;" alluding, as some authors suppose, to the form of the port; or, according to others, to the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Allured by the advantages of its situation, the Cumæans, a commercial and enterprising people, invaded the island and drove the Siculi from this settlement; they were in their turn overpowered by a band of Samian adventurers, who made way for a colony of citizens of Messene, and under these masters it changed its name to Messana. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; for in the 28th year before Christ it was destroyed by the Mamertines, a warlike unprincipled <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> inhabiting the south part of Bruttium. These <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> being received into Messana on their return to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, where they had served as mercenaries in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Agathocles, took an opportunity of massacring the inhabitants and usurping their possessions. The city was now called Mamertina; and, in order to support themselves against the resentment of the Sicilian powers, the Mamertines implored the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who, eager to extend their dominion beyond the limits of Italy, and jealous of the growing power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, made no scruple to succour these assassins with a consular army. This step brought on the first Punic war. The Mamertines reaped no other fruit from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> but a more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>; for such was the real <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their connexion with Rome, whatever name it might be disguised under. Messina was, however, always distinguished by particular attentions and favours from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; and, excepting a short period during the wars of the triumvirate, appears to have tasted all the sweets of Roman prosperity, without partaking of the bitter draughts of adversity. Its fate, in the ruin of the empire, was similar to that of the rest of Sicily. In 829 Messina fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Saracens, but obtained very honourable terms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>; for half the city was left to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, where they were to be governed by their own laws, and profess their own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> undisturbed. In the other resided the bey of one of the five provinces into which the Arabian conquerors had divided the island. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, Messina was the first to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off the yoke in 1037, when George Maniaces landed an army of Greeks and Normans on the shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>. It afterwards held out against the whole Mussulman force, till the feeble state of a distracted empire shut out all hopes of assistance from Constantinople. This unfortunate city then opened its gates to the army of the caliph, and felt very severely the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his resentment, but it did not long groan under the yoke; for in less than 20 years Roger the Norman took it by surprise, and delivered it from Mahometan oppression. During the crusade our Richard Coeur de Lion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France wintered here in their way to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; a sojourn marked by continual quarrels, conflagration, and bloodshed. The Messinese were particularly tardy in entering into the national <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of 1282, but afterwards exceeded the rest of the insurgents in deeds of cruelty: This, and the importance of their situation, singled them out for the first objects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>'s vengeance. He invested their city very closely, and declared so openly his determination to refuse all terms whatever to the besieged, that they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> no hopes of safety but in an obstinate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Their courage, perseverance, and sufferings, were excessive; at length their strength and resources began to fail rapidly, and every circumstance seemed to denounce their speedy destruction, when Roger Lauria appeared off the harbour with the Arragonian fleet, forced the king to retire with precipitation across I give my blessing to you and all your city, and agree to become your protectress. In the 42d year of my Son, the 1st of the indiction, the 3d <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and the 27th of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, at Jerusalem." Not to dwell upon the astronomical blunders in these dates, let it suffice to observe, that Lascaris was not aware that Denis the Little, a Syrian monk in the 6th century, was the first who made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the era that commences at our Saviour's birth. the straits, and in his sight defeated and destroyed his naval armament. Robert, grandson of Charles I., also made a fruitless attack; but in the disturbed reign of Frederic III., Messina was delivered up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> king of Naples and his consort <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Joan, who entered it in triumph. In a few years it returned to its former possessors. The year 1672 was remarkable for the revolt of the Messinese.—They threw off the Spanish yoke, and swore <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to Louis XIV., king of France. They were for some time vigorously assisted by the French; but before the Spaniards had gained the least advantage to excite any hopes of recovering so valuable a possession, Louis found himself necessitated from motives of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> his new subjects, and leave them to the mercy of their old incensed masters. The horror of being thus abandoned, and the chastisement inflicted by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, broke the fierce spirit of the Messinese; they were still stunned with the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> and effects of this blow, when the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> in 1743 was introduced from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, and swept away more than half the inhabitants. From this chain of calamities, the opulence, trade, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Messina, have been gradually sinking; and unless very favourable circumstances happen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> every year <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> lower. The number of its inhabitants does not now exceed 30,000. The following particulars are added from M. Houel, who visited this city since the late earthquakes, which completed its destruction. On the front of the cathedral there is a square, which, though not regular, is far from being <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>. This was not the largest square in Messina before its overthrow; but it was the most elegant, the most splendidly adorned, and the best frequented. There stands in this square an equestrian statue of Charles II. of Spain, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, which has been spared by the earthquake. It stands on a marble pedestal, in the middle of the square. Opposite to this statue is an elegant marble fountain, ornamented with a variety of figures, representing men and other animals, all of them spouting out water in great abundance; which used, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, to spread an agreeable and refreshing coolness over the square, that induced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> to assemble here. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> streets terminated here. The cathedral forms a part of the square. It is dedicated to the blessed Virgin; the occasion of which has been already mentioned. There is an anniversary feast celebrated in Messina, which is called the feast of the Letter. A lock of the Virgin's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which she sent to the Messenians at the same time with the letter, is carried through the city in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> in a crystal vessel. She made also a present of her <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> to the Messenian deputies. It is placed over the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>. None but the canons of the cathedral are permitted to touch, or take up on their shoulders, the silver shrine in which the crystal vessel with the Virgin's hair is deposited. Eight of those canons, with mitres on their heads, bear this shrine in the procession. The canopy suspended over it is supported by six senators in their robes. The picture and the hair are shown to strangers. This procession, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies of this festival, are followed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races. The spirits of the people being already elevated by their religious exercises, they engage with amazing eagerness in these and the other diversions with which they are accompanied: a tumultuous joy reigns over the city; and the evening concludes with illuminations and fireworks. The ships in the harbour pay the citizens the compliment of entertaining them with a discharge of their guns on the occasion. Through a square called the Square of the Great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, runs a large and impetuous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, the Porto delle Legni. It is precipitated from those lofty mountains which overlook this city on the south side. The channel which it has cut out for itself is at times entirely full. It would, on such occasions, overflow the square and other parts of the city, were it not confined by walls which have been built on both sides to prevent such accidents.—Another stream of a similar origin, called the Torrent of La Bocetta, runs through another part of the city, it is also confined within walls to prevent it from overflowing. The Square of St John of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> is one of the largest in Messina. In the middle of this square is a fine marble fountain, ornamented with a variety of sculptured figures and jets d'eau. Beside the fountain there used to stand a large reservoir for horses to drink out of. In the time of the annual festivals, there used to be exhibited on the water of the reservoir a galley, or rather a fictitious representation of a galley, with galley-slaves, soldiers, officers, and a commander on board, all in arms, and the galley properly equipped as a ship of war. This galley was decorated with great art; and by night the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and every other suitable part, were hung with lamps, which illuminated it in a very splendid manner. Every thing around was so artificially disposed, that when the fire-works were played off, the spectator was led to think, though he perceived only one galley, that the noise which he heard was produced by a naval <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>; and that the other ships were concealed from his view by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> occasioned by the guns and fireworks. This, when properly conducted, was a noble spectacle. The senate repaired thither from the cathedral, attended with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> and a numerous company. In one carriage sat six senators, the governor of the city, and sometimes the archbishop. It was exceedingly large and drawn by six <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> horses very richly harnessed. Other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> followed, with the train who attended the governor and the senators. Almost all festivals owe their origin to some extraordinary event, or some singular story either true or false. It is said, that when the splendor with which the feast of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPTION">Assumption</a> de la <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARA">Bara</a> was celebrated at Messina, first began to attract foreigners to the city, on that occasion such crowds repaired thither as to alarm the inhabitants with the fears of a famine: But one year, when the number of strangers was greater than usual at the time of this festival, the magistrates were very much at a loss how to supply them with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; and at length, every other resource failing, no hopes of relief remained but from the kindness of the Blessed Virgin. Fervent prayers were addressed to their patroness: and next morning by day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> three brigantines appeared entering the harbour with full sails. They proved to be loaded with corn. It was eagerly purchased: and the people of the city hasted to appease their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. But when they came after refreshing themselves to pay the corn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, neither ships nor merchants could be found. After their first emotions of surprise had subsided, they naturally concluded that such a seasonable supply must undoubtedly be a present from the Virgin, who, being pleased with the zeal of her Messenian votaries, and desirous to prevent the concourse of strangers who attended the festival from diminishing, had interposed in this miraculous manner to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> them from the distresses of famine. A new festival was celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to their generous benefactress. Three small vessels of silver were made, and dedicated to the Virgin in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the event; and these are at present used as lamps in the cathedral. The senate likewise decreed, that the clergy should pay annually a small tax, to be laid out in constructing a small gallery to swim on the fountain, and in defraying the expenses of the fireworks. The profits of the clergy are so considerable on the occasion of the festival, that they may be supposed to pay the tax with great cheerfulness. In Messina, as in the other cities of Sicily, the women wrap themselves in a large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mantle above the rest of their dress. The stuffs are richer or plainer according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and circumstances. People who are not rich enough to have fine clothes of their own, hire them at so much an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. There are women who make a livelihood by lending out their clothes. The mantle covers the wearer from head to foot.—It reduces the old and the young, the ill-shaped and the handsome, pretty much to an equality in point of appearance. This must naturally appear very unfavourable to the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. But yet, on proper occasions, at church or in a public walk, the ladies of Messina find means to open and adjust the mantle so as to display all their beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> and shape, and to attract the affections of lovers, perhaps more powerfully than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their dress were suited to display their charms in a more ostentatious manner. Between Messina and the tower of Faro there stands a small church called the Madonna of the Grotto. It was anciently a temple of a round structure, and ornamented with columns like the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at Rome. Modern columns now supply the place that was occupied by the ancient. There are large niches in the rock adjoining to the temple, which are thought to be of equal antiquity. These contain no sculptured figures; but in Pagan times they might possibly contain some. Messina being situated between Mount Ætna and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Charybdis, and being likewise at no great distance from the volcanoes of Lipari and Stromboli, must have been in all ages liable to suffer by earthquakes. Such terrible events, however, appear to have been more unfrequent in ancient than in modern times, and have actually alarmed the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> oftener than any other. In the year 1693 a fourth part of the cities of Sicily was destroyed by an earthquake. Messina merely felt the shock; all its buildings, however, suffered. In the year 1742 it suffered another equally violent. A plague which followed in 1743 retarded the repairs necessary after the earthquake. In the year 1780 this city <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, for more than six months, to suffer from new earthquakes. Were the state of the elements, previous to these dreadful events, carefully examined, it might perhaps be found to undergo certain changes which might be considered as prognosticating them. The autumn of the year 1782 was unusually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and rainy. Fahrenheit's thermometer was often as low as 56 degrees. The succeeding winter was dry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> never fell under 25 degrees: And, what is uncommon in that season, storms were now and then observed to arise from the west. The pilots in the channel observed that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> no longer rose at the usual periods, and the gulf of Charybdis raged with extraordinary fury. On the 5th of February 1783, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> was heavy and calm; the sky obscured with thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> seemingly all in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. About half after twelve at noon, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> began to shake with a dreadful noise. The shocks continually increased, and became at length so violent as to open the ground, and to overturn in two or three minutes a considerable part of the buildings. A long white cloud appeared to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west; and soon after another, very dark, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the heavens. The latter in a moment spread over the whole horizon, and deluged the city with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with dreadful claps of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. The inhabitants fled in the utmost terror to the fields and the ships in the harbour. From mid-day till five in the afternoon the earthquake continued almost without interruption. The shocks then became somewhat less frequent. The cries of the dying; the shrieks of those who were half buried under the ruins; the wild terror with which others, who were still able, attempted to make their escape; the despair of fathers, mothers, and husbands, bereft of those who were dearest to them; then formed altogether a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of horror, such as can but seldom occur in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the calamities of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Amid that awful scene, instances of the most heroic courage and the most generous affection were displayed. Mothers, regardless of their own safety, rushed into every danger to snatch their children from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Conjugal and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> affection prompted deeds not less desperate and heroic. But no sooner did the earthquake cease, than the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> wretches who had escaped began to feel the influence of very different passions. When they returned to visit the ruins, to seek out the situation of their fallen dwellings, to inquire into the fate of their families, to procure food and collect some remains of their former fortunes—such as found their circumstances the most wretched became suddenly animated with rage, which nothing but wild despair could inspire. The distinction of ranks, and the order of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> were disregarded, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> eagerly violated. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>, rapine, and lawless robbery, reigned among the smoking ruins. About one in the morning another shock of the earthquake was felt, which overturned most of the houses that were still standing. Most of those whom want, or avarice, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, still detained among the ruins, now shared the same fate with their friends whom the former shocks had buried under them. The succeeding day scarce alleviated the distress of this dismal night: the few wretches who still survived found themselves destitute of every necessary. At length order was in some degree re-established; and in two days after every person was supplied at least with some small portion of the necessaries for subsistence. None yet thought of returning to take up their abode among the ruins. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people fixed their residence on the plain of Porto Salvo, near the town of Salleo. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, magistrates, and merchants, took up their abode on another plain, on the other part of the stream Porto de Legno; the soldiers at Terra Nuova. Some violent shocks which were again felt on the 7th of February and the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> completed the destruction of the city. The corn magazines, however, escaped without damage: and the public ovens and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a> were but little injured. From these facts it may perhaps be inferred, that had not the houses of Messina been, in general, hastily built at the first, and afterwards carelessly repaired, fewer of them would have been overthrown by the earthquake. The neighbouring villages having suffered but little, were the first to relieve the remaining inhabitants of Messina in their distress. Maltese galleys for some days supplied necessaries to the poor and the sick with a generosity which merits the highest praise. They brought surgeons and whatever was needful for the cure of the wounded. The supplies sent by the king of France were refused, for what reason we know not. What money was needed for the support of the people was taken from the treasury of the city of Messina; for what the king of Naples sent was seized and spent by the garrison. It is said that not more than 800 or 900 persons perished by this earthquake. The sea during that convulsion of the land was slightly agitated in the harbour. Farther out the sea was more violently agitated; but none of the ships in the harbour were dashed to pieces. The waters rose so high as to be injurious in a very considerable degree to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHAROS">Pharos</a>, as well as along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a> and Bagmara. This earthquake was not of a momentary duration, like that by which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> was destroyed, and like many others; for more than sixty days from the 5th of February to the beginning of April, Messina continued to be shaken, and in that time felt more than 200 shocks; and even after that period the alarm was again and again renewed. Not only the magistrates, the soldiers and the people, but the priests likewise, with their tabernacle and altar, retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. The nuns, too, deserted their cloisters, and sought a retreat without the walls. Some of them confined themselves to the gardens of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>; others mixed indiscriminately with the people. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> damage which the public buildings within the city suffered was the fall of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> of the church of Purgatory. Only the walls were left standing; and even these had suffered considerably. One half of the steeple of the cathedral was beaten to the ground. The magazines of Porto Franco were likewise very much shattered. The fort of St Salvator, being built on an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> foundation, the side next the sea is there fallen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; but on the other side, where it is founded on a rock, it has stood unmoved by all the shocks of the earthquake. On the 5th of February, when the earthquake was more violent than at any time afterwards, a strong smell of sulphur was felt. The earth was affected somewhat in the same way as if it had been borne up on a fluid; and seemed to reel with the shocks much like a ship tossed with the waves. This tremendous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was felt all over Sicily; but towards Pharos it became weaker. On the following days the sky was cloudy; the mountains of Sicily and the shores of Calabria continued covered with a thick fog like smoke. North and north-east winds raged with the most violent impetuosity. The disastrous year of this earthquake was scarce concluded, the chasms which it had opened in the ground were still yawning, and the poor inhabitants of the adjacent country still trembled with terror, when the elements again renewed their fury to ravage this miserable land. On Tuesday the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1783, about sunrise, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> began to blow softly from the north-east. The sea gradually swelled, rose beyond its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> with rapid impetuosity, overflowed the quay of Messina, and lashed with its billows the ruins of the Palazzata. It loosened and displaced many of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>, spread over the whole street, and attacked the pedestals of the statues which had been spared by the earthquake, and still stood firm among the ruins. The same furious wind which swelled the sea in so extraordinary a manner, ravaged the whole coast from Messina all the way to Syracuse.

MESSUAGE

Pages 599-599

MESSAGIUM, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> adjoining assigned for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. By the name of messuage may a garden, shop, mill, cottage, chamber, cellar, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>.—In Scotland, messuage denotes what is called in England the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>-house, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> dwelling-house within any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>.

META

Pages 599-599

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, was a pile of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of a pyramidal form, intended as a boundary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chariot course.—When the meta was passed the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> was concluded. The greatest art and management were required in avoiding the meta, and yet going as near it as possible. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they went too near, they were in the greatest danger of breaking the chariot to pieces; and if they took too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a circuit in the turn, they gave their rivals an opportunity of getting within them, besides losing a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ground. The boundary of the Grecian stadium, or course, was called ἐπίστας, ἐπίστας, ἐπίστας and ἐπίστας ἐπίστας; to which last name Horace probably alludes, in calling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> "ultima linea rerum." The meta at Rome were first of wood, afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius made them of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, or rather gilded them. In the Roman circus there were two metæ, one at the entrance of the course, and the other at the end of it. An <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> was placed upon the top of the meta.

METACARPUS

Pages 599-599
or METACARPIUM, (from μέτα, behind, and κάρπος, hand), in Anatomy, that part of the hand between the wrist and the fingers. See ANATOMY, No. 55.

METAGITNIION

Pages 599-599

the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year, answering to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and

METAL

Pages 600-600

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> used in heraldry, by way of colours, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, in blazon called <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> and argent. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of arms these metals are represented by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, which are the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> colours of those metals. In engraving, gold is expressed by dotting the coat, &c. all over; and silver, by leaving it quite blank. It is a general rule in heraldry, never to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> metal upon metal, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> upon colour: so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the field be of one of the metals, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> must be of some colour; and if the field be of any colour, the bearing must be one of the metals. METALEPSIS. See Oratory, No. 59.

METALLISATION

Pages 600-600

is defined to be the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> by which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are formed in the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.

METALLURGY

Pages 600-600

in a more general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, comprehends the whole art of working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, from the state of ore to the utensil; and in this sense, essaying, smelting, refining, parting, smithery, gilding, &c. are only branches of metallurgy. But in a more limited sense it includes only the operations which are followed in separating metals from their ores. For an account of these processes, see Ores, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">Reduction</a> of; and for the practical branches, see Gilding, Parting, Purifying, Refining, Smithery.

METAMORPHOSIS

Pages 600-600

in general, denotes the changing of something into a different form; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it includes the transformation of insects, as well as the mythological changes related by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets. Mythological metamorphoses were held to be of two kinds, apparent and real: thus, that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> into a bull, was only apparent; whereas that of Lycaon into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, was supposed to be real. Most of the ancient metamorphoses include some allegorical meaning, relating either to physics <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> morality; some authors are even of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> is couched under them; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> and Dr Hooke have attempted to unriddle several of them.

METAPHOR

Pages 600-605

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>. See Oratory, No. 54. Metaphor and Allegory, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>.—A metaphor differs from a simile, in form only, not in substance: in a simile the two subjects are kept distinct in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, as well as in the thought; in a metaphor, the two subjects are kept distinct in the thought only, not in the expression. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> resembles a lion, and upon that resemblance many similies have been raised by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and other poets. But instead of resembling a lion, let us take the aid of the imagination, and feign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> the hero to be a lion; by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> the simile is converted into a metaphor; which is carried on by describing all the qualities of a lion that resemble those of the hero. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> here, that of resemblance, belongs to the thought. An additional pleasure arises from the expression: the poet, by figuring his hero to be a lion, goes on to describe the lion in appearance, but in reality the hero; and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is peculiarly beautiful, by expressing the virtues and qualities of the hero in new terms, which, properly speaking, belong not to him, but to the lion. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> better be understood by examples. A family connected with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, resembles a tree, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> and branches of which are connected with a common root: but let us suppose, that a family is figured, not barely to be like a tree, but to be a tree; and then the simile will be converted into a metaphor, in the following manner: Edward's sev'n sons, whereof thyself art one, Were sev'n fair branches, springing from one root; Some of these branches by the dest'ries cut: But Thomas, my dear <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, my Glo'ster, One flourishing branch of his most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> root, Is hack'd <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> leaves all faded, By Envy's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>'s bloody axe. Richard II., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> i. sc. 3. Figuring <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life to be a voyage at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. There is a tide in the affairs of men, Which, taken at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, leads on to Fortune: Omitted, all the voyage of their life Is bound in shallows and in miseries. On such a full sea are we now afloat: And we must take the current when it serves, Or lose our ventures. Julius Caesar, act iv. sc. 5. Figuring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be a garland of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>: Hotspur. Wou'd to heav'n, Thy name in arms were now as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as mine! Pr. Henry. I'll make it greater ere I <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> from thee; And all the budding honours on thy crest I'll crop, to make a garland for my head. First Part of Henry IV., act v. sc. 9. Figuring a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who hath acquired great reputation and honour to be a tree full of fruit: Oh, boys, this story The world may read in me; my body's mark'd With Roman swords; and my report was once First with the best of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. Cymbeline lov'd me; And when a soldier was the theme, my name Was not far off; then was I as a tree, Whose boughs did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> with fruit. But in one night, A storm or robbery, call it what you will, Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my leaves; And left me bare to wither. Cymbeline, act iii. sc. 3. "Blest be thy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, thou <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of shells, said Swaran of the dark-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> shield. In peace, thou art the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the mountain-storm. Take now my hand in friendship, thou noble king of Morven." Fingal. "Thou dwellest in the soul of Malvina, son of mighty <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>. My sighs arise with the beam of the east: my tears descend with the drops of night. I was a lovely tree in thy presence, Oscar, with all my branches round me: but thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> came like a blast from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>." An allegory differs from a metaphor; and a figure of speech differs from both. A metaphor is defined above to be an act of the imagination, figuring one thing to be another. An allegory requires no such operation, nor is one thing figured to be another: it consists in choosing a subject having properties or circumstances resembling those of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> subject: and the former is described in such a manner as to represent the latter: the subject thus represented is kept out of view: we are left to discover it by reflection; and we are pleased with the discovery, because it is our own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. (See the word Allegory.) Quintilian gives the following instance of an allegory. O navis, referent in mare te <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">novi</a> Fluctus. O quid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGIS">agis</a>? fortiter occupa portum. Horat. lib. ode 14. and explains it elegantly in the following words: "Tosusque ille Horatii locus, quo navim pro republica, fluctuum tempestates pro bellis civilibus, portum pro pace atque <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCORDIA">concordia</a>, dicit." In a figure of speech, there is no fiction of the imagination employed, as in a metaphor; nor a representative subject introduced, as in an allegory. This figure, as its name implies, regards the expression only, not the thought; and it may be defined, the using a word in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> different from what is proper to it.—Thus youth, or the beginning of life, is expressed figuratively by morning of life: morning is the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and in that view it is employed to signify the beginning of any other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, life especially, the progress of which is reckoned by days. See Figure of Speech. Metaphor and allegory are so much connected, that it seemed proper to handle them together: the rules particularly for distinguishing the good from the bad, are common to both. We shall therefore proceed to those rules, after adding some examples to illustrate the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of an allegory, which, with a view to this article, was but slightly illustrated under its proper name. Horace, speaking of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to Pyrrha, which was now extinguished, expressed himself thus: Me tabula sacer Votivae paries indicat uvida Suspendisse potenti Vestimenta maris Deo. Carm. lib. i. ode 5. Again: Phœbus volentem prælia me loqui, Victas et urbes, incerepit, lyra Ne parva Tyrrhenum per sequor Vela darem. Carm. lib. iv. ode 15. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>. Great lords, wise men ne'er sit and wail their loss, But cheerly seek how to redress their harms. What though the mast be now blown overboard, The cable broke, the holding <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> lost, And half our sailors swallowed in the flood! Yet lives our pilot still. Is't meet that he Should leave the helm, and, like a fearful lad, With tearful eyes add <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the sea, And give more strength to that which hath too much; While in his moan the ship splits on the rock, Which industry and courage might have sav'd? Ah, what a shame! ah, what a fault were this! Third Part of Henry VI. act v. sc. 5. Oroonoko. Ha! thou has rous'd The lion in his den; he stalks abroad, And the wide forest trembles at his roar. I find the danger now. Oroonoko. act. iii. sc. 2. "My well beloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill. He fenced it, gathered out the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> thereof, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a wine press therein; he looked that it should bring forth <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and it brought forth wild grapes. And now, O inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done? Wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes? And now go to, I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down. And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged, but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> that they <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> no rain upon it. For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant." Isaiah v. 1. The rules that govern metaphors and allegories are of two kinds. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of these figures comes under the first kind: the propriety or impropriety of introduction comes under the other.—To begin with rules of the first kind; some of which coincide with those already given for similes; some are peculiar to metaphors and allegories. In the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, It has been observed, that a simile cannot be agreeable where the resemblance is either too strong or too faint. This holds equally in metaphor and allegory; and the reason is the same in all. In the following instances, the resemblance is too faint to be agreeable. Malcolm. ————But there's no bottom, none; In my voluptuousness: your wives, your daughters, Your matrons, and your maids, could not fill-up The cistern of my lust. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, act iv. sc. 4. The best way to judge of this metaphor, is to convert it into a simile: which would be bad, because there is scarce any resemblance between lust and a cistern, or betwixt enormous lust and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cistern. Again: He cannot buckle his distemper'd cause Within the belt of rule. Macbeth, act v. sc. 2. There is no resemblance between a distempered cause and any body that can be confined within a belt. Again: Steep me in poverty to the very lips. Othello, act iv. sc. 9. Poverty Metaphor. Poverty here must be conceived a fluid, which it resembles not in any manner. Speaking to Bolingbroke banished for six years: The sullen passage of thy weary steps Esteem a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, wherein thou art to set The precious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a> of thy home return. Richard II. act ii. sc. 6. Again: Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, lady, And every word in it a gaping wound Issuing life-blood. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, act. iii. sc. 3. Tantae molis erat Romanam condere gentem. Æneid. i. 37. The following metaphor is strained beyond all endurance: Timur-bec, known to us by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a> the Great, writes to Bajazet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Ottomans in the following terms: "Where is the monarch who <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> resist us? where is the potentate who doth not glory in being numbered among our attendants? As for thee, descended from a Turcoman sailor, since the vessel of thy unbounded ambition hath been wreck'd in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of thy self-love, it would be proper, that thou shouldst take in the sails of thy temerity, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the anchor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> in the port of sincerity and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, which is the port of safety; lest the tempest of our vengeance make thee perish in the sea of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> thou deservest." Such strained figures, as observed above, are not unfrequent in the first dawn of refinement; the mind in a new enjoyment knows no bounds, and is generally carried to excess, till <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> discover the proper limits. Secondly. Whatever resemblance subjects may have, it is wrong to put one for another, where they bear no mutual proportion. Upon comparing a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> to a very low subject, the simile takes on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>; and the same will be the effect where the one is imagined to be the other, as in a metaphor; or made to represent the other, as in an allegory. Thirdly. These figures, a metaphor especially, ought not to be crowded with many minute circumstances; for in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is scarcely possible to avoid obscurity. A metaphor above all ought to be short: it is difficult, for any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to support a lively image of a thing being what we know it is not; and for that reason, a metaphor drawn out to any length, instead of illustrating or enlivening the principal subject, becomes disagreeable by overstraining the mind. Here Cowley is extremely licentious. Take the following instance. Great and wise conqu'ror, who where'er Thou com'st, dost fortify and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there! Who canst defend as well as get; And never hadst one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up yet; Now thou art in, thou ne'er will part With one inch of my vanquish'd heart; For since thou took'st it by assault from me 'Tis garrison'd so strong with thoughts of thee, It fears no beauteous enemy. For the same reason, however agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> allegories may at first be by their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, they never afford any lasting pleasure: witness the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">Fairy</a> Queen, which with great power of expression, variety of images, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of versification, is scarce ever read a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time. In the fourth place. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> carried on in a simile, being in a metaphor sunk by imagining the principal subject to be that very thing which it only resembles; an opportunity is furnished to describe it in terms taken strictly or literally with respect to its imagined nature. This suggests another rule, That in constructing a metaphor, the writer ought to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of such words only as are applicable literally to the imagined nature of his subject: figurative words ought carefully to be avoided; for such complicated figures, instead of setting the principal subject in a strong <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, involve it in a cloud, and it is well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the reader, without rejecting by the lump, endeavour patiently to gather the plain meaning, regardless of the figures: A stubborn and unconquerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> Creeps in his veins, and drinks the streams of life. Lady Jane Gray, act i. sc. 1. Copied from Ovid: Sorbent avidæ præcordia flammæ. Metamorph. lib. ix. 172. Let us analyze this expression. That a fever may be imagined a flame, we admit: though more than one step is necessary to come at the resemblance: a fever, by heating the body, resembles fire; and it is no stretch to imagine a fever to be a fire: again, by a figure of speech, flame may be put for fire, because they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> conjoined; and therefore a fever may be termed a flame. But now admitting a fever to be a flame, its effects ought to be explained in words that agree literally to a flame. This rule is not observed here; for a flame drinks figuratively only, not properly. King Henry to his son <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry: Thou hid'st a thousand daggers in thy thoughts, Which thou hast whetted on thy stony heart To stab at half an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of my frail life. Second Part Henry IV. act iv. sc. ii. Such faulty metaphors are pleasantly ridiculed in the Rehearsal: Physician. Sir, to conclude, the place you fill has more than amply exacted the talents of a wary pilot; and all these threatening storms, which, like impregnable clouds, hover o'er our heads, will, when they once are grasp'd but by the eye of reason, melt into fruitful showers of blessings on the people. "Boyce. Pray mark that allegory. Is not that good? "Johnson. Yes, that grasping of a storm with the eye is admirable. Act ii. sc. i. Fifthly. The jumbling different metaphors in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, beginning with one metaphor and ending with another, commonly called a mixt metaphor, ought never to be indulged. K. Henry. K. Henry.—Will you again unknit This churlish knot of all abhorred war, And move in that obedient orb again, Where you did give a fair and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> light? First Part Henry VI. act. v. sc. r. Whether 'tis nobler in the mind, to suffer The stings and arrows of outrageous fortune; Or to take arms against a sea of troubles, And by opposing end them. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>, act iii. sc. 2. In the sixth place, It is unpleasant to join different metaphors in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, even where they are preserved distinct: for when the subject is imagined to be first one thing and then another in the same period without <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, the mind is distracted by the rapid transition; and when the imagination is put on such hard duty, its images are too faint to produce any good effect: At <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a> gravi jamdudum saucia cara, Volnus alit venis, et eceo carpitur igni. Æneid. iv. 1. Est mollis flamma medullas Interea, et tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus. Æneid. iv. 66. Motum ex Metello consule civicum, Bellique causas, et vitia, et modos, Ludumque fortunae, gravesque Principum amicitias, et arma Nondum expatiis uncta cruroribus, Periculoso plenum opus alee, Tractas, et incedis per ignes Subpositos cineri doloso. Horat. Carm. lib. ii. ode 1.
