They obtained their name from the exact regularity of their lives; which gave occasion to a young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of Christ church to say, "Here is a new set of Methodists sprung up;" alluding to a sect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians which went by that name. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> regularity, however, soon brought a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> against them, perhaps not altogether without foundation, of being too scrupulous, and carrying their sanctity to too great a height. In particular it was urged, that they laid too much stress upon the rubrics and canons of the church, insisted too much on observing the rules of the university, and took the scriptures in too literal a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and to the name of Methodists two others were quickly added, viz. those of Sacramentarians and the Godly Club. The principal person in this club while in its infancy appears to have been Mr Morgan, and next to him Mr John Wesley. They visited the sick, and instituted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the relief of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; and the better to accomplish their benevolent designs, Mr Wesley abridged himself of all his superfluities, and even of some of the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and by proposing the scheme to some gentlemen, they quickly increased their funds to £2l. per annum. This, which one should have thought would have been attended with praise instead of censure, quickly drew upon them a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>; some of the seniors of the university began to interfere, and it was reported "that the college censors were going to blow up the Godly Club." They found themselves, however, patronised and encouraged by some men eminent for their learning and virtue; so that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, though they had suffered a severe loss in 1730 in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mr Morgan, who had indeed been the founder of it. In the month of October 1735, John and Charles Wesley, Mr Ingham, and Mr Delamotte son to a merchant in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> along with Mr Oglethorpe, afterwards General Oglethorpe. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of this voyage was to preach the gospel to the Indians. By this time, however, it appears that Mr Wesley had embraced such notions as may without the least <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> be accounted fanatical. Thus in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Samuel, he conjures him to banish from his school "the classics with their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>," and to introduce instead of them such Christian authors as would <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> together with him in "<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> up his flock in the knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of God." During the voyage such a profession of worship was observed, as we cannot help thinking savoured more of a Pharisaical than Christian behaviour; an account of which, as a similar strictness would certainly be inculcated upon the disciples, and consequently must give a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> idea of the principles of the early Methodists, we shall here transcribe from Mr Wesley's life. "From four in the morning till five, each of us used private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; from five to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> we read the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> together, carefully comparing it (that we might not lean to our own understandings) with the writings of the earliest ages; at seven we breakfasted; at eight were the public prayers; from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> to twelve learned the languages and instructed the children; at twelve we met to give an account to one another what we had done since our last meeting, and what we designed to do before our next; at one we dined; the time from dinner to four we spent in reading to those of whom each of us had taken charge, or in speaking to them separately as need required; at four were the evening prayers, when either the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> lesson was explained (as it always was in the morning), or the children were catechised and instructed before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>; from five to six we again used private prayer; from six to seven I read in our cabin to two or three of the passengers, of whom there were about 80 English on board; and each of my brethren to a few more in theirs; at seven I joined with the Germans in their public <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, while Mr Ingham was reading between decks to as many as desired to hear; at eight we met again, to instruct and exhort one another; between nine and ten we went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, when neither the roaring of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> nor the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the ship could take away the refreshing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> which God gave us." As they proceeded in their passage, this austerity instead of being diminished was increased. Mr Wesley discontinued the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of wine and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; confining himself to vegetables, chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and biscuit. He ate no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>; and his bed having been made wet by the sea, he lay upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, and slept soundly till morning. In his Journal he says, "I believe I shall not find it needful to go to bed, as it is called, any more;" but whether this was really done or not, we cannot say. The missionaries, after their arrival, were at first very favourably received, but in a short time lost the affections of the people entirely. This was owing to the behaviour of Mr Wesley himself, who appeared not only capricious but frequently despotic. He particularly gave offence by insisting upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of children by immersion; and his excessive austerity with regard to himself Methodists himself did not tend to give his hearers any favourable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> either of the superior sanctity or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of their teacher. At last, on account of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> with Mr Causton the storekeeper and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVANNAH">Savannah</a> which ended in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, he was obliged to return to England. Thus the cause of Methodism seemed to be entirely lost in Georgia. But Mr Wesley was soon succeeded by a more popular and successful champion, viz. Mr George Whitefield; who having spent his time during the voyage in converting the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> with whom he sailed, arrived at Savannah in Georgia on the 7th of May 1738. Here he was received by Mr Delamotte, was joined by several of Mr Wesley's hearers, and became intimate with some other ministers. Mr Ingham had made some progress in converting a few runaway Creek Indians, who had a settlement about four miles from Savannah; but being obliged to return to England in a few months, this design was frustrated, and the Indians in a few years separated. During the short time that Mr Whitefield resided at Savannah, he became extremely popular; and indeed the instances of his success in the way of making converts are very surprising. However, he was obliged to return to England in the autumn of that year, that he might receive priests orders. On his return to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in October 1739, he landed at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, and instantly began his spiritual labours as in other places; being attended with astonishing success not only there but wherever he went. Passing through the colonies of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and South Carolina, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of converts continually increased; but on his arrival at Savannah, he found the colony almost deserted. He now resumed the scheme he had formerly projected of building an Orphan-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and for this he made the first collection at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a> in South Carolina, amounting to about 70l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. His zeal in the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, or of the colony, were not, however, sufficient to procure him the favour of those in power. On his return to Philadelphia, after a short stay at Savannah, the churches were denied him; but he was made ample amends by the success which attended his field preachings and private efforts. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> were everywhere set up, and many were converted with symptoms of enthusiasm, different according to their various tempers and constitutions. During this excursion, he was so successful in his collection for the Orphan-house, that on his return to Savannah he brought along with him <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> to the value of 500l. sterling. The success in Georgia was now greater than ever; but the many charities which it was necessary to supply, rendered it necessary in a short time for him to undertake another journey to Charlestown. Here his principles met with the greatest opposition. He had lost the favour of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> by his field-preaching, and was denied the sacrament. The opposition, however, was altogether fruitless; the number of converts increased wherever he went, and he now undertook a voyage to New England. In this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> also the established clergy were his enemies; but the usual success attended his other endeavours, and procured 500l. more for the use of the Orphans in Georgia. From the year 1741 to 1743 America was deprived of Mr Whitefield's preaching, he having spent that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> in England; but in 1744 he again set out for Methodists, the western continent. The remarkable success which had hitherto attended his labours now stirred up many opponents; and these had met with the greater success, as none of the Methodist preachers whom he had left were possessed of such abilities either to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the favour of those who heard them, or to defend their doctrines against objections. Mr Whitefield's success, however, was the same as before: he even found means to inspire the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> class with such sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Pepperell could not undertake his expedition against Louisbourg without first consulting Mr Whitefield; and great numbers of New-Englanders went volunteers, confident of victory, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the discourses of their teacher. From the continent of America Mr Whitefield took a voyage to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERMUDAS">Bermudas</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; and here, as everywhere else, he met with the most surprising success. Here also collections were made for the Orphan-house in Savannah, which were transmitted to that place. Supposing it to be better for his cause to visit different countries, than to take up a permanent residence in one, Mr Whitefield left Bermudas in a few months, and did not return to America till 1751, when the Orphan-house was found to be in a very flourishing situation. After a short stay, he set sail again for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Here he remained two years, and then set out on another visit to America, landing at Charlestown on the 27th of May 1754. His presence constantly revived the spirits and cause of his party, and added to their numbers wherever he went. Next year he returned to England; but after labouring in the usual manner, and meeting with the usual success there till the year 1763, he set sail again for America, and arrived at Virginia in the latter end of August. He now visited all the colonies, and found that great progress had been made in converting the Indians. On his arrival at Georgia, matters were found in a very flourishing situation, and he received the thanks of the governor and principal people for the great benefit he had been to the colony; which shows, that the stories which had been so industriously propagated, concerning the avarice of him and other Methodist preachers, were, partly at least, unfounded. In 1765 he returned to England; and in 1769 made his seventh and last voyage to America, landing at Charlestown on the 30th of November the same year. He was still attended with the same success; and indeed it is impossible to read, without admiration, on account of the efforts made by himself and Mr Wesley, to propagate their tenets in the different parts of the world. For a very considerable time Mr Whitefield was the only Methodist who paid any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to America; and in that country he was more popular than even in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Towards the end of his life, several Methodists having emigrated from Britain, formed distinct societies in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> and Philadelphia. These quickly increased in number; and, about the time that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Britain began, their numbers amounted to about 3000 in Virginia, Maryland, New York, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>. They would probably have increased much more, had it not been for the imprudence of some of their preachers, who intro- Vol. XIII. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. Methodists introduced politics into their discourses, and thus rendered themselves obnoxious to the people among whom they lived. Among those who hurt the cause in this manner was Mr Wesley himself, who, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a piece entitled *A Calm <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">Address</a> to the American Colonies*, would in all probability have ruined it, had not a gentleman, with whom he was connected, destroyed or sent back to England the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> as soon as it arrived in America, so that its existence was scarce known in that continent. At the conclusion of the war, Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, who in 1776 had left a curacy in England in order to join Mr Wesley, paid a visit to his friends in America; though it had been imagined that a total separation had taken place between the American and European Methodists. This breach was, however, made up by a manoeuvre of Mr Wesley; for no sooner had the Americans obtained their independence, than he, who had hitherto branded them with the name of rebels, sent a congratulatory letter on their freedom from the "State and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">Hierarchy</a>," and exhorting them to "stand fast in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> with which God had so strangely made them free." To show his zeal in their service still farther, he gave ordination, by laying on of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, to several preachers who were to embark for America, and consecrated Dr Coke one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the Methodist Episcopal church in that country. He extracted also from the liturgy of the English church one for the American Methodists, taking particular care to expunge every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> that had a particular respect to the regal authority. Such proceedings in one who had formerly professed such extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the English church, could not but require an apology; and this was accordingly made in a pastoral letter transmitted to the American societies, and addressed "to Dr Coke, Mr Astbury, and our brethren in North America." In this letter he makes the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his conduct. "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s account of the primitive church convinced me, many years ago, that bishops and presbyters are the same order, and consequently have the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to ordain. For many years I have been importuned, from time to time, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> this right, by ordaining part of our travelling preachers. But I have still refused, not only for the sake of peace, but because I was determined, as little as possible, to violate the established order of the national church to which I belonged. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is widely different between England and North America. Here there are bishops who have a legal jurisdiction: in America there are none, neither any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> ministers: so that for some hundred miles together, there is none either to baptize, or to administer the Lord's supper. Here, therefore, my scruples are at an end; and I conceive myself at full liberty, as I violate no order, and invade no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s right, by appointing and sending labourers into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. It has indeed been proposed to desire the English bishops to ordain part of our preachers for America; but to this I object. 1. I desired the bishop of London to ordain only one, but could not prevail. 2. If they consented, we know the slowness of their proceedings; but the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> admits of no delay. 3. If they would ordain them now, they would likewise expect to govern them; and how grievously would that entangle us. 4. As our American brethren are now totally disentangled, both from the state and the English hierarchy, we dare not entangle them again either with the one or the other. They are now at full liberty simply to follow the scripture and the primitive church; and we judge it best, that they should stand fast in that liberty wherewith God has so strangely made them free." Dr Coke, on the consecration of Mr Astbury to the office of a bishop, made another apology. "The church of England (says he), of which the society of Methodists in general have till lately professed themselves a part, did for many years groan in America under grievances of the heaviest kind. Subjected to a hierarchy which weighs everything in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of politics, its most important interests were repeatedly sacrificed to the supposed advantages of England. The churches were in general filled with the parasites and bottle-companions of the rich and great. The humble and most unfortunate entreaties of the oppressed flocks, yea the representations of a general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> itself, were contemned and despised. Everything sacred must bow <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at the feet of a party; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of mankind be sacrificed to their views; and the drunkard, the fornicator, and the extortioner, triumphed over bleeding <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZION">Zion</a>, because they were faithful abettors of the ruling powers. The memorable revolution has struck off these intolerable fetters, and broken the anti-christian union which before subsisted between church and state. And had there been no other advantage arising from that glorious epoch, this itself, I believe, would have made ample compensation for all the calamities of the war; one happy consequence of which was the expulsion of most of those hirelings, who "ate the fat, and clothed themselves with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, but strengthened not the diseased," &c. The parochial churches in general being hereby vacant, our people were deprived of the sacraments through the greatest part of these states, and continue so still. What method can we take in so critical a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>? God has given us sufficient resources in ourselves; and, after mature deliberation, we believe that we are called to draw them forth. "But what right have you to ordain?" The same right as most of the churches in Christendom; our ordination, in its lowest view, being equal to any of the presbyterian, as originating with three presbyters of the church of England. "But what right have you to exercise the episcopal office?" To me the most manifest and clear. God has been pleased to raise up, by Mr Wesley, in America and Europe, a numerous society well known by the name of Methodists. The whole body have invariably esteemed this man as their chief pastor under Christ. He has constantly appointed all their religious officers from the highest to the lowest, by himself or his delegate. And we are fully persuaded there is no church office which he judges expedient for the welfare of the people entrusted to his charge, but, as essential to his station, he has power to ordain. "But, do not you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the succession?" The uninterrupted succession of bishops is a point that has long been given up by the most able Protestant defenders of episcopacy. Bishop Hoadley himself, in his celebrated controversy with Dr Calamy, allows it to be unnecessary. His words are, 'To the 13th question I answer, that I think not an uninterrupted line of succession so grants the authenticity of the anecdote given us by St Jerome, which informs us, that the church of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> had no regular succession from the time of St Mark the evangelist, the first bishop of that church, to the time of Dionysius, a space of 200 years; but the college of presbyters, on the death of a bishop, elected another in his stead. We are also informed, from the epistle of St Clement to the Corinthians, written soon after the death of St Paul, a writer whose works are next in precedence to the canon of scripture, and probably written by immediate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, that the church of Corinth was then governed only by a college of presbyters. And from the epistle of Polycarp to the church of Philippi, written in 116, we also find that the Christian Philippians were then governed only by a college of presbyters. So that the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were so far from esteeming the regular succession as essential to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of a Christian church, that, in some instances, episcopacy itself was wholly omitted. Such was the defence urged by Mr Wesley for this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> of episcopal powers: a conduct, however, of which he afterwards repented, as tending to make a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> separation betwixt his followers and the church of England. Yet it does not appear that this had any bad effect on the minds of his American brethren; for Dr Coke, on his arrival on the western continent, found the societies numerous and flourishing. His first efforts were directed against the slave trade; and not only the abolition of that traffic, but the release of all those who were actually slaves at the time, seem to have been his favourite objects. By interfering in this matter, however, perhaps with too much zeal, he involved himself in danger. Some riots took place, and a lady offered the mob 50 guineas if they would give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> 100 lashes. This piece of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> would have been inflicted, had it not been for the interposition of a sturdy colonel; and the Doctor had not only the satisfaction of escaping the intended <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, but of seeing his doctrine so far attended to, that some slaves were emancipated. Mr Hampson, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Mr Wesley, observes, that "the colonists, in the infancy of Methodism, conducted themselves with more propriety than the English. There was little or no persecution, nor anything like a riot, except in one or two instances which have been mentioned as the consequence of the animadversions on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>; and even these were productive of no mischief. Not a creature was materially injured; no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were broken, nor any lives lost; which was not the case in this country. Here many thousands of innocent people were subjected to the grossest indignities, and several were eventually sacrificed to the fury of their persecutors." "While we commend the Americans for their behaviour in opposition to the brutality of English mobs, it may be proper to inquire into the sources of this distinction. Something of this may have arisen from similarity of sentiment. The Americans, from the first beginnings of colonization, had been accustomed to the doctrines of the old puritans and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONCONFORMISTS">nonconformists</a>, which in many respects have a near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to the Methodist tenets. The origin of Methodism in America was seldom, if ever, attended, either under the Methodist discourses of Mr Whitefield's or Mr Wesley's preachers, with those ridiculous effects with which it was accompanied in these kingdoms. Most of the preachers, who went over to the continent, having laboured for some years in Europe previous to their having crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, had exhausted their wildfire; so that their discourses were more scriptural and rational than those of the primitive Methodists. Another reason may be found in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the Americans. As a people, they are better cultivated than the body of the English; they are chiefly composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and a respectable gentry; and there is but a small proportion of that class, so superabundant here, which we distinguish by the name of mob. "The only exception we have heard, to their exemption from the extravagancies which in this country marked the infancy of Methodism, is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> they have introduced in Maryland and Virginia. Frequently, at the conclusion of a sermon, the whole congregation began to pray and to praise God aloud. The uproar which this must create may easily be conceived. Some we are told, are great admirers of this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of enthusiasm, in which every man is his own minister, and one sings and another prays, with the most discordant devotion. But we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not dignify such indecency with such a name. Its proper appellation is fanaticism. We hope, that, for the future, religion will never appear in this country under so odious a form; and greatly is it to be lamented, that, among the friends of Christianity, any such absurdities should arise, to furnish infidels with occasions of triumph." Our author informs us, that the occupation of the Methodist preachers in America was very laborious. In the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> they frequently rode 20 or 30 miles, preaching twice or thrice, and sometimes to considerable congregations. Notwithstanding this labour, however, few or none of them ever thought of returning to Britain. Several reasons may be assigned for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> they took in this laborious exercise. "Their excursions (says Mr Hampson) through immense forests abounding in trees of all sorts and sizes, were often highly romantic. Innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and falls of water; vistas opening to the view, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> with the uncultivated wild; deer now <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> across the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and now scouring through the woods, while the eye was frequently relieved by the appearance of orchards and plantations, and the houses of gentlemen and farmers peeping through the trees; formed a scenery so various and picturesque, as to produce a variety of reflection, and present, we will not say to a philosophic eye, but to the mind of every reasonable creature, the most sublime and agreeable images. "Their worship partook of the general simplicity. It was frequently conducted in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The woods resounded to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the preacher, or to the singing of his numerous congregations; while their horses, fastened to the trees, formed a singular addition to the solemnity. It was indeed a striking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>; and might naturally impress the mind with a retrospect of the antediluvian days, when the hills and valleys re-echoed the patriarchal devotions, and a Seth or an Enoch, in the shadow of a projecting rock, or beneath the foliage..." Methodists of some venerable oak, delivered his primeval lectures, and was a "preacher of righteousness to the people." The American hospitality is supposed by Mr Hampson to have been another reason for the assiduity of the Methodist teachers, as well as the consciousness of being well employed, and the satisfaction resulting from considerations of public utility. As many of the preachers were men of fervent piety, this reflection would have its full <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and the instruction of the ignorant and the reformation of the profligate would be considered as the best recompense of their labours. Spreading themselves through the continent, they took in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, Georgia, with the principal places in both <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAROLINAS">Carolinas</a>, Virginia, Maryland, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a>, Pennsylvania, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, and New York; numbering upwards of 43,000 members of their society, exclusive of about 80 itinerants, and a considerable number of local preachers, who took no circuits, but assisted occasionally in the neighbourhood of their respective residence. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and expensive buildings which the colonists have erected for public worship, almost exceed credibility; and several colleges are founded for the instruction of youth. How far the proposed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of uniting genuine religion and extensive learning will be carried into execution, time only can discover. It must materially depend on the character of the presidents and tutors, and the provision that shall be made for their support. Men of real erudition will never be procured at low salaries; and it is in vain to attempt establishments of this sort without a liberal provision for the professors of every branch of science. Two of these places are called Cokesbury and Wesley Colleges. How they are endowed, or whether they propose to obtain authority to confer degrees, we are not informed. But perhaps they are rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> than colleges; which indeed is a circumstance to be wished, as good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> schools are of the utmost service to the progress of literature. The great success which attended the Methodist preachers in America naturally determined Mr Wesley to try the West <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> islands. The Moravians had already attempted to establish their principles in some of these islands; and in 1786 some preachers were sent from the Methodists in England to the West Indies. In many of these they met with success. Societies were formed in Barbadoes, St Vincent's, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>, St Christopher's, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a>, Antigua, St Eustatius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORTOLA">Tortola</a>, and St Croix, amounting in all to near 5000 persons. At this time the whole number of Methodists in America and the West Indies amounted to about 43,302. These societies consisted both of whites and blacks: on the continent they were mostly whites, but in the islands <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. "But it is to be observed (says Mr Hampson) that the subjection of the negroes, and the obedience in which they are trained, must inculcate a docility peculiarly favourable to the purposes of a mission." Some of the missionaries went also to St Vincent's, where they met with some success, and have established some schools, in which their children are carefully instructed in the principles of religion. "In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1789 (says our author), Dr Coke paid a visit to Jamaica, and gave them several sermons. As he made but a short stay, it could hardly be considered as a fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. Should a mission be established here, as well as in the other islands, which will probably be the case, it is hoped it will be the means of correcting one vice at least, and that is dwelling; a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> relic of Gothic barbarity, by which all the islands have for many years been distinguished. Perhaps too it will give some check to the spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and dissipation; and teach the planters, if it be found impracticable to emancipate their slaves, at least to treat them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>." It has been debated among the leading men of the Methodistical profession, whether the cause might not be served by sending missionaries to the East Indies and to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; but these projects were dropped, as there was no invitation, nor any prospect of success if it had been adopted. A mission has been formed to the new settlement called <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENTUCKY">Kentucky</a>, on the confines of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> territories, near the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>. The danger of the missionaries at the time they undertook this service was certainly very great; yet such was their zeal for the cause, that they voluntarily offered themselves: but we are not yet informed what success they have met with. While Methodism was thus making rapid progress in America, its teachers were equally indefatigable in Britain. A most remarkable particular, however, occurs with regard to Mr Wesley himself; for though he had gone to Georgia, as has been already related, to convert the Indians to Christianity, yet on his return to England in 1738, he took it into his head that he, their teacher, was not yet converted: the reason was, that he had not the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of assurance. This, however, was not long wanting. He arrived in England on the first day of February, and was blest with the assurance on the sixth of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> following. This was immediately announced to the public; and the consequence, if we may believe him, was, that God then began to work by his ministry, which he had not done before. Being joined by one Kinchin, a fellow of Corpus, they travelled to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, Holms Chapel, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, and other places, where they preached, exhorted, and conversed on religious subjects, in public houses, stables, &c., sometimes meeting with success and sometimes not. During this peregrination Mr Wesley certainly displayed a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, which we must undoubtedly suppose to have been communicated to his hearers, and to have caused them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> on many occasions in a very ridiculous manner. An instance follows: "The next day (says he), March 11th, we dined at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>, and, soon after we left it, were reproved for our negligence there (in letting those who attended us go without either exhortation or instruction) by a severe shower of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>!" About the latter end of March or beginning of April he and his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> began to pray extempore, leaving off entirely the forms of the church of England, to which he had formerly been so devoted. The doctrine of instantaneous conversion, which his imagination had suggested to him as a work performed on himself, was greedily received by some of his hearers; and all the converts to the new doctrine confirmed themselves, and contributed greatly to persuade others, by declarations of their experiences, as they called them: how- This new doctrine of an instantaneous, and in fact miraculous impulse, though greatly relished by the enthusiastic part of the society, was very much disliked by others, particularly Mr Charles Wesley his brother, who warned him of the mischief he was doing; though he himself was soon converted, and, what is very astonishing, two days before John Wesley himself. The particulars related of these miraculous conversions are truly disgraceful, and could not but bring into contempt the society which consisted of such enthusiasts. "Many (says Mr Hampson) are represented as falling suddenly to the ground, in horror and agony not to be conceived, and rising again with equal expressions of peace and consolation." Their conversions were usually attended with these violent symptoms; and, for several years, few meetings occurred where Mr Wesley presided, without one or more instances of the same kind. It was not possible that such transactions should <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without notice. The confusion that too often prevailed, the emotions of the persons affected, and the exultations of the rest, which were severally animadverted upon, gave great and general offence. Many insisted, that it must either be occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the rooms, and the agitation of the animal spirits under discourses of the most alarming <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; or that it was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> artifice and hypocrisy. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, two of the sons of a Mrs Hutton in London, happening to become converts to the new doctrine, this lady was so much offended, that she wrote to Mr Samuel Wesley, informing him, that she was of opinion his brother John had lost his senses; and requesting, that the next time he came to his house, he, Mr Samuel, would either confine or convert him. All that could be done, however, to prevent the progress of the new doctrine was insufficient; and the first Methodist society was formed in London on the first of May 1738, when about 50 agreed to meet together once a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, for free conversation, begun and ended with singing and prayer. All this time, however, it seems that the conversion of Mr Wesley was far from being so complete as that of many of his hearers. He had preached and converted others, while he himself was absolutely unconverted. The knowledge of the true saving faith was only revealed to him on the 6th of March, and he did not <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> its power till the 24th of May; and even after this, his doubts and fears were still so great, that on the 13th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> he undertook a voyage to Germany, where, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Zinzendorff, his faith seems to have been thoroughly confirmed. On Mr Wesley's return, September 16th, 1738, he applied himself with the greatest assiduity and success to the propagation of his doctrine. Multitudes of converts were made in various parts of the kingdom; and the reproaches poured upon him by his opponents, seemed to have rendered his zeal more fervent if possible than before. It is remarkable, however, that some of his old friends were now so much offended with his conduct or his principles, that they absolutely refused to keep company with him. His original plan seems to have been, to make an union of Methodist clergymen, and disseminate his principles by their means. But in this he succeeded so ill, that in a letter written in 1742, he wished for a clerical assistant, were he only in deacons orders: but adds, "I know of none such, who is willing to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> with us; and I scarce expect I shall, because I know how fast they are rivetted in the service of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and the world before they leave the university."—Finding at last that nothing could be done with them, he was obliged to have recourse to lay preachers; and easily selected those who appeared to have the greatest talents for prayer and exhortation in the private meetings appointed for that purpose. Thus he at once raised himself to be the head of a sect; as the lay preachers willingly yielded obedience to him who had the advantages of superior learning and abilities, and was besides in orders as a clergyman; and this obedience he did not fail on every occasion to exact. If his doctrine had formerly given offence to the established clergy, the appointment of lay preachers was reckoned much worse; and their being appointed without any form of ordination whatever, which almost all of them were, subjected them to contempt and reproach, which their want of learning, and very often of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> abilities, did not contribute to remove. Thus finding the churches shut against him and his followers, he was obliged to preach in the fields, and made his first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> in this way on the second of April 1739, in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>; Mr Whitefield having set him an example the day before. The success of those ignorant and itinerant preachers, with their absurd and uncharitable discourses and behaviour, so provoked their adversaries, that a persecution was soon commenced against them. Mr Wesley himself was calumniated in the harshest manner, being sometimes said to be a Jesuit, sometimes an illiterate enthusiast, as the people took it into their heads. Many pretended to answer him in writing, without being able to do so: the consequence was, that their deficiency of argument was supplied by invective, and the most scandalous performances made their appearance. Some of the English clergy so far forgot themselves as to instigate the mob against them, and the most cruel outrages were committed upon them in various places. For some time the persecuted party adhered to the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> obedience and non-resistance, which their inhuman adversaries did not fail to take the advantage of.—The less they were opposed, the more insolent they became. The Methodists were frequently in danger of their lives. Men, women with child, and even children, were knocked down and abused with the same undistinguishing fury. Houses were stripped of their furniture, vast quantities of furniture carried off, featherbeds cut in pieces and strewed over the streets, several reputable people were forced into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, &c. To the disgrace of magistracy also it was found, that when application was made to the justices of the peace, redress was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> denied; nor was a step put to these shameful proceedings without a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> mandate for the purpose. From the year 1738 to 1747 Mr Wesley and his itinerants were employed in various parts of England. Methodists. In 1747 he went over to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, where a society had been formed by one Mr Williams, a clergyman. Here they proved so successful, notwithstanding the number of Papists, and the violence of their other opponents, that in 1750 they had erected meeting-houses in every part of the kingdom, and had formed 29 circuits, which employed 67 itinerants, besides a considerable number of local preachers. An invitation was given to Mr Wesley, in 1751, to visit Scotland, by an officer in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUSSELBURGH">Musselburgh</a>. He accordingly took a journey thither the same year; but left the place, after preaching in it once or twice. In 1753 he returned to Scotland, and visited Glasgow. Societies were at length formed in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, as well as at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>, Aberdeen, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, and a few other places; but his success was by no means equal to what it had been in other parts; for in 1790 the number of circuits in Scotland was no more than eight, which were supplied by 20 itinerants. Mr Whitefield, the other great labourer in the vineyard, was equally indefatigable, and probably more successful than Mr Wesley. Before entering into orders, he had formed a society of religious persons at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>; here he preached his first sermon on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a> and Benefit of Religious Society; here he became extremely popular, as well as at Bristol and London, while preparing to set sail for Georgia for the first time; and in all places to which he came, large collections were made for the poor. He maintained the same doctrine with Mr Wesley as to the new birth; which likewise gave offence to the clergy when delivered by him, as it had done with Mr Wesley. In the various intervals of his voyages to America, he employed himself with the very same assiduity in Britain and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, which we have already taken notice of in the western continent. His success was everywhere prodigious. In 1741 he was invited to Scotland, and preached his first sermon there at Dunfermline. From thence he went to Edinburgh, and preached in several of the established churches, but differed with Messrs Ralph and Ebenezer Erskine; so that he, as well as Mr Wesley, proved unsuccessful in forming a coalition with any other religious party. In the private way, however, his success was very considerable, at Edinburgh, Glasgow, Aberdeen, Dundee, and other places. In 1742 he paid a second visit to Scotland, and a third one in 1748. In 1751 he visited Ireland for the first time; and preached to great multitudes, without being molested, even in places where others had been mobbed. From thence he returned to Scotland the same year, and speaks in very favourable terms of the attention the people there paid to their Bibles. In 1752 and 1753 he again visited the same kingdom, and the last time distinguished himself by preaching against the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a> in Glasgow. In 1756 he returned; and by his animated discourses at Edinburgh against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> and arbitrary power, was owned to have contributed very much to the increase of courage and loyalty in this country. Next year he again visited the Scottish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> during the time that the General Assembly sat, and his sermons were attended by several of the members. At Glasgow he made a large collection for the poor of that city, and from thence took a voyage to Ireland. He was received with the usual Methodist affection by the lower classes of Protestants; but the Popish rabble, exasperated at his success, almost murdered him with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. After passing through a great part of Ireland, visiting England and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, he paid another visit to Scotland, where four clergymen now <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> him their pulpits. His last visit was in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1758, when his congregations were as large as ever; and it is to his endeavours principally that we are to ascribe the great number of Methodist societies now existing in Scotland. With regard to the religious principles of the Methodists, we cannot enter into any particular detail; neither indeed are there any doctrines peculiar to all included under that name, except the single one of universal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>. In March 1741, Mr Whitefield being returned to England, entirely separated from Mr Wesley and his friends, "because he did not hold the decrees."—Here was the first breach, which warm men persuaded Mr Whitefield to make, merely for a difference of opinion. Those indeed who believed universal redemption, had no desire at all to separate; but those who held particular redemption, would not hear of any accommodation, being determined to have no fellowship with men that "were in such dangerous errors." So there were now two sorts of Methodists so called; those for particular, and those for general redemption. Not many years passed, before William Cudworth and James Rolly separated from Mr Whitefield.—These were properly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTINOMIANS">Antinomians</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> avowed enemies to the law of God, which they never preached or professed to preach, but termed all legalists who did. With them, preaching the law was an abomination. They had nothing to do with the law. They would preach Christ, as they called it; but without one word either of holiness or good works. Yet these were still denominated Methodists, although differing from Mr Whitefield both in judgment and practice, abundantly more than Mr Whitefield did from Mr Wesley. In the mean time, Mr Venn and Mr Romaine began to be spoken of; and not long after Mr Madan and Mr Berridge, with a few other clergymen, who, although they had no connexion with each other, yet preaching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> by faith, and endeavouring to live accordingly, to be Bible Christians, were soon included in the general name of Methodists. And so indeed were all others who preached salvation by faith, and appeared more serious than their neighbours. Some of these were quite regular in their manner of preaching; some were quite <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, (though not by choice; but necessity was laid upon them, they must preach irregularly, or not at all); and others were between both; regular in most, though not in all particulars. In 1762, George <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a> and a few other persons began to speak great words. In the latter end of the year they foretold that the world would be at an end on the 28th of February. Mr Wesley, with whom they were then connected, withstood them both in public and private. This they would not endure; so, in January and February 1763, they separated from him, under the care of Mr Maxfield, one of Mr Wesley's preachers. But still Mr Maxfield and his adherents, circumstances, &c., in opposition to empirics and charlatans, who use violent medicines, and pretended secrets or nostrums.

METHUSELAH

Pages 793-793

the son of Enoch and father of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAMECH">Lamech</a>, was born in the year of the world 687, begat Lamech in 874, and died in 1656, being the very year of the deluge, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 969, which is the greatest age that has been attained by any mortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> (Gen. v. 21, 22, &c.). According to the text of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, Methuselah must have lived 14 years after the deluge; and according to other copies, he died six years before it: but it is generally agreed on, that these copies, as well as the Septuagint, are corrupted in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

METHYMNA

Pages 793-793

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the island in greatness, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and opulence. Its territory was fruitful, and the wines it produced excellent. It was the native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, and of Arion the musician. When the whole island of Lesbos revolted from the power of the Athenians, Methymna alone remained firm to its ancient allies.

METOEICI

Pages 793-793

a name given by the Athenians to such as had their fixed habitations in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, though foreigners by birth. The metoeici were admitted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a>, and entered in the public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>. They differed both from the πολίται and ξένοι; because the πολίται <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "citizens" were freemen of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and the ξένοι or "strangers" had lodgings only for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; whereas the metoeici though not freemen of Athens, constantly resided upon the spot whether they had removed.

METONYMY

Pages 793-793

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, is a trope in which one name is put for another, on account of the near relation there is between them. See ORATORY, No. 51.

METOPE

Pages 793-793

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> space between the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGLYPHS">triglyphs</a> of the Doric frieze, which among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used to be painted or adorned with carved <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, representing the heads of oxen or utensils used in sacrifices.

METOPOSCOPY

Pages 793-793

the pretended art of knowing a person's dispositions and manners by viewing the traces and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Ciro Spontoni, who has written expressly on metoposcopy, says, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> lines are examined in the forehead, and that each line is considered as having its particular planet: the first is the line of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the third of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, &c. Metoposcopy is only a branch of physiognomy, which founds its conjectures on all the parts of the body.

METRE

Pages 793-793

μέτρον, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a system of feet of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> length. The different metres in poetry, are the different manners of ordering and combining the quantities, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short syllables; thus hexameter, pentameter, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBIC">iambic</a>, sapphic verses, consist of different metres or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. See HEXAMETER. In English verses, the metres are extremely various and arbitrary, every poet being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to introduce any new form that he pleases. The most usual are the heroic, generally consisting of five long and five short syllables, and verses of four feet, and of three feet, and a caesura or single <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, by variously combining and transposing their quantities, made a vast variety of different measures.

METRICAL VERSES

Pages 794-794

are those consisting of a determinate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short syllables; as those of the Greek and Latin poets.—Capellus observes, that the genius of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is incompatible with metrical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>.

METROCOMIA

Pages 794-794

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, signifying "a borough <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> village that had other villages under its jurisdiction."—What a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> was among cities, a metrocomia was among <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The ancient metrocomiae had each its choripiscopos or rural <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, and here was his see or residence. See METROPOLIS and CHORIEPISCOPUS.

METRONOMII

Pages 794-794

the name given by the Athenians to five officers in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and ten in the Piraeus, whose duty it was to inspect all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> except those of corn. The Piraeus was the greatest mart in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>.

METROPOLIS

Pages 794-794

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Arcania, a little to the south of Stratos.—Another, of Lydia; situated between Colophon and Priene, near the Cayster.—A third, of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>; sacred to the mother of the gods, who was here worshipped.—A fourth Metropolis of Epirotis, a district in Thessaly, to the east of Comphi, and the last town of that district. Metroplites, the people.

METULUM

Pages 794-794

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBURNIA">Liburnia</a>, at the siege of which Octavius Cesar was wounded. Said to be the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, and situated on two eminences, intersected by a valley (Appian). Now generally thought to be Metting in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. N. Lat. 46. 5.

METZ

Pages 794-794

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and strong town of France, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Messin, with a citadel and a bishop's see, whose bishop used to hold the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is one of the finest in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> called Costin and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the governor are worth seeing. The Jews live in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town by themselves, where they have a synagogue. The sweetmeats they make here are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Moselle and Seille. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 16. N. Lat. 49. 7.

MEURSIUS

Pages 794-795

JOHN, a learned and laborious writer, was born at Losdam, near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, in 1579. He early discovered a fondness for polite literature and the sciences; and went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> at Orkans with the son of Barneveldt, whom he accompanied in his travels. In 1610 he was made professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and afterwards Greek professor. In the following year, the magistrates of the United Provinces proved how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was of his abilities, by fixing on him to write the history of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Meursius married in the year 1612. His wife, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> Catharina Bilberbeccia, descended from a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family in Angermund a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Pomerania, possessed many amiable qualities, and rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> remarkably happy, while he discharged the duties of his professorship with an assiduity equal to his abilities. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the republic of letters did not lose the advantages to be derived from his labours; for during the fourteen years of his residence at Leyden, the works which he published were more numerous than those which had been presented to the world by the whole body of professors from the original foundation of the university in 1575. Meursius's writings had now spread his reputation in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; nor was the fame of his diligence and talents as a professor less known. In so high a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, indeed, did he stand among his literary contemporaries, that Christian IV. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of historiographer <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and invited him to undertake the professorship of history and politics in the academy of Sora, which was founded by King Frederick II., although the revival of its honours and dignities may be dated from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, when it seemed to be again founded under the auspices of Christian IV. Meursius and his family left Leyden in the year 1635. On his arrival at Sora, he was received with the most friendly tokens of regard by his majesty and the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and more particularly by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> Rosenkrantz, on whom he has bestowed very ample praises in one of his letters. Here he resided, equally beloved and admired, for above twelve years. His pupils were not very numerous, but his exertions never relaxed. Those hours likewise which were not devoted to the duties of his professorship, he employed in revising the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> and in philological disquisitions. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> did not suffer by the intenseness of application, till in the year 1638 he had a violent attack of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, from which disorder he had suffered severely. In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Vossius he thus describes his melancholy condition: "The state of my health during the whole of the last winter has been truly deplorable. My sufferings from the stone have been really dreadful. I have voided so many, that the repeated discharges brought on a wound which emit- ted blood for above four months. I was next attacked by a tertian fever, which increased constantly, and produced an universal lassitude of body, a dejection of spirits, and a total loss of appetite. But, thank heaven, I have now in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> recovered my strength, and gotten the better of these complaints." He recovered from this attack; but in the following year the disorder returned with redoubled violence, and brought on a consumption, which terminated his existence on the 29th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of September 1639. He left behind him a son who was named after him, and one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. So mild were the dispositions of Meursius, that in all his writings he constantly avoided literary disputes. He was sometimes unavoidably drawn into them; but constantly endeavoured to promote a reconciliation rather than widen any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>, by his replies to the attacks of his adversaries. In his friendships he was firm and affectionate. Of his domestic life, whatever is known has been gathered from his letters. The same easy tranquillity seems to have attended him in every situation. In his family he was particularly fortunate. In his son, to whom he gave his own name, he seemed to behold his own youth renewed. The same application, the same eagerness in the pursuit of knowledge, marked the conduct of this promising young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; who did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> survive his father, but died soon after he had recommended himself to the notice of the learned world by his publications. They were only three in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; but displayed so much <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> learning that they have been assigned to the father, John Meursius, by l'Abbé Beughem and others. This mistake was occasioned as much by the similitude of their names, as by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their works, and their manner of treating philological subjects. His works may be divided into four classes, of which each might form a separate volume <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were ever to be republished. Meursius himself indeed, in one of his letters to Vossius, proposes such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. From that epistle, and from another which the younger Meursius sent to G. I. Vossius, who strongly advised him to republish the whole of his father's writings, and from the collections of his posthumous works which have appeared from Struvius, Grosschupius, Moller, and some others, a catalogue of his works might be formed. Some assistance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> also be derived from the indexes published in their respective works, by Hankins, Desselius, Wettenius, and Bartholinus. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which Meursius recommends for publishing his works, is to insert in the first volume all that he has written relative to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, his historical pieces; in the third his miscellaneous dissertations; and in the fourth, the various authors which he published, with his notes and corrections. A scandalous and indecent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is entitled *Meursii elegantiæ Latini sermonis*, and has *Aloisia Siggeae Satyrae Sotadicæ* annexed to it, is very falsely attributed to Meursius; nor indeed are the *Satires* with more reason assigned to Aloisia Siggea, who was a Spanish lady eminent for her piety and virtue. The real author of these infamous productions was Westerius, an advocate at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, who probably assumed the name of Meursius, in order to shield himself from the disgrace which would naturally have attended the writer of such a performance.

MEVANIA

Pages 794-794

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Cispennine Umbria; seated at the confluence of the Tina and Clitumnus, on the Via Flaminia, famous for its herds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cattle brought up there for sacrifice; the white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> said to be owing to the waters of the Clitumnus (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). Mevania was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Propertius. Mevenates the people. Now said to be Bevagna, in the territory of the Pope.

MEWING

Pages 795-799

the falling off <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> change of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, feathers, skin, horns, or other parts of animals, which happens in some annually, in others only at certain stages of their lives; but the generality of beasts mew in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. An old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HART">hart</a> casts his horns sooner than a young one, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in the months of February and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>: after which they begin to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> in March or April: and as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> grows strong, and the season of the year puts forth the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, so their heads grow, and are summed full by the middle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. It is to be observed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a hart be gelt before he has a head, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> never have any; and if he be gelt after he has a head, he will never <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his horns; again, if he be gelt when he has a velvet head, it will always be so, without fraying or burnishing. --- **<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">MEXICO</a>,** A <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">Province</a> of the Spanish empire in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, once a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, the most powerful and civilized in the new world; lying between the 14th and 21st degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between 91 and 103 degrees west <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; being near 2000 miles in length, and in some places 600 miles in breadth. The Toltecan are the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Mexican <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of which we know anything. They were expelled, as we are told, from their own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> (supposed by Clavigero to have been Tollan, to the northward of Mexico) in the year 472; and for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> led a wandering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In whatever <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they determined to reside for any considerable time, they erected houses and cultivated the ground. Thus their migrations were extremely slow, and it was not till 104 years after they set out that they reached a place about 50 miles to the eastward of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mexico, where they settled for 20 years, giving to their new place of residence the name of Tollantzinco. From thence they proceeded about 40 miles farther to the west, where they built a city called, from the name of their country, Tollan, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TULA">Tula</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> settlement of the Toltecans, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was changed into a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. Their first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> began his reign in 667, and their monarchy lasted 384 years, during which time they reckon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> eight princes. We are not, however, to imagine that each of their kings lived <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to make up this space.
