The good effects of this, he tells us, have often astonished him: and when given early in the disease, he says he can depend as much upon it for the cure of an haemoptysis, as on cinchona for the cure of an intermittent. He agrees with Dr Cullen, however, that in those cases where there is any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and which almost always happens, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for venesection. A cool regimen, and quiet of body and mind, are certainly useful; but Dr Cullen observes that some kinds of gestation, such as sailing, and travelling in an easy carriage on smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, have often proved a remedy. When the cough is very troublesome, it is absolutely necessary to exhibit frequently a small dose of an opiate. Dr Dickson also informs us, that the nitre joined with spermaceti, or pulv. tragacanth. comp., has produced equally good effects with the electuary above mentioned; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of which he at first considered the conserve only as a vehicle for the nitre, though he means not to insinuate that the former is totally destitute of efficacy. When this haemorrhage has resisted other modes of cure, and there is reason to apprehend, even from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> quantity of blood evacuated, that the patient may sink under the discharge, blisters, particularly when applied to the breast, are often had recourse to with great advantage; and the sulphuric acid, properly diluted,

STOMACE

Pages 409-409

Sauv. gen. 241. Lin. 175. Vog. 85. Sag. gen. 177.** <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">Species</a>: Scorbutica, Purulenta, &c.

SUPPRESSION OF URINE

Pages 496-498

Ischuria, Sauv. gen. 293. Lin. 167. Vog. 129. Sag. 212. Home's Clinical Experiments, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. xv. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is distinguished into various <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, according as the seat of it is in the kidneys, the ureters, the bladder, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>; and hence these species are named renalis, ureterica, vesicalis, and urethralis. 1. Ischuria renalis, or a suppression of urine from an affection of the kidneys, happens but rarely; however, Dr Home in his Clinical Experiments describes such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. In the end of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1774, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a full <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, aged 35, was seized with shivering, coldness, and severe cough. Three days after, his urine appeared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-coloured, was passed with pain, and in small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. About the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1775, he was attacked with violent pains in the small of his back, over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, and in the ankles, with pain in the region of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> when pressed. A general swelling was afterwards observed all over the body, but chiefly in the ankles and abdomen, which last was tense and hard. These were attended with vomiting, bad appetite, and considerable thirst. When he entered the clinical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> (January 21st), the cough, sickness, and vomiting, had gone off, but the suppression of urine remained. The little which he made was passed with his stools, so that Dr Home <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it but once; and then it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> powder at bottom. The pains and swellings which retained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of the finger, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>; he had a headache, and a very slow <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> only 48 strokes in a minute. He had taken a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many diuretic medicines before his admission. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after his reception, he was seized with a spontaneous diarrhoea, which continued during the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Crystals of tartar were exhibited in doses of half an ounce each morning; at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he took 20 drops of tincture of opium with a scruple of nitre, and continued this course for eight days without any increase of urine. The stronger and heating diuretics were then tried, as an infusion of juniper berries and pills of garlic; but they were attended with no manifest advantage. Whenever the pulse became so strong that he could bear bleeding, eight ounces of blood were taken away, which was sify. This was thrice repeated; he appeared easier after each bleeding, his pulse bore it well, and the swellings and other symptoms abated. The heating diuretics, in this state, were given up, and a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> and nitre was substituted in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in each dose of which, taken every two hours, there was a scruple of nitre. Fermentations were applied to the region of the kidneys, and camphorated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> was afterwards rubbed on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. He was ordered the semicinium, which, from a deficiency of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at that time, he got only once; and which then seemed to have a good effect, as he passed a gill of urine when he was in it. Notwithstanding this, however, the disease continually gained ground; he became comatose, delirious, and died ten days after his admission. On dissection, the kidneys were found of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> form; some watery vesicles appeared on their surface, containing <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> gritty particles like fine sand; and the lower part of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> kidney was considerably inflamed. The pylorus, part of the duodenum, and a considerable part of the small intestines, were much inflamed. In the abdomen were found about five pounds of fluid, and in the cavities of the thorax about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. The lungs were a little inflamed, and full of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> on their surface and in their substance; the heart was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and a polypus in each ventricle. About six ounces of fluid were found in the pericardium; in the brain nothing preternatural appeared, except about an ounce of water in each ventricle. Dr Home seems to have been at a loss for the remote cause of this suppression of urine, which manifestly had its immediate origin from the kidneys having lost the power of performing their functions. He thinks the inflammation which appeared in the right kidney was scarce sufficient to have occasioned the distemper, as the other would have supplied its place; for which reason also he thinks that the ischuria was owing to a general affection of the system; and that it was of an arthritic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, the patient having been troubled with complaints of that kind for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time before. 2. The ischuria ureterica is also a rare disease, unless the obstruction proceeds from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or clot of blood stopping up the passage. Gravel or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, indeed, are very frequently formed in the kidneys; and, by falling into the ureters, occasion an ischuria, with violent pain, and symptoms more or less urgent in proportion to the size and shape of the stones. Sometimes it is attended with coldness of the extremities, nausea, vomiting, and spasmodic constriction of the precordia, a difficulty of making water, constipation of the belly, difficulty of breathing, stupor of the thigh, retraction of the testicle, inquietude, loss of strength, syncope, and convulsion fits. When the violent pain has continued for several days and nights without intermission, and has brought the patient exceeding low, and the suppression of urine is complete, with coldness of the extremities and convulsions of the tendons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Nor is it a good sign when the stone continues long in the ureter; for then the appetite decays, a nausea and retching to vomit supervene, and the patient is consumed with a hectic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Sometimes the pain is attended with an inflammation of the stomach and intestines; and sometimes the disease ends in a dropy of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a>, which soon carry off the patient. The indications of cure are, to exclude the stone as easily as possible, and prevent the breeding of others. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the patient be of a sanguineous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>, Sydenham recommends to take away ten ounces of blood from the affected side; and then to give the patient a gallon of posset-drink in which two ounces of marshmallow roots have been boiled, injecting at the same time an emollient glyster. After the posset drink has been vomited up, and the clyster returned, give a pretty large dose of an opiate. But if the patient be old or weak, or subject to nervous affections, bleeding may be omitted, especially if his urine at the beginning of the fit be coffee-coloured, and mixed with gravel; but as to the other things, the cure is the same. Huxham highly recommends an emollient bath prepared of a decoction of marshmallow root, lintseed, fenugreek seed, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of chamomile, to which may be added a few white poppy seeds. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this bath he says he has seen the most cruel fit of the gravel suddenly ended, when neither copious bleeding nor opiates had the least effect. Mild diuretics are also of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Hoffman recommends dulcified spirit of nitre as proper to relax the spastic stricture. It is to be taken with suitable distilled waters and syrup of poppies; or in broth, with a few spoonfuls of oil of sweet almonds. Turpentine glysters are also accounted very serviceable; and may be prepared with ten ounces of a decoction of chamomile, with half an ounce of turpentine dissolved in the yolk of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and about as much <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. The sal diureticus, or acetic potassae, is much esteemed by some, when taken along with an opiate. But when the stone is too big to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, Arbuthnot recommends a cool and diluent diet to hinder the further growth of it. Whey, infusion of lintseed, decoction of marshmallows, and gently resolving diuretics, are also proper. To put a stop to the vomiting, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> tincture of benzoin, formerly named balsamum traumaticum, has sometimes been used with success, when almost every other means have failed. 3. The ischuria vesicalis may arise from a stone in the bladder; and this indeed is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cause of it; but there are certain <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, in which, though the usual quantity of urine, or perhaps more, be passed, the patient dies from the retention of a still greater quantity in the bladder. Of this Dr Hume gives the following instances. A man of 58 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, of a strong spare habit, and never subject to the gravel, had, during the winter of 1777, a cough with expectoration, which went off in the beginning of 1778. About the 17th of February 1778 he felt some difficulty in passing his urine, and much pain about the region of the bladder. He continued in this way for ten days, after which he became easier on application of some medicines. The abdomen then swelled, and he had pains in his loins and thighs. On the 3d of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> he was admitted into the clinical ward; his abdomen was then swelled and tense; and an evident fluctuation was felt, which some that touched him thought was somorous and produced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. A tumor was discovered between the navel and spine of the os ilium on the left side, which gave him much pain, especially when pressed. This tumor became more easily felt after the swelling of the abdomen decreased, seemed round, and very near as large as the head of a child. It appeared very much on the left side, even when the patient lay on the right, and it then became dependent. He passed urine frequently, and rather more than in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, as it was computed at four pints a day. It was always clear, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. His body had a strong disagreeable smell; his skin was dry, belly bound, and his appetite entirely gone, so that he had hardly taken any food for 12 days. His legs swelled slightly for some days in the evening. His pulse was generally regular, sometimes slower than <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and sometimes a little quicker; being once felt at 64, and another time at 92. He was often seized, especially after eating or drinking, with hiccough; which increased and lasted till his death. On the 22th day of his disease, after some doses of squills, the general swelling of his abdomen fell, became much softer, and more distinctly discovered the swelling of the left side. The next day a vomiting came on; he became delirious, and died the day following. The body being opened, it appeared that the tumor which was so distinctly felt on the left side of the abdomen, was owing to a distention of the bladder with urine. Its fundus reached to about the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the norta into the Epispistes, the iliacs; it entirely filled the pelvis, and contained between five and six pounds of urine of a pale colour. On examining the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> surface, its neck, and the beginning of the urethra, were found to be surrounded with a scirrhus, which impeded the evacuation of the urine. The bladder itself was much thickened, but not more in one part than another. The ureters entered naturally; but were much thickened in their upper half near the kidney. The kidneys were somewhat enlarged; particularly the left, which had several watery vesicles on its external surface. These organs were not in their usual situation; but lay <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> on each side of the spine, and very near the aorta; so that the renal vessels were very short. What was very singular, the lower end of each arose over the spine, and they were united together by their membranes, the aorta passing beneath the union. The bladder had pressed considerably on this part; and the peritoneum covering them was considerably thicker than natural. The lungs adhered everywhere to the pleura, and in some places very firmly; they were of a loose texture and black colour; and the veins of the lower extremities were turgid with blood. It does not appear that this patient got any medicines farther than a few dried squills, which diminished the swellings and brought off much wind. He also got a mixture of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, and afterwards of opium, for his hiccup; but without success. His disease was mistaken for an ascites; and the catheter was not tried; but in another case the use of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> was apparently of more service than any internal medicines. This last patient was about 90 years of age, and laboured under symptoms very similar to those already mentioned. When admitted into the clinical ward, he had the hypogastric region swollen, and difficulty of passing his water; but without pain, vomiting, or hiccup. He had lost all appetite; was thirsty, and constive. His pulse was 110, and weak. In the evening about three English pints of pale clear urine were drawn off by means of the catheter: the next day all the symptoms were gone off or abated. After this he continued to pass some urine, sometimes voluntarily, sometimes involuntarily and insensibly; but so much always remained behind, that his bladder was constantly full, unless when the urine was drawn off, which was done twice every day. The urine was sometimes pale, sometimes of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour; and once there was some blood mixed with it, which perhaps might have been occasioned by the catheter. About the sixth day the urine was very putrid, with much purulent like <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> at the bottom, and was passed with more pain. About the 11th, the putrid smell went off. The next day all the urine passed insensibly except what was drawn off; and an hiccup, though not very severe, had come on. In this way he continued without fever, though frequently troubled with the hiccup, especially during those nights in which the urine had not been drawn off. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after admission, the bladder, with the assistance of the catheter, was almost entirely, though insensibly evacuated, and the hiccup had left him; he had no other complaint but that of voiding his urine insensibly, the natural effect of a scirrhus bladder, and which was probably incurable. With this patient the hot bath and mercurials were tried, in order to soften the scirrhus of the bladder, but without effect. 4. The ischuria urethralis arises from some tumor obstructing the passage of the urethra, and thus hindering the flow of the urine. It is no uncommon distemper, and often follows a gonorrhoea. Dr Home gives us an example of this also.—The patient was a man of 60 years of age, who had laboured under a gonorrhoea six months before, and which was stopped by some medicines in two or three days. He felt soon afterwards, a difficulty in passing his urine, which gradually increased. About 10 days before his admission into the clinical ward, it was attended with pains in the glans, and ardor urinis; he had passed only about eight ounces the day before his admission, and that with very great difficulty; and the hypogastric region was swollen and pained. On introducing the catheter, three pounds of urine were drawn off, by which the pain and swelling were removed. The instrument required force to make it pass the neck of the bladder, and blood followed the operation: and the finger, introduced into the anus, felt a hard tumor about its neck. He was treated with mercurial pills and ointment, by which the swelling about the neck of the bladder soon began to decrease; but at the same time a swelling of the right testicle appeared. He was vomited with four grams of turbithe-mineral, the subulphas hydrargyri flavus of the present pharmacopoeia, which operated gently; and here Dr Home observes, that though these vomits are little used, from a mistaken notion of their severity, he never saw them operate with more violence than other vomits, or than he could have wished. The swelling diminished in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the emetic and some external applications; and the cure was completed by bleeding and a decoction of mezereon root. GENUS CXXIV. DYSURIA.

WHETHER THERE BE ANY OTHER

Pages 365-366

r there be any other means of radically curing the gout, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> is not able to say. There are histories of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of the gout, in which it is said, that by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> emotions of mind, by wounds, and by other accidents, the symptoms have been suddenly relieved, and never again returned; but how far these accidental cures might be imitated by art, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> would succeed in other cases, is at least extremely uncertain. The practices proper and necessary in the treatment of the gout, are to be considered under two heads: First, As they are to be employed in the intervals of paroxysms; or, secondly, As during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of these. In the intervals of paroxysms, the indications are, to prevent altogether the return of paroxysms; or at least to render them less frequent and more moderate. During the time of paroxysms, the indications are, to moderate the violence and shorten the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of them as much as can be done with safety. It has been already observed, that the gout may be entirely prevented by constant bodily <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and by a low diet; and Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a> is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that this prevention may take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> even in persons who have a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> disposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Even when the disposition has discovered itself by several paroxysms of inflammatory gout, he is persuaded that labour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> absolutely prevent any returns of it for the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. These, therefore, are the means of answering the first indication to be pursued in the intervals of paroxysms. Exercise in persons exposed to the gout, in Dr Cullen's opinion, operates by answering two purposes: One of these is the strengthening of the tone of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> vessels; and the other, the guarding against a plethoric state. For the former, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> exercise be employed early in life, and before intemperance has weakened the body, a very moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of it will answer the purpose; and, for the latter, if abstinence be at the same time observed, less exercise will be necessary. With respect to exercise, this in general is to be observed, that it should never be violent; for if violent, it cannot be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, and must always endanger the bringing on an atony in proportion to the violence of the preceding motions. It is also to be observed, that the exercise of gestation, though considerable and constant, will not, if it be entirely without bodily exercise, answer the purpose of preventing the gout. For this end, therefore, the exercise must be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> that of the body; and must be moderate, but at the same time constant and continued through life. In every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> and circumstance of the gout in which the patient retains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, bodily exercise, in the intervals of paroxysms, will be always useful; and in the beginning of the disease, when the disposition to it is not yet strong, exercise may prevent a paroxysm which otherwise would have come on. In more advanced states of the disease, however, when there is some disposition to a paroxysm, much walking will bring it on; either as it weakens the tone of the lower extremities, or as it excites an inflammatory disposition in them; and thus it seems to be that sprains or contusions often bring on a paroxysm of the gout. Abstinence, the other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the regimen for preventing the gout, is of more difficult application. If an abstinence from animal food be entered upon early in life, while the vigour of the system is yet entire, Dr Cullen has no doubt of its being both safe and effectual; but if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> for this diet shall not have occurred till the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> has been broken by intemperance, or by the decline of life, a low diet may then endanger the induction of an atonic state. Further, If a low diet be entered upon only in the decline of life, and be at the same time a very great change from the former manner of living, the withdrawing of an accustomed stimulus of the system may readily throw it into an atonic state. The safety of an abstemious course will be greater or less according to the management of it. Animal food especially disposes to the plethoric and inflammatory state, and that food is to be therefore especially avoided; but on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, vegetable aliment of the lowest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is in danger of weakening the system too much by not affording sufficient nourishment, and more particularly of weakening the tone of the stomach by its acescence. It is therefore a diet of a middle <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> that is to be chosen; and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> is precisely of this kind, as containing both animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. As approaching to the nature of milk, and as being a vegetable matter containing the greatest portion of nourishment, the farinaceous seeds are next to be chosen, and are the food most proper to be joined with milk. With respect to drink, fermented liquors are useful only when they are joined with animal food, and that by their acescence; and their stimulus is only necessary from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. When, therefore, animal food is to be avoided, fermented liquors are unnecessary; and by increasing the acescence of vegetables, these liquors may be hurtful. The stimulus of fermented or spirituous liquors is not necessary to the young and vigorous, and when much employed impairs the tone of the system. These liquors, therefore, are to be avoided, excepting as custom and the declining state of the system may have rendered them necessary. For preventing or moderating the regular gout, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is the only proper drink. With respect to an abstemious course, it has been supposed, that an abstinence from animal food and fermented liquors, or the living upon milk and farinacea alone for the space of one year, might be sufficient for a radical cure of the gout: and it is possible that, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of life, in certain circumstances of the constitution, such a measure might answer the purpose. But this is very doubtful: and it is more probable, that the abstinence must, in a great measure, be continued, and the milk diet be persisted in, for the remainder of life. It is well known, that several persons who had entered on an abstemious course, and had been thereby delivered from the gout, have, however, upon returning to their former manner of full living, had the disease return upon them with as much violence. violence as before, or in a more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and more dangerous form. It has been alleged, that, for preventing the return of the gout, blood-letting or scarifications of the feet, frequently repeated, and at stated times, may be practised with advantage; but of this Dr Cullen tells us he has had no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; and the benefit of the practice is not, as far as we know, confirmed by the observation of any other practitioner.
